THE DAISY QUEEN. Merrily, merrily, here they go, Five little children all in a row. What are they doing? what do they mean Crowning the middle one Daisy Queen. Five little faces beaming and bright, Happy as long a 3 the day is light; Quick little feet fast hurrying on, Sweat little voices singing a song. What is the song? and what do they mean? Crowning the middle one Daisy Queen. I'll tell you then what I heard them say, As they passed me by, laughing and gay; 'Twas somebody's birthday, so they said, A daisy crown she should wear on her head. Queen of the fields and flowers was she, Whatever she willed or wished should be. All must be merry, good-tempered, and glad, Nothing, if possible, make their Queen sad. Merrily, merrily, on they went, Singing aloud in their heart's content. Far, far away, they may still be seen, Loving and crowning their Daisy Queen. Little Folks" Magazine for April.

TOOTHSOME ADVICE. The following verses, by Mr. Edwin Waugh, have been w-ritten at the spesial request of the Ladies Committee of the Manchester Domestic DWI:10111y Classes, to whom the copyright belongs. We are permitted to reproduce them in our columns:— " Eh, Nanny; thoe'rt o' out o' gear; Do, pray tho, go peep into th' glass; Thou looks dirty, an' dt:awly, an' queer; Whatever's to do witho, lass ?" "Bless yo, Mary; if folk Tiobbat knew The trouble I have wi' y on lad!— He's at th' alehouse again, th' owd crew; It's enough to drive ouy mon mad! '' Eh, my wench; I'm mich owder than An' it grieves me to see tho like this; So pray tho, now, hearkei, to me; An' don't go an' tak it amiss: Thou once war nice-lookin, an' mild, An' tidily donned, too, as well; But, now, thou'rt quite sluttish an' wild About both thi house an' thiser. "It's hard to keep things reet with aught That a body can manage to do , Bat a mon's sure to stray when he's nought Bat dirt an' feaw looks to come to: If thou wants to keep Jamie i'th house, Thou mun bait th' trap with comfort, my lass; Or, there's lots o' nooks, canty an' crouse, Where he'll creep with his pipe an' his glass. "Thou mun keep his whcarn pleasant and sweet; An' everything fit to be seen Thou man keep his hearth cheerful an' bract; Thou mun keep thisel' tidy an' clean ; good-temper't wife trill entice To a fireside that's cosy an' trim; Men liken to see their wives nice; An' I'm sure that it's so wi' yor "Thou man have his meals cooked to his mind, At th' rest time, an' daicently laid; Tak pains; an' thou'll very soon find Row nice a plain dish can be made: Goad cookie' keeps likin' alive, With a woman that's nooan short o' ; An' there's never a craiter i'th hive But's fond of a toothsome tit bit!" "Eh, Mary! I'm nought of a cook, But just rough and ready, yo' known; As for roasting and boiling, bi th' book, I'm o' little more use than a atone!" "Don thi bonnet, and his tho me, I'll soon put tho rest if el:it'll come; An' I'll lam tho some cookin', thou'll see, That'll help to keep Jamie at whoam!" March, MM.

You just take a bottle of my medicine," said a quack doctor to a consumptive, "and you'll never cough again." "Is it as fatal as that ?" gasped the consumptive. If there is one time more than another when a woulan shoold be left entirely alone, it is when a hankie of clothes, which the has just washed and hung out to dry, comes down in the mad. Mr. X.'s eon (just returned from abroad, to new Irish butler, engaged during his absence): "Do you belong here?" Butler: " Bedad, sir, I do ; an' if I didn't belong here, sure I wouldn't be long here." . ANECDOTE OF GENERAL Wassitroroia.—Renben Rouzy, of Virginia, was indebted to General Washington about one thousand pounds. While he was President of the Milted States, one of his agents brought an action for the mousy,' judgment was obtained, and execution issued against the body of the defendant, who was taken to gaol. He had a considerable landed estate, but this kind of property cannot be sold in Virginia for debts, unless at the discretion of the proprietor. He had a large family, and for the sake of his children preferred lying in gaol to selling his land. A friend hinted to him that perhaps General Washington did not know anything of the proceeding, and that it might be well to send him a peLition, with a statement of his circum- stances. He did sa, and the very next post from 'Philadel- phia (after the arrival of his petition !meat city) brought him an order for his immediate release, together with a full discharge, and 3. severe reprimand to the agent for having acted in such a manner. Poor Rouzy was in consequence restored to his family, who never laid down their heads at night without presenting prayers to heaven for their "be- loved Washington." Providence smiled upon the labours of the grateful family, and in a few years Rouzy enjoyed the exquisite pleasure of being able to lay the one thousand pounds, with the interest, at the feet of this truly great man. Washington reminded him that the debt was die- sharged. Rouzy replied, the debt of his family to the father of their country, and preserver of their parent, could never be discharged; and the General, to avoid the pleasing importunity of the grateful Virginian, who would not be denied, accepted the money, only, however, to divide it among Rouzy's children, which he did immediately. COLD AND HEAT NEAR THE Pots.—We are accustomed to associate this geographical position with extreme cold. But the rocks of Greenland tell us that, although this is the case now, it was not the case in some former ages, and con- sequently that there is no necessary connection between an extremely low temperature and a position near the Pole. They tell us, in short, that this association is purely tem- porary and accidental. It is striking and curious enough to fual, in the bleak headlands ef the Isle of Mull, on our own coasts, the leaves of an abundant forest vegetation—the large leaves of the plane-tree, the ever-green needles of the taxodiurn, of the yew, and of the pine, and mixed with these the frond-like leaves of the tree called by botanists " Sans- buria," which is now an inhabitant of Japan. But the curi- osity of this contraet between the present and the past, as regards climatal cOntitions, is pothing to the still greater contrast in this matter which is presented by finding the lame fossil flora in the reeks of Greenland—rocks whose sur- faces are now almost wholly bare of vegetation, and all the higher elevations of which are covered with eternal ice and snow. And yet even this contrast is not the contrast high- est in degree which the rocks of Greenland present. The Miocene Flora, to which those leaf beds belong, is a very old flora now, but there was another flora much older,which we have never seen in life, and which, from its nearest liv- ing analogies, we are accustomed to think must have been associated with almost a tepid and steamy atmosphere. This is the flora of the coal. measures. Yet this flora, too, inlong ages before the Miocene, b,. certainly flourished on the area which is now occupied by Greenland. It is needless to point out what curious questions these facts raise.—The Duke of Argyll, in" Good Words" for April. TARTAR HORNES.—In ordinary times they "made great raids on their own account into Poland, or campaigned against the Cossacks, who were kept up by the Russians as a check upon them. Being often pursued and hard pushed , on these occasions, their animals were obliged to be "fit." The training the beet of them underwent as a preparation for the business was something appalling, and to anyone unacquainted with the strength of constitution and iron hardness of the Tartar ponies would be completely in- credible. Their method of training a horse, or rather the ordeal they made him pase through before he was considered suitable for the "war-path"—which they admit used to kill _two out of five who underwent it, and was, of course, only compatible with the possession of an unlimited number of animals coating nothing or next to nothing to keep, being grazed on the steppe all the summer, and half starved On. a little dry fodder during the winter—was in this wise : " After picking out a likely one, rising seven or eight— before which age no horse was allowed to be selected for raiding --- they loaded him on a saddle with a sack of earth or sand, at first only the weight the rider, but gradually increased for eight days, till the horse carried 20 stbne or 22 stone. As the weight was increased, the horse's ration of fond and water He was trotted and walked six or seven miles daily. After the first eight days they gradually, for other tight days, decreased the load, still, however, decreasing the feed until the sack was empty; finally giving him for two Or three days absolutely nothing at all, but merely tighten- ing up the girths at intervals. About the 19thdaythey worked him hard until he sweated, when they unsaddled him, and poured buckets of ice-cold water over the anima Irons head to tail. He wig then picketed, all wet, to a peg on the open steppe, allowed to graze, or fed sparingly, giving lu—oi every day a little more feed and more rone for seven or eight days more, after which he was turned loose to run with the herd as usual. A horse that had undergone this discipline WAS considered a valuable animal, and a sort of fortune to a man, being able to travel almost continuously for four or five days together, with only a handful of fodder once in eight or ten hours and a drink of water once in the 21. This training was, oicourse, a sort of epitome of what the animals often had to go through on an actual foray, whott-thOy had frequeney to swim semi-frozen rivers, to 'Wry great weights, to go for days almost without food, to be paluketed on the steppes, perhaps sweating from a long jot:mile*, In snow and sleet, without any cor,ring„" &T,C.— " The Book of the Horse," for April, 'The niedinal pr •,t,ssion are now ordering Cadbury's COOO7 Etssence in thousamis of cases, heeause it contains more nutri- tious and flado-f,rming elemen-s than any other beverage, Inc Is preferabte to the thick starchy cocoa ordinarily sold. div.head: INTERESTING PRESENTATION.
div.p: INTERESTING PRESENTATION.

A. very interesting ceremony took place on Monday even- ing at the Bank Quay Mission School-room, Liverpool-road, Warrington, when a presentation was made to Mr. and Mrs. Long, by the employes of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, soap manufacturers, in whose service Mr. Long has been for a period of 55 years. Mr. Long is retiring from work in con- sequence of failing health, and his fellow-workmen determined on the presentation as a means of evincing the respect and esteem in which he is held by them. The gift took the place of a handsome silver coffee service and castor, which were supplied by Mr. Robinson, of Warring- ton, and purchased by subscriptions from the workmen.

Mr. WILLIAM Hi:As-r occupied the chair, ..a-p,;siiion, he said, which he was glad to hold, in order to give honour where honour was due—to an old servant who had worked with them so long a time. He was sway that through a misunderstanding as to the arrangements there were not as many of their friends present as could have been wished, but under the circumstances they must make the best of it. They would excuse him making a speech, and he would simply call on the choir to proceed with the programme. Several musical selections having been given, Mr. JOHN WILLETT made the presentation. Perhaps in the first place, he said, he had better explain that there bad been some slivht misunderstanding as to the meeting, for which, he believed, he was to blame, and he was extremely sorry. He felt himself in a very humble position in being asked to pre- sent the testimonial to their esteemed friends Mr. and Mrs. Long. When the committee asked him to present it he said that he bad rather that someone who was older than him wdtald undertake the duty, but they would have no nay, and so he would endeavour to do the best he could. Mr. Long was now retiring from business. He had been connected with Bank Quay Soap Works for some- thing like 55 years, which was a long time for a man to work in one place. On Mr. Long retiring through ill health they thought it advisable to make some kind of a presenta- tation to him, and what was decided upon was what they saw on the table before him. It was not perhaps as good as they should have liked it, but they had done their best. (Applause.) They were only giving honour where it was due, and there were many in the room who would bear him out in saying that many of them had had Mr. Long's counsel and advice on many occasions, and not only had they had that, but whenever it had been required his purse had been open to their wants. (Applause.) He then presented the coffee service to Mr. Long, reading the inscription, " Pre- sented to John Long by the employes of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Bank Quty Soap Works, as a token of respect and esteem on his retiring after 55 years' service." (Ap- plause.) Mr. LONG, in reply, expressed his thanks. The testimo- nial would be valued by him as a token of sympathy, even more than he should value it for its intristic worth. It was 55 years since he first came to work with Messrs. Crosfield and since that day to the present, he could say, he had, done his duty. He would have preferred to have seen more of his fellow workmen amongst them, but, of course, mis- takes would occur, and be would ask those who were present to tell those who were not, from him, that he should never forget, as long as he lived, what they had done for him. (Applause) Mr. WILLETT then presented the silver castor to Mrs. ' Long, on behalf of the workmen. He hoped that she and her husband might be long spared to use it and, in fact, that ' they might always have something to use it with. (Ap- plause.) They would all feel glad that Mr. Long was in better health now than he had been, and be hoped that be ' would long be spared to come amongst them, and if they did not see him amongst them at work they would know ' that they had his hearty sympathy and affection. Mrs. LONG, replying, said that this was not the first Oken ' of respect that her husband's fellow-workmen had shown
her. Twelve years ago there were many in that room who contributed to a handsome token of respect to her late hus- band, Dnd she should now like to thank them as she bad

never had the opportunity of thanking them before for what they bad done in the past, and also to thank them for that present token of their esteem. Mr. Middleton, Mr. Knight, Mr. J. Roughlev, and Mr. Monks also spoke of their respect and affection for Mr. Long. The programme of music was then proceeded with, and at the dos,: a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman.

A grave-digger, walking the streets the other day, chanced to turn, and noticed two doctors walking behind him. He stopped till they passed, and then followed on behind them. "And why this?" said they. " I know my place in the pro- cession " returned he. , _ .

Many years since a St. Louis newspaper contained an ad- vertisement of one cent reward for a runaway apprentice to the doctor's trade, copies of which are yet preserved by anti- quarians. The boy for whom that reward was offered has been for many years a prominent banker in the Mississippi Valley, and a millionaire. "I believe I'll go out and stretch my legs a little," said a tall gentleman, as a train stopped at a station. "Oh, don't," said a gentleman passenger who had been sitting opposite to him, and who had been much embarrassed by the legs of the tall gentleman; "don't do that. Don't stretch those legs any more. They are too long already." In 1717 the following singular commitment to the Bastile was made out by order of the Duke of Orleans, Regent during the minority of Louis XV. of France Laurence d' Henry, for disrespect to King George I. in not mentioning him in his almanack as King of Great Britain." How long this unlucky almanack-maker remained in prison is unknown. A very charming foreign actress, who has not been for- tunate in her marriage, was at Washington not long ago, and, meeting an old friend, made sundry inquiries concern- ing the welfare of their common acquaintance. "How ees A?" asked the actress. "A ? Oh, he died about a year ago." "And how see B ?" " B ? Why, didn't you know ? He has been dead these three years." "Has he, eendeed? And that zat good C, how ees he ?" "Poor C! He died last month." " Ah!" said the lady, sadly, " eferybody dies— eferybody dies—except "—with deeper melancholy—" mine huspand '—Harper's Magazine. At a station on the overland route the keeper got rather short of provisions—in fact, had nothing left but a bottle of mustard and some bacon. As the stage stopped there one day to change horses the solitary passenger seated him- self at the table, and the host said, "Shall I help you to a piece of bacon ?" "No, thank von; I never eat bacon," said the traveller. "Well, then," said the station keeper, "help yourself to the mustard !" It is a proverb in newspaper offices that the best sayings of the editors never get into the papers. Scenes like the following, we are told, take place almost daily in the offices of the dullest newspapers. A certain philadelphia paper has a political correspondent stationed at Washington, whose duty it is to send frequent letters. • But the corres- pondent holds also a lucrative post, under the Government, and owing to this, perhaps, is somewhat indolent at times, and neglects to send on his letter', though he never forgets to draw his pay all the same. gust day, towards the end of a silent week, he wired to the editor:—" No time to write letter; send cheque." To which the editor wired back : "No time to write cheque; send letter." It came,

The crash hat of the male is now matched by the "pocket bonnet" of the female, which can be folded up and put away, when necessary, in the pocket. But whoever heard of a case where a woman had any desire to put a new bonnet out of sight? THE BELFRY OF BRUGES.—The great bell-tower compels 'one's attention, and ends by laying so firm a hold on the imagination that at no moment of day or night is one wholly unconscious of its solemn protecting presence. By day and night its chimes float through the air like fairy bells, weird and soft, to warn the listener that time indeed is flying even in this drowsy city. It is the first object that catches his eye as the traveller approaches Bruges. It is the last he loses sight of, with a sigh as for a well-tried friend, when the train steams away again through the flat green country. It has watched for six hundred years over the varying fortunes of its city, and has gained that pre- cious quality which, as Mr. Ruskin says, is the greatest ! glory of a building:—" Its glory is in its age, and in that deep sense of voiceftaness, of stern watching, of mys- terious sympathy, nay, even of approval or condemnation, which we feel in walls that have long been washed by the passing waves of humanity."—Rose Kingsley in "The Eng- lish Illustrated Magazine.

QtrEER RELATIONSHIPS.—A correspondent of the Drawer Is involved 'in domestic perplexities. He writes got acquainted with a young widow, who lived with her step- daughter in the same house. I married the widow; my father fell, shortly after it, in love with the stepdaughter of my wife, and married her. My wife became the mother-in- law and also the daughter-in-law of my own father; my wife's step-daughter is my step-mother, and I am the step- father of my mother-in-law. My step-mother, who is the step-daughter of my wife, has a boy; he is naturally my step-brother, because he is the son of my father and of my step-mother; but because he is the son of my wife's step• daughter so is my wife the grandmother of the little boy, and I am the grandfather of my step-brother. My wife has also a boy; my step-mother is consequently the step-sister of my boy, and is also his grandmother, because he is the ' child of her step-son; and my father is the brother-in-law of my son, because he has got his step-sister for a wife. I am the brother of my own son, who is the son of my step- mother; I am the brother-in-law of my mother, my wife is the aunt of her own son, my son is the grandson of my father, and I am my own grandfather.—llarper's Kagazine. _ . _

_ Tourn DRAWING EXTRAORDINARY.—The fashionable and eccentric physician, Dr. Mousey, who lived in Sir Robt. Walpole's time, took so keen a delight in drawing teeth by this particular process that, in the absence of a patient with a fee for the service, he would sometimes be his own dentist, and operate on himself from a pure love of art. The pro- cess was this. Round the tooth to be drawn the doctor fastened a strong piece of catgut, to the other end of which a bullet was attached. A pistol having been charged with this ballet and a full measure of powder, the operation was performed effectually and speedily. The doctor could rarely prevail on his friends to let him remove their teeth in this singular and startlingly simple manner. Once a gentleman, who had agreed to make trial of the novelty, and had even allowed the apparatus to be adjusted,turned craven at the last moment. "Stop ! stop!" he exclaimed, " I've changed my mind." "But I hav'nt changed mine, and you are a coward for changing yOttrS," answered the doctor, pulling the trigger. Even at this distance of time it would be pleasant to discover that the patient of this comedy was his grace of Grafton, and that, to avenge himself for the loss of a place in the Lord Chamberlain's gift, the operator attached the catgut to the wrong :tooth.—Leisure Hour. MONEY.—When bartering is going on, each sheep must be paid for separately. Thus, suppose two sticks of tobacco to be the rate of exchange for one sheep, it would sorely puzzle a Dammara to take two sheep and give him four sticks. I have done so, and seen a man put two of the sticks apart, and take a sight over them at one of the sheep he was about to sell. Having satisfied himself that one was honestly paid for, and finding to his surprise that exactly two sticks remained in hand to settle the account for the other sheep, he would be afflicted with doubts; the transaction seemed to come out too "pat" to be correct, and he would refer back to the first couple of sticks; and Olen his mind got hazy and confused, and wandered from one sheep to the othef, and he broke off the transaction until two sticks were put into his hand, and one sheep driven away, and then the other two sticks given him, and the second sheep driven away. For another example of the slow progress men make in their methods of transacting business, we do not require to go out of our Own country, nor to refer farther back than our own nineteenth century. It was not until the year 1826 that keeping accounts by" Tallies" was completely abolished in our own country, and from our own public offices. The tally was a willow stick not longer than five feet, about one inch in depth and thickness. On one of the four sides of this stick the amount owed was expressed in notches. On each of the two sides next the notched side the description of the payment was written • the stick was then split in half through the notches, a half being given to each party, and a claim was established by these halves fitting. it is better not to inquire into the sure working of such a sys- tem, for it is apparently very far from perfect; and yet in this present century it was in such a manner that the accounts of the Chancellor of the Exchequer were kept.— "The World of Wonders," for April.

No time should now be lost in setting hens, and as this is the great hatching month, as fast as broody hens and eggs can be got they may be put down, of course allowing for the space at disposal. Individual judgment is required in every case' but we still always feel that by the 15th or 20th of April we should have the major portion of eggs under hens that we wish to hatch in the season. Watering the outside of the nests should never be forgotten, and it will very materially influence the hatching returns.

Two ART OF SELF•CULTURE.—Great men have, com- monly, been workers on one subject. They have been astronomers, geologists, chemists, engineers, mechanicians, historians, painters, poets, but no man has been all these. Each could say, This one thing I do. Each of you should have one thing to do; one subject to which to give your- self. Since lam speaking now, not of your business in life, which is probably already fixed for you, but of the cultiva- tion of your knowledge, and of your taste, and, through them, of your mind, you may, I believe, make free choice of the subject towards which your inclination lies—that which enlists your love—all the better if it be a passionate love. What is your subject, the subject you greatly desire to know? As a first step you must answer this question. You need not answer it aloud, and therefore you need not have the fear of being thought ambitious or presumptions. Whisper the high ambition in your own heart. Better the ambition should be high. Choose no ignoble consort for your study. If you set about acquiring anything, let it be a real treasure, costly, and so worth the having.—The Venerable Archdeacon Gore in "27C Quiver."

A young man asked the lady 1 his affections the other evening how she liked the look of his new style standing collar. After critically surveying him and the collar, she replied, "Very nice, indeed. It looks like, a whitewashed fence round a lunatic asylum." J. R. Randal tells the story of a black soldier who ran away at Murfeaboro battle, and was asked if he thought any- one would have missed him had he been killed? "No," he replied; "they don't miss white men, much less niggers, but I would have missed myself, and that's the pint with me." A young lady who has enjoyed every kind of love gives the following as the result of her experience :—" The sweetest love is a mother's love; the longest, a brother's love; the strongest, a woman's love; the dearest, a man's bye; and the sweetest, longest, strongest, dearest love, is the love of a bonnet.'"
Y, APRIL 12,

_ RANCE MISSION. A musioal temPerince entertainment was given at the Workingmen's Club, Market-place Warrington' on Satur- day evening, by Mr. W. H. Whitehead, of Manchester. There was a good attendance. The Rev. Thomas Rippon presided, and referred to the successful meetings conducted by Mr. John Bennett Anderson, in connection with the Temperance Union. Many pledges had been taken, the enthusiasm was high, and the results were in every sense satisfactory. As their friend Mr. Roberts said the other evening, they meant to work with a will and with patience until the flag of temperance was placed upon the proud sum- ' mit of their endeavour. There was every reason why they should go on working, for strong drink was still asserting itself on every side. He then referred to the case ef an "infant drunkard," reported in the papers as having been admitted into an hospital suffering from delirium tremens, and also to a case heard at the Warrington Police Court, when a man named John Rowan made his 81st appearance. He did not know whether John Rowan was now serving his month, or whether he was in that room, but if he was in that room be (the Chairman)should like to shake hands with him to say as a fellow Englishman that he had a heart full of sympathy for him, and if what he could say would lead him, to sign the pledge again and take the blue, he would do his very best to help him. They should treat the poor drunkard tenderly. He might have been like that poor youngster that they had been reading about, and have been trained to the dank front his birth, so that it might not be his fault that he was what he was. They had just now a great deal of kindness shown to them by temperance reformers, but at the same time they had a great deal of opposition and that from quarters where they expected that help would be given. He was very sorry to read in the columns of the local papers a short time ago that a gentleman spoke, he believed, on that platform, disapprovingly of two things that as temperance reformers they wanted to see brought about Ile alluded to local option and Sunday closing. That gentleman was a clergyman, and speaking on local option he laid it down as a premise that local option interfered with the liberty of the subject, and as regarded Sunday closing he was understood to have said that where it had been tried it had proved a failure. He held in his hand a book entitled "Social Wreckage," by Francis Peak, and in the chapter on the licensing laws and intemperance ' there WAS a sentence that referred to Sunday closing which I would perhaps bring a little light home to his ecclesiastical 1 friend—" The Irish Sunday Closing Act, which came into force in October, 1878, seemed to have had a very beneficial effect, for the Government returns showed that in the ensu- ing six months the arrrests for drunkenness on Sunday throughout Ireland, save in the five excepted towns, were 707 as against 2,364 in the corresponding period of the I previous year." (Applause.) He was not dealing with clap-trap, but with simple facts, anti if his ecclesiastical friend held that Sunday closing was a failure he wished him to correspond with the author of "Social ' Wreckage" and settle the matter with him. It seemed to him that if they had Sunday closing in ' this country the worst class of public-houses would be put a stop to, for many of them were greatly dependent upon Sunday trading. He was pleased to find that at the last meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, the chair- man introduced a resolution bearing upon this subject to strengthen the hands of Mr. Stevenson when he introduced his measure the other night in the HOliSe of Commons, and he was very sorry to see that the resolution was negatived. He Viought that Town Councils and other public bodies would do honour to themselves in supporting such an ob- ject.

GENERAL NEWS.
----------------------------- - Mr. Henry George was entertained at dinner on Satur- day in London, on the eve of his departure for the United States.

The honour of knighthood has been offered to Mr. James allport, a director of the Midland Railway Company, and for many years its successful manager. At Kingstown Police Court, en Monday, Edward Dayitt, labourer, was committed for the murder of Mary Carless, at Blackrock, by striking her on the head with a shovel in a quarrel.

A Danish sailor named Edward Peache, who had been arrested for frequenting the Tyne Dock for an unlawful purpose, hanged himself on Monday in a police cell at South Shields with a leather strap which he wore instead of braces.

The sentence of three months' imprisonment imposed upon a Lancaster cattle dealer and butcher named Fell for having in his possession a quantity of diseased meat alto- gether unfit for human food was on Monday annulled by the Court of Quarter Session at Lancaster on appeal. At a meeting of the Newry Town Commissioners, on Mond ry, the chairman propos.d a vote of condolence with the Duchess of Albany. The Nationalists rose one after another and protested, and, when the motion was carried, expressed their satisfaction that the vote was not unani- mous.

THE MURDER IN LONDON. —On Saturday, the Home Secretary decided to offer £lOO reward, in addition to £lOO offered by the city authorities, for the discovery of the Inc- defer of Perkins near London Bridge. The funeral of the deceased took place at Ilford Cemetery, on Saturday after- noon, in the presence of a large crowd. FIFTEEN MILE SENTENCED TO DEATH. The Supreme Court of Midrid h 45 delivered judgment in the appeal against the sentence of the Xeres Court on 15 members of the Black Hand, found guilty of murder in 1882. The Xeres Court had sentenced seven of the accused to death, and eight to 17 years' penal servitude. The Supreme Court has however, sentenced all 15 to death. RAVAGES OF A MAD DOG.—A valuable pointer dog belonging to Mr. Walter Hewkin, of Saddleworth, attacked with rabies through being bitten by another dog, has cona- mittcd some frightful ravages. It appears to have roamed through the district and attacked every animal with which it came in c mtact. No fewer than 23 dogs, some of them very valuable, and four cats have been destroyed in conse- quence. THE INVINCIBLE PLOT. An official and categorical denial is given to the published statem, Ws regarding a "plot" to rescue the Inyincibles incarcerated in Mountjoy Prison, Dublin. The story seems to have been worked out from an accidental discovery that messages from one of the convicts had been clandestinely conveyed to friends outside, and that measures of ,greater watchfulness were then adopted by the authorities.

FRIGHTFUL ACCIDENT—An inquest was held at Hanley, on Monday mornint, on the body of a youth named John Chadwick, aged 16, who met with his death at Berry Hill Ironworks on Saturday. Whilst larking near the rolls in the forge the revolving machinery caught his scarf, and dragged him through head first, the mangled body going completely round the rolls three times. The remains were afterwards gathered up in a bag. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

A VETERAN IN HARNESS. M. Chevreul, the veteran chemist and director of the Gobelins Manufactory, though he has reached the age of 98, has so strongly objected to being placed on the retired list, that the order has been rescinded. M. Chevreul is a tremendous worker; he does not care about wine, and never takes it; he is spare in his diet, takes but two meal a day, and devotee a quarter of an hour to each. "jam very old," it is reported that he said 10 years ago, "and must not waste time in eating."—British Medical Journal. MINERS' DISTURBANCE AT DURHAM.— Owing to non-pay- inent of their wages, the miners employed at the Thornley Colliery, Durham, created a great disturbance there on Sat- urday. A report obtained circulation that in the rioting two men had been killed, but there is no truth in the statement. The manager sold three locomotives, and offered the men an instalment of 5s in the pound, but this was refused, and the miners prevented a removal of the engines by tearing up the rails. A large body of police was present, but no collision between them and the men occurred. AmeucTiote AT LIVERPOOL —On Saturday afternoon a young man named Robert Alexander Hill was committed for tiial by the Liverpool county magistrates on a charge of abducting Dorothy Snowdon. aged 14, and causing a false entry to be made in a marriage register. The girl is the daughter of a milk dealer, in whose employment Hill for- merly was. The other morning she went out with the milk, as usual, but instead of returning she met the accused and went with him to the parish church, where they were mar- ried, the prisoner representing to the clergyman that the girl was 18. AN IMPORTANT VERDICT SET AslDE.—Some weeks ago the widow of a Mr. George J. Smith, average adjuster, Glatt. gow, obtained a verdict against the Midland Railway Com- pany for £3,500 in a suit for compensation for the loss of her husband. Mr. Smith was killed by a fall down the hoist at the St. Pancras Hotel, and the jury who tried the case, believing there was evidencs of negligence against the com- pany's servants, returned a verdict as before stated. A court composed of Justices Mannisty and Williams, however, has ordered the verdict to be set aside, on the ground that there was no evidence of negligence and that it was against the weight of evidence. THE EDUCATION QUESTION.—Mr. Foreter and Mr. Mun- della were present at a meeting of managers of London Board Schools on Saturday. Mr. Forster, in the course of a short speech, said that compulsion in the matter of school attendance had generally been successful, and the necessity for it was becoming less and less. He thought the outcry against over-pressure had come from people who did not properly understand the question of education. Mr. Mun- della said the One defect of the School Board system was not having sufficient managers to take a full share of the work. The right hop, gentleman paid a high tribute to the work which was being done in Liverpool, which was, he said, enough to make the heart of any man rejoice. DEATII FROM THE BITE OF A CAT.—Mr. Payne, the London coron.?r, held an inquiry at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, on Saturday, as to the death of Robert Wallis Warren, 21 years of age, who died from hydrophobia brought on by the bite of a cat. About a month ago the deceased, while caressing a, favourite cat, was bitten by it on the hand. The wound was very slight, and after it had been attended to the deceased appeared to suffer no incon- venience. About a week back he complained of feeling ill and was advised to go to the hospital. When admitted he was found to be suffering from hydrophobia in an acute form. He died on Tnesday, the cause of death being hydrophobia. —ln reply to the coroner the house-surgeon observed that it was not generally known that the bite of a cat was equally liable to cause hydrophobia with that of a dog.— The jury returned a verdict of accidental death. MR GLADSTONE ON FRUIT FARMING.—(To the editor of the Examiner.)—Sir, Referring to the Premier's speech at the aenual tent audit at Hawarden, Mr. Gladstone is incor- rect in stating that preserves are charged from 7d to 9d a lb, and that this is owing mainly to the energy of the French, Belgian, Dutch, German and American fruit growers. All the gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, black currants, damsons, and blackberries used by me are entirely English—no foreign whatever being used—and to prove that the quantity is not particularly small, my usual season's make is :—Goeseberry, 300 tons. Raspberry, 300 tons. Strawberry, 200 tons. Black currant, 400 tons.. Damson, 500 tons. Blackberry, 100 tons. And they can be bought retail from ready-money grocers in two and three. pound stoneware jars at the following prices :.—Gooseberry, 5d to 5p per lb. Raspberry, 6d to 6d. Strawberry, 6d to (iid. Black currant, sp. Blackberry, 50. Raspberry and Gooseberry, Slid. Plum, 4d. Greengage, ed. Damson, 7d. Orange Marmalade, 4d. Jars extra_, one penny each. Yours, &c., WM. P. HARTLEY.—BootIe, Liverpool. BILLS IN PARLIAMENT.—W est Cheshire Water Bill.— On Monday, in the House of Commons, this Bill, which has passed the House of Lords, came before the Examiner of Standing Order Proofs (Mr. Robinson). The Bill incor- porates the West Cheshire Water Company, and confers upon them powers for the construction of works and the supply of water. There was no opposition, and the further stand- ing orders of Parliament were declared duly complied with.--Chester and Connah's Quay Railway Bill.—On the committee of the House of Commons meeting again OR Monday morning, Admiral Egerton in the chair, Mr. Find- lay, the general manager of the London and North-Western Railway, was examined. The objections, he said, to the proposed line were that it was totally unnecessary, that there would be no traffic to justify its construction financially, and that it would unfairly prejudice Parliament in respect toethe suggested line to Birkenhead.—Mr. Pope, Q.C., then proceeded to address the committee on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway. The learned counsel had not concluded his address when the committee adjourned. SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—A meeting of the council of the South-west Lancashire Liberal Association was held on Monday at the Reform Club, Liverpool, Mr. Thomas Brocklebank presiding. After the chairman had made a statement with regard to the work of the sub-committees, the secretary (Mr. G. H. Croaden Powell) read the report, which was adopted on the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. A. Eccles (Huyton).— Mr. A. Sinclair (St. Helens) moved the following resolu- tion :—" That this meeting of the South-west Lancashire Liberal Association is gratified that the Prime Minister has brought forward a Pr inchise Bill so comprehensive and so just, and urges upon the Government the necessity of using all the means in their power to pass it into law, believing that the stability of our institutions and the loyalty of the people of these realms will be greatly increased thereby."— The resolution was seconded by Mr. W. Tyrer (Prescot)ie supported by Mr. J E. Johnson-Eerguson (Kenyon), and I adopted.—Mr. J. B. Leach (Widnes) moved the subjoined resolution, which was seconded by Mr. W. S. Barrett (Birk- dale), and carried :—" That this meeting views with the gravest apprehension the tendency of the present line of obstruction in the House of Commons, believing it to be uncalled for and of a factious character, degrading to the tone of our representative assembly, and prejudicial to the highest interests of these realms, and prays the Government to adopt such means as shall ensure the proper criticism of public measures, and put down the prevalent vexatious method of dealing with important national interests."—A vote of thanks baying been conveyed to the chairman, on the motion of Mr. G. W. Rawlins (Rainhill),, seconded by Mr. F. F. Kennedy (Walton), the proceedings terminated. tmerozseeowe—The main cause of nervousness Is Indigestion, and that is caused by weakness of the stomach. LORD SALISBURY'S VISIT TO MANCHESTER —The Pre' gramme of Lord Salisbury's engagement in Manchester in Hester week has had to be shortened. As at present arranged, Lord Salisbury will address a meeting of the COO' servative party in the Free Trade Hall on Wednesday o'o' log, and on Thursday night he will be entertained at a ban- quet in the same building. MURDER Taut. tie .Donute.—At the Dublin Commission Court, on Ttlealay, a labourer named Goulding was tried for the murder of a woman named Malone. The case for the prosecution was that the prisoner, after beating the woman, threw her into the Liffey. The prisoner went Cu log to the police, and stated that the woman accidentally fell in when lacing her boot, and that he was forcibly Pre; vented from rescuing her. He had previously ill-treaten the deceased. A FISHERMAN DROWNED—On Saturday afternoon John Mayor, a fisherman, aged 21 years, was found drowned 10 Morecambe Hay. He had gone out early trawling in Cora' pany with other boats, but was in sole charge of his father'! boat. At the conclusion of the fishing operations Mayor? lboat was seen drifting out to sea. His brother Thorne', who was in another boat, went in pursuit, and deceased boat was eventually found empty. It is thought that he must have fallen overooard whilst putting up Wei sail. Iris 'body was found on a sandbank in the course of the after' MACCLYSVIELD COTTON OPERATIVES AND VirEll, GRIEVANCES.—A mass meeting of cotton operatives Ira' held at Macclesfield on Tuesday night to consider the re' port of the executive committee who had waited on the directors of the Globe Spinning Company during the del In order to see if a settlement of the dispute could be el' rived at. The directors refused to give the operatives the Blackburn list, and it was unanimously resolved to rerosin out until their demands were conceded. Other districts are giving help, but many operatives are suffering extras privation. •THE.WORKING CLASSES AND DIVORCE.—A clergYol writing to the Times says:—" A working man in my Pr% has a faithless wife, who has deserted him in the nwt. shameful way. It does seem to ar'' either that these courts ought to be abolished altogether of that a respectable working man ought to obtain redress f° a sum proportionate to his means." Government Bill and the London Government Bill was an insult to common sense and unworthy of the greatness of the question. There was a certain amount of truth in the statement that the Reform Bills hitherto passed had largely improved the constitution of the country. At the same time we were suffering some inconveniencies from the enlarge- ment of the constituencies. Members had not learned the exact footing on which they ought to stand wi,h reference to the electors, and there were other dangers and difficulties which the House must be careful not to increase. If a large body of new voters were admitted to the constituencies without proper preparation t'my would fall into the hods of those who would manipulate them on principles destruc- tive of individual freedom and responsibility. (Opposition cheers.) The Prime Minister said that they would not be able to deal with redistribution till after the Franchise Bill and the Registration Bill were passed. When would that be? The Registration Bill could not be introduced this year. Mr. GLADSTONE.—I know no reason why it should not be. (Cheers.) Sir S. NORTHCOTE remarked that the Hausa was getting information by degrees respecting the intentions of the Go- vernment, and for that must thank the noble lord who had brought forward the amendment. (Opposition cheers.) In his opinion, however, it was necessary to deal with redistribu- tion first and registration afterwards. The Prime Minister admitted that it was desirable to have all these measures passed by the same Parliament; but he (Sir S. Northeote) doubted whether that would be possible, and he accused the Government with treating the House unfairly in delaying so long. With regard to the proportion of members to be as- signed to the three kingdoms the Prime Minister said that some were to be taken from England. [Mr. Gladstone shook his head.] Sir S. such a step, but he did not see why the Corporatien should not accept an enlargemeot of its action. The Government had, therefore, determined in the effort they were making to establish a central government for London to take as the found ition of their scheme the ancient Corporation of Lon- don, the object of the present bill being to adapt that body to the purposes for which it was originally intended, viz, the good government of the great Metropolis of the United Kingdom. As to the area to be in- cluded under the new government, that of the Metropolitan Government Act of 1855 hal been adopted. The qualifications of the citizens under the bill would be the sauce as those in other municipal towns, and in the new Corporation would be merged all the powers at present administered by the Commissioners of Sewers, the Common Hall, the Wardmotes, and the exist- ing Corporate body itself. The new body would also have transferred to it the powers of the present Metropolitan Board of Works, as well as of the vestries under the Metro- politan Management Act of 1855, and the powers of the Justices of the Pe tee for the Metropolitan counties. The bill, however, did not propose to interfere with the existing management of the poor, with the arrangements under the Education Act, or with the present administration of the police. The new Metropolitan body would appoint all its ewn officers, and the present authority of Commons Hall would be abolished. For elective purposes, London would be divided into municipal districts, the districts taken in the first instance being those of the existing vestries and dis- trict Boards. The number of the Common Council would be 240, and the representation would be in joint ratio with the population and rateable value. The number of munici- pal districts would be 39, including the City, and they would be represented by numbers varying from 12 or 14 to one or two. The Lord Mayor would be annually elected by the whole body, which would be fairly representative of the four millions of inhabitants of the metropolitan area. It was also proposed to have a deputy Mayor, who should be a paid officer, and capable of acting in the absence of the lord Mayor. It was proposed to transfer the magisterial authority of the court of aldermen to stipendiary magistrates while the other functions of that court would be vested in the Common Council. The election of members of the Council would take place triennially in the same manner as in the case of the .Bchool Beards. In order to enable the work of so large an area to be performed without too great a pressure on the central body, district boards would be elected, with a certain proportioa of members belonging to the Common Council, sum to maintain a connection between the two district bodies acting under authority delegated to them by the general body, and submitting budgets to the Common Council, upon which the latter would make the necessary rates. It was also proposed to include the whole Metropolitan district in the county of the city of London, and the bill would come into operation on Jan 29th after its passing. The first election, however, by the citizens would onty be of 150 members of the council, the other 90 being supplied by the 46 members of the present Metropolitan , Board of Works and by 44 persons to be elected by the pre- sent council of London. The existing Lord Mayo: would retain his position until the month of May, when the newly appointed body, although elected in January, would begin to act. The right hon. gentleman entered into r. number of smaller details dealt with by the bill, and concluded, by stating that in this measure the Government had made an honest, painstaking effort to grapple with the ffifficulties of governing four millions of people. (Cheers.)—Leave was then given to bring in the bill. The bill was afterwards brought in and read a first time, the 24th last being fixed for the second reading. Mr. PARNELL called attention to the taxation imposed on the city of Qurk for extra police. Tin Corporation had made y,nsuccessful attempts to obtain a decision on the legality of this taxation, but had never been able to carry it beyond the Recorder's court. Mr. TRETELNAN, speaking on behalf of the Government, contended that the city of Cork, in regard to its police rating, compared favourably with Londonderry and Belfast, the maintenance charge at Cork being only Id in the pound, against 4,p at Londonderrty, and 5d at Belfast. After some remarks from Mr. Gray, Sir J. APKenna, Mr. Deasy, Mr. O'Brien, and Mr. Sexton, Mr. HEALY called at— tention to the conduct of the Government in the discharge of the prisoner charged with the murder of a Nationalist named Maguire. The hon. member proceeded at some length to criticise the conduct of the executive, and was describing the circumstances attending the death of Michael Waters in Mountjoy Prison, when, noticing that the Chief Secretary was smiling, he said: It is all very well for the right hon. gentleman to smile in that callous way at the sufferings of an Irish prisoner. Mr. TRRYBLYAN thereupon sprang to his feet and ex- claimed: That is an absolute falsehood.

The SPEAKER interposed, and said Mr. Healy' s speech had reached "a high level of violence," but on the latter raising as a form of order the question of the word " false- hood," the Attorney-General explained that Mr. Trevelyan was smiling at something that was said in a private conver- sation. Several members sought to address the House, and on Mr. Healy interrupting the Attorney-General, the Speaker threatened to " name " him amid cheers from the House. Finally Mr. Trevelyan withdrew the word " false- hood," used, be said, on the impulse of the moment. Mr. Healy then resumed his speech without further reference to his conflict with the Speaker and Mr. Trevelyan. The dis- cussion was continued by Mr. Harrington, the Solicitor- General for Ireland, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, and on the ques- tion being put from the Chair, the Irish members chal- lenged a division, with the result that the motion was agreed to by 85 votes against 27. ACCIDENT CCO AN EXPRESS' TRAIN AT lIIITTON QUARRY.— On Tuesday afternoon, as the half-past three express train from Lime-street to Manchester was approaching Huyton Quarry at full speed, one of the valves of the engine burst, -and the train .came to a standstill in the statim. The engine was uncoupled with the object of running it into a shed, but it could not be made to act. The Huyton Quarry officials were prompt in their action, and after a delay of about 15 minutes another locomotive took the disabled one and the carriages forward to Manehecter.. .

HITYTON LOCAL BOARD ELEcrrox.—The counting of the votes took place at the Board-room, on Friday. Mr. F. Dobell was the returning officer, assisted by the clerk (Wm. Swift) and the assistant overseer (H. Makin). Mr. Hatch- man and Mr. A. E. Hall were present on behalf of the can- didates and ratepayers. The following was the result : George Banner 566, * Richard Brown 445, * Edward J. Grimehaw 397, Tom Dalzell 366, John Duncan 320, * John 3owett 288, George Hatchinan 232, Charles H. Fairclough 134. There was a large number of bad votes, over 100 being disqualified by being without a signature. It will be seen that one of the retiring members will be thrown out; he has been a member since the formation of the Board, and the chairman for several years. The park residents have carried three out of four of their nominees. * The asterisk denotes the retiring members.

An alarming fire occurred on Tuesday at the chemical works of Messrs. P. Moir Crane and Co., Clayton, Manches- ter. A still containing several gallons of oil burst, and the oil flowing out was set on fire. The flanas were not ex- tinguished before considerable damage had been caused.
