I He then searched for the body of the child, and discovered it under the washhand stand. The child was dead, and had a handkerchief twisted twice or thrice round its neck. It j was his opinion that the child had had a separate existence ; and had died from strangulation. That, however, he coed , not swear to without a post-mortem examination. The j jury thereupon adjourned the inquest upon the body of the child, and returned a verdict in regard to the mother of "Death from hemorrhage, after giving birth to a child."

div.head: RETURN OF TROOPS.
div.p: THE RETURN OF TROOPS.

MALTA, TEXTRSDAY.—Her Majesty's troopship Jumna has arrived here from Suakina, and will sail hence to day for Devonport. She has on board the 10th Hussars, a battery of Artillery, the first battalion of the York and Lancaster Regiment, the second battalion of the Royal Irish Fusiliers, and a detachment of Royal Marines. DISQUIEFING NEWS FROM BERBER.

WEDNESDAY.—lntelligence from Berlin announces the arrival there of the messenger who left Khartoum on March 27th. He states that affairs at Khartoum are in a critical condition, the irregular troops having mutinied.. No official confirmation of this news has yet been re- ceived. The Daily News received the following from Cairo on , Tuesday night : The news from Berber is mat alarming. Very shortly our communication with that town an Don- gola will doubtless be cut off. No messages can pass be- tween Berber and Shendy, so that news from General Gor- don is impossible. The Daily News says :—With respect to the position of , General Gordon at Khartoum, we have reason to believe that he has, in the plainest terms, compatible with the peen- liar persmal circumstances attending his undertaking of the mission, been urged by the English Government to I vacate Khartoum. He has continuAd to express confidence in the ultimate success of his mission, and has on various grounds declined to obey this request. At the date of the last communication from him he was in a position to have withdrawn from Khartoum and retired the garrrison in safety. MESSAGE FROM GENERAL GORDON.—SHELLING THE ARABS. REPORTED MUTINY AT KELAR-

TOUM. WEDNESDAY.—Sir Evelyn Baring has received a despatch from General Gordon, dated March 30th, stating that on March 24th General Gordon sent a steamer to shell HaHyeb, bet the shells fell short. Another steamer was subsequently sent up the Nile, accompanied by a barge mounting a Krupp gun, which made good practice. On March 25th the General disarmed 250 Bashi-Bazouks who .ref used to march. On March 26at tbe rebel camp on the Blue Nile was shelled, the enemy losing 40 killed. The rebels fired on Khartoum on March 27th, from a village opposite, which they evacuated, however, at sunset, with a loss of 50 men. OW March 30th the rebels drove the Bashi-Bazquks from a village opposite Khartoum, but retired an hour afterwards. The White Nile district is quiet, and the Khartoum market Is well supplied. The Mandi is reported to have sent to the rebels four mountain guns and two Nordenfelts. The gun which the rebels captured on M trch 16th is stated to be spiked, but it had only two rounds when it fell into their hands. General Gordon estimates the • number of the rebels at from, 1,500 to 2,000, of whom perhaps not more than 150 are determined men. Intelligence from Berber announces the arrival there of a messenger who left Khartoum on March 27th. He states that affairs at Khartoum are in a critical condition, the irregular troops having mutinied. No official confirmation of this news has yet been received. ATHENS, WEDNESDAY.—British Consular reports from Hedjaz state that Arab feeling is opposed to the Mandi. The Government has received information that Admiral

Hewett has reached Ma9sowah in her Majesty's Euryalus on his way to Abyssinia to confer with King John. THE FIGHTING AT KHARTOUM. The Times publishes the following telegrams from its cor- respondent at Khartoum:— MARCH 28 —The rebels are moving away from their camp in retreat towards Sennaar. Three steamers are plunging shell among them. A messenger has come in say- ing the English are at Eldamer. Four of our officers write saying they are prisoners with the rebels. General Gordon has arranged for their escape to-night. NIGIIT.—There is a dropping fire from the other side of the river, but none of us have been hit. All is quiet in the town. 1 Meilen 20—To-day we took a Krupp 20. pounder gun to the north side of the Blue Nile and shelled the rebel pimp ; every shell told. Mauna 30.—The Bashi-Baaouks went out into the plain to-day, but were driven back by the Arab cavalry. The Arabs occupied the village opposite, and are now firing On the palace. A man in the palace has been killed. We are shelling the village opposite. The Bashi-Bazapks lost one man in the cavalry charge. Arwtr, 1.—Yesterday some Bashi Bazouks were sent to thd village opposite to look for firewood. This was a signal for a descent of the rebels from their camp. Of course the Bashi Baz9uks retreated towards the two twtified houses ei - posits, but owing to the way in which a Krupp 20-pounder at the Palace covered the retreat, they only lost one man by the rebels' magnificent cavalry charge. The rebels then poured into the village and opened fire on the Palace with Itemingtons. We replied with canister ana shell. A few

shots from Gel, Gordon had the effect of silencing the Arab fire, but uLt AI a clerk looking out of a window of the Palace had been shot through the brain. The night passed quietly; early in the morning, however, the Arabs sent some ballets into the Palace, but no notice being taken, ceased firing. There was a game ot hide and seek in the village, but, of nurse, when the least danger began the Bashi Bazouks retired. It is reported that the rebels lost yesterday, by the fire of the Krupp gun, 40 killed and 8 wounded, and 16 horses. It is reported that the rebels have captured the post, but it is unknown whether it was ours going or the Cairo post coming in. We have received no communication from the outer world since March 10. Last night the Arabs opened fire on the Palace, but we silenced them.

div.head: SATURDA.Y, APRIL 12, 1884.
div.p: SATURDA.Y, APRIL 12, 1884.
FOREIGN NEWS.
THE WRECK -
OF AN ATLANTIC STEAMER.-GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

_ NEW YORE, SATURDAY.—The Daniel Steinmann struck at 10 o'clock on Thursday night, about 300 yards from Sambro Light, during a terrific gale and dense fog. The steamer was immediately backed off, but the next moment again struck with terrible force upon another shoal. An immense h.le was knocked in her bottom, through which the water poured and speedily tilled the hold. In a few minutes the vessel sank. So far as is at present known one lifeboat only was launched. About midnight some men on Sanabro bland observed a boat making for the shore, and I guided it to a Safe landing place by torches. The occupants proved to be five of the crew and two of the passengers of the Daniel Steinmann. When daylight Came two persons were perceived clinging to the rigging of the wreck, and a boat put off from the lighthouse to their rescue. They were the captain of the steamer and a boy passenger. The cap-1 tain fears that 90 passengers have been drowned. No females have been saved.

EVINING.—The Daniel Steinmann was about eight miles out of her course when she struck. The captain states that he experienced fine weather, with the exception of the last two days. during which a heavy fog prevailed, rendering it impossible for any observations to be taken. At ten o'clock on the night of the 3rd inst. he saw a light ahead, which he at first took for the Chebucto Light, the fog making it ap- pear about five miles off. He now thinks, however, that it could not have been more than one mile distant. On nearing it he discovered it to be the Sambro Light, and before speed could be slackened the vessel was among the ledges on the Inorth east of the island. She struck twice and began filling fast. He then tried to run her ashore buL wi.b.mt success, the vessel sinking in a few minutes. When the ship first struck, he ordered the passengers on deck. • In a short time the heavy seas which swept over the vessel carried them nearly all into the sea. Five of the crew and two passengers succeeded in launching a boat, and reached Sambro Island. The ship went down stern first. The captain, who was at the time on the bridge, took refuge in the fore-rigging, but the vessel sank so rapidly that he was obliged to let himself float. He fortunately succeeded in getting hold of the top-gallant-yard, and clung there with one other passenger, who hal also managed to keep afloat, until five o'clock the following morning, when they were reacued by a boat from the island. NENI Yong, Sum:ay.—None of the bodies of those who were drowned in the wreck of the Daniel Steinmann have yet been washed ashore. It is stated by some people on Sambro island that the weather was clear enorieh for the steamer to be seen from the islamd at the time of the disaster. The captain, however, maintains that fog prevailed, and that no fog whittle woe blown an the 'sited. The folldwing are the names of the persons saved:— Captain Schoonhaven, Commander of the Daniel Steinmann; Fritz Veck, of Stralsund; Charles von Louis, Frank Disseri, and Petro Lingens, of Antwerp; Otto Krang, of Wittchen- dorf ; John Nederman, of Echenbofen ; Vincenzo Lacco, an Italian; and Eugene Nickels, of Mulfort. Naar Yoax, APRIL 7.—Eleven bodies have been washed ashore from the ill-fated steamer Daniel Steinmann. They are all terribly mutilated from contact with the rocks, and the features of some are quite unrecognisable. Among them I are the corpses of the mate and of three children, two of them girls. No adult female has been found. On only one of the bodies were any valuables discovered. On one a ticket was found taken in the name of August Richter, of Daeseldorf. Noce of the cargo has drifted ashore or floated. The wreck remains in the same position. Considerable indignation is felt here at the mismanagement of affairs on Sambro Island. It is pointed out that there was no lifeboat or rocket apparatus available, although Sambro is one of the most dangerous places on the coast. It is stated that a lifeboat could have caved at least fie persons. The only people that escaped were by a boat from the steamer. The New York Times declares that the captain is directly 'responsible for the accident by having pushed on in the fog when for two days he had been unable to take any ob- servations. The journal also severely censures the failure to keep a lifeboat on the island. HALIFAX, TUESDAY.—The official inquiry into the loss of the Daniel Steinmann has been opened. Divers have been sent out to inspect the wreck. They saw no bodies, but did not enter the cabin or the steerage. It is believed that the corpses of the victims have been carried out to sea by the undertow. Some of the cargo has been recovered. EGYPT.—THE CABINET CRISIS AT CAIRO. CAIRO, MONDAY, 11-10 A351.--.Efforts are being msde to induce Nubar Pasha to remain in office. The differences be- tween him and Mr. Clifford Lloyd have been referred to the Britieh Government. Meanwhile Nubar Pasha attends to his official duties as usual. Major. General Graham arrived here this morning. Lieu- tenant-General Stephenson will hold a review to-morrow of troops just returned from Suakin'. Mr. Clifford Lloyd arrived here from Alexandria this morning, and has since bad an interview with Sir Evelyn Baring. Canto, TIIICSDAY.—The decision of the British Govern- ment with reference to the differences between Nubar Pacha and Mr. Clifford Lloyd has not been received. To-day Sir Evelyn Baring, accompanied by Mr. Lloyd, paid a visit to Nubia racha and other members of the Ministry for the purpose, it is presumed, of endeavouring to arrange matters, but Nubar persists in his determination to resign unless Mr. Clifford Lloyd agrees to retire. Gam% THURSDAY.—The difference between Nubar Pasha and Mr. Clifford Lloyd has been satisfactorily arranged. Both will retain office. In virtue of the understand:lag arrived at Mr. Lloyd will limit his action to the functions of under secretary, and is to be censidered an Egyptian not an English official. CONFERENCE WITH OSMAN.DIGNA. .

TRUBSDLY.—The Sheikh El Margham received a letter, yesterday, from Osman Digna stating that he would send some Sheikhs on the 12th inst. to meet El Morgham at a point two tours' march from Suakin', where a conference could be held.

div.head: LORD DUFFERIN AND THE PORTE.
div.p: LORD DUFFERIN AND THE PORTE.

ATHENS, WEDNESDAY.—In consequence of the urgent representations of Lord Dufferin, a number of claims of ffritish subjects in Turkey are now in course of settlement. Lord Dufferin has received instructions from Earl Granville settling the question of the coasting trade at Smyrna. ADEN, MONDAY.—The mission under the command of Major Hunter, which left here at the beginning of Feb- ruary for the African coast, has returned after visiting Harrar, Berbera, and Zaila. The tribes are peaceably dis- posed towards the Egyptian Government, and there is con- sequently no cause for anxiety. The Berbera Somah tribe had threatened to revolt in consequence of the harsh treat- ment of the Bey, but owing to the intervention of Major Hunter a better feeling now prevails. The state of affairs, however, is still disquieting, but there is no cause for alarm I so long as a British war vessel remains in the vicinity. It is believed that the gun vessel Arab will shortly proceed to cruise off the coast. The position of affairs in the Soudan has caused great excitement among the various tribes. There are four French war vessels in the Gulf of Aden.

div.head: RUSSIA.-TilE MURDER OF COL SUDEIKIN
div.p: RUSSIA.-TilE MURDER OF COL SUDEIKIN

BERLIN, TIIESDAY.—.A. despatch from Moscow states that one of the assassins of Colonel Sudeikin was arrested there yesterday. The individual in question is not, how- ever, Degaieff. THE ANNEXATION OF MERV.

Trms, Mont:ay.—The Journal Caucasus publishes the following telegram from General Komaroff, dated Askabad, March 26:—" During the march to Mery our detachment was surprised on the night between March 14th and 15th by a band of marauders coming from Konhutchankala, who were repulsed with considerable lose by three volleys from two of our rifle companies. On our side one soldier was killed. On the following day our troops occupied Kechut- chankala when all was quiet. The administrative authori- ties of the district have entered upon their duties, the erec- tion of a fort has been commenced, and Mervians are em- ployed on the works." CAN ADA.—FURTRER RAILWAY EXTENSIONS AND SUBSIDIES. OTTAWA MONDAY.—In order to secure the establishment of ocean termini within the Dominion in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Government offer a subsidy of $960,000 for a railway between Montreal and Quebec, together with $1,000,000 for a line between New Glasgow and the Straits of Canso in Nova Scotia, be- sides $3,500,000 in fifteen annual payments of $231,000 each as a subsidy or guarantee of the interest on the bonds of the company agreeing to construct a short line of railway connecting Montreal, St. John, New Brunswick, Halifax, and Louisburg, in Cape Breton Island.

div.head: GERMANY, THE RETIREMENT OF PRINCE BISMARCK.
div.p: GERMANY, THE RETIREMENT OF PRINCE BISMARCK.

- -- BERLIN, MONDAY.—The impending retirement of Prince Bismarck from the Prussian Ministry forms to-day the sub- ject of an article in the North German Gazette, which ex- plains that the step is in consequence of medical advice. Prince Bismarck was informed that his power to work could only be maintained if his labours were reduced in e4tent, and he was therefore absolutely ordered to give up some of the business which he had previously been in the habit of transacting. The Chancellor accordingly decided to retain the Imperial business. and to renounce his control over Prussian affairs.

_ AUSTRIA.—EXPLOSION OF A BOMB AT TRIESTE. TRIESTE, MONDAY.—A bomb was exploded here last night close to the barracks, without, however, doing any damage. Brume, Monnev.—An Anarchist named Ziffer has been arrested here, charged with having procured money for the purposes of agitation by obtaining goods under false pre- tences, and afterwards selling them at a very low price. •50 HOUSES BURNED DOWN. VIENNA, TUESDAY.—A fire has occurred in the Moravian village of Graegan, causing the destruction of 50 houses. One woman and ten children perished in the flames.
ROUMANIA.-RESIGNATiON OF THE MINISTRY.

BUCHAREST, TURSDAY.—The members of the Cabinet tendered their resignation to the King to-day in consequence of a hostile vote of the Chamber of Deputies, yesterday, upon the Premier's policy in regard to the date for the com- mencement of the debate upon the Bill for the Revision of the Constitution.

BUCHAREST, WEDNESEAT.--The Ministerial crisis is at an end. In the Chamber of Deputies to-day, M. Bratiano, the Premier, announced that the King had informed him that in consequence of yesterday's vote of confidence in the Government he considered the resignation of the Cabinet as annulled. The Chamber then commenced a debate on the revision of the Constitution. HALF A CITY DESTROYED.
Snits, Wauxasnev.--futelligence has been received here from Burmah reporting that a great fire has occurred at Mandalay, ciusing the destruction of half the city
THE -TRUCE BETWEEN CHILI AND BO LI %'IA.

Pews, WEDNESDAY.—A despatch received by the Chilian Minister to France states that under the terms of the truce concluded on the 4th instant between Chili and Bolivia, the portion of the Bolivian territory occupied by the Chilian forces will remain under Chilian law. Trade will be free between Chili and Bolivia. FRANCE AND_TONQUIN.—MASSACRE OF

div.head: MISSIONARIES.
div.p: MISSIONARIES.

Penis, WEDNESDAY.—Tbe Ultramontane journal Le Monde to-day states that a telegram .ha i reached Paris an- nouncing the massacre of five French missionaries and 30 ,catechists in the province of Than Roe, in Western Tonquin. TURKEY.—OVERFLOW OF THE TIGRIS. CONSTANTINOPLE, TIECTICSDAY.—The floods caused by the overflow of the Tigris have assumed alarming proportions. According to news from Bagdad dated the Bth inst., the river had risen to such an extent on the previous day that 21<lykes had been broken down and several places inun- dated. The town of Bagdad is surrounded by water. The whote extant of the inundation is not yet fully known. The crops rin the neighbourhood of Bagdad, which were very promiting, have been destroyed. The town is for the present out of danger, owing to the vigorous measures taken by the governor.

div.head: SWETZERLAND.-EXPULSION OF SENOR ZORRILLA.
div.p: SWETZERLAND.-EXPULSION OF SENOR ZORRILLA.

PARIS, rEURSDAY.—In consequence, it is said, of repre- sentations made by the Spanish Government to that of Switzarland, Senor Ruiz Zorrilla, the Republican leader, has been obliged to quit Swiss territory. His present whereabouts, however, are unknown.

div.head: – EARLESTOWN•
div.p: - EARLESTOWN•

SERMONS AT THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—The annual sermons in aid of the trust fund were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, Earleetown, on Sunday last, by the Ray. D. T. Maylott, of Darwen. Both in the morning and evening there was a large congregation, and the collections realised about £4. In the afternoon of the same day the Rev. D. T. Maylott gave an earnest and impressive address to the scholars on mission work at Fer- nando Po, where he had formerly been stationed as a mis- sionary. RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—About six o'clock on Monday evening a brakesman named Richard Pascluill, residing at Daubhill, near Bolton, when engaged uncoupling wagons in motion, at Barlestown, met with a rather serious accident. He was kneeling on the buffers of the wagon, his right leg being extended from the wagons, when it came into contact with some trucks standing in another siding, knocking him off the wagons and breaking his leg. He was also severely cut about the bead. After having his injuries attended to by Dr. Handysidei be was removed to the Liverpoel Infirmary.

THE EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL JONIOR CHALLENGE CUP. —The whole of the ties have now been completed in the first round of the competition for the Challenge cup pre- sented by the Earlestown Association Football Club. The results were as follows :—Earlestown Association (2nd) de- feated Earlestown Wanderers (2nd) by six gosis to one ; St. Helens St. Thomas's (let) beat Etrlestown Ramblers (2nd) by ten goals to oce ; Haydock Temperance (2nd) beat Got- borne (2ml) by four goals 14 none; Earlestown Wanderers (Ist) defeated Earlestown limbless (Ist) by four goals to none; Newton St. Peter's (Ist) defeated Etriestown Revers (let) by one goal to none; Haydock St. James's (2nd) de- feated Haydock Recreation (Ist) by two goals to one. The draw for the second round of the competition took place on Thursday evening week, when the remit was awaited with considerable interest. The clubs were drawn together as follows :—St. Helens St. Thomas's (Ist) v. Earlestown Association (2nd); Newton St. Peter's (Ist) v. Haydock St. James's (2nd) ; Haydock Temperance (2nd) s. Earlestown Wanderers (Ist). The ties have to be played off on or before Saturday next, April 12th, the first-named club in each tie having the choice of ground.

Tau VIADUCT INsTrruvu SOIREE.—The festivities in con- nection with the Viaduct Institute soiree wer-; continued on Saturday evening, when a concert and ball were held in the same room at the works in which the proceedings on the previous Wednesday evening took place. The decorations remained as they were on the latter occasion. The concert room was again crowded, and Mr. H. J. Darman accom- panied the singing on the pianoforte. Mr. P. Hastie very effectively sang "Polly," and was rewarded with a deserved encore; after which Miss Bothwell sweetly sang "The wishing cap." Mr. J. White gave "The vagabond," and was succeeded by Mr. Jackson, of Golborste, whose render- ing of the humorous piece, "Why did I marry Martha Box?" excited loud laughter. On being recalled, he gave' " The runaway musketeer." Miss Bothwell very nicely sang "The blue Alsltian mountains," and Mr. Thistle was again recalled for his capital song, "The mousquettire." Mr. Durman sang a comicar piece, entitled "The little th scrub,"ou?, Jackson a n r.Wesointe againeff ct idveelliyg delighted dg th‘e' humorous songs, " Oh, dem golden slippers," and *The wooden leg brigade,' and the concert then concluJed, shortly after eight o'clock. The ball which was afterwar,l6 AalUideeiLC we h ebr y e ci:st held was still more largely attended. The Golborne Brass Band played the selections for dancing, which was heartily kept up until about eleven o'clock.

NEW PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOLS.—The Primiti we Method6ts of Earlestown have long felt the wast of better and more convenient school accommodation, anal active steps are now being taken with the view of remedyinz the disad- vantages under which the Sunday school workers have la- boured for some considerable time. It has been decided that the work of erecting pew school premises s'aall be com- menced forthwith, and tenders are being asked for in con- nection with the undertaking. The school will be built upon a plot of land in Lord-street, behind the present chapel and school in Legh-street, and a portion of the present chapel yard will also be built upon. It is proposed that the large room shall seat about 500 persons. There will be five large class-rooms along the aide of the school, and there will also be an infants' schoolroom. We understand that the work will be proceeded with as soon as convenient after the contract has been let.

THE CEIURCII DISPUTE AT EARLESTOWN.— DISGRACEFUL SCENES: EXTRAORDINARY AD- DRESS BY THE VICAR.--THE VICAR MOBBED. Since the commencement of the dispute at St. John's Church, Earlestown, the particulars' of whith are wella known to oar readers, many disgraceful scenes have been occasioned both inside and outside the church, bat the oc- currences witnessed an Sunday last were far worse than any previous proceeding in Connection with the dispute. , Last weekend a rumour obtained ciedence that something un- usual might be expected on the Sunday. but nothing,ile- finite as to the intention of the Vicar (the Rik. T. R. Mat- thews) could be obtained: It was authoritatively stated , that a meeting of the churchwardens and sidesmen was held last Tuesday week, and one result was that a request was forwarded to the vicar that he should select the hymns which were to be sung on the Sunday and hand them to the organist. But Mr. Durman did not receive the hymns; and the sequel to the demand of the officers of the churah was evidenced 03 Sunday morning. It appears that the vicar had obtained the services of a gentleman from Liverpool, who kindly consented to preside at the organ on Sunday. But it is stated that the gentleman in question was not aware of the dispute existing at the church until he arrived thereat. However, on Sunday forenoon he proceeded to the organ, while the choir and congregation gathered in their places. Mr. J. Darman, the organ'st hitherto, also occupied his accus- tomed seat amongst the choir. As the service was pro- ceeded with, the organist engaged for the day played the organ at the appointed times, but neither the choir nor congregation took any part in the service. One or two per- sons is the church, however, did respond to the prayers and sing the psalms and hymns which were played, but as a whole the congregation remained silent throughout the service. The preacher was the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate), bile no allusion to the disagreement was made by that gentleman. In the afternoon the statement that the church- wardens and sidesmen had held a meeting, and that they bad decided to take some definite action in the matter drew together a large congregation, the church being filled. Con- siderable excitement was manifested by the congregation, and the rapid moving about of various officials of the church; the passing backwards and forwards in and out of the vestry by the Vicar tended to still further increase the uncertainty as to what the upshot of all the "mysterious movements" would be. But the congregation had not long to wait. Four sidesmen were noticed to make their way to the back of the organ, and the congregation quickly came to the conclusion that they proceeded thither simply to prevent the new organist playing the organ. This opinion turned out to be the cor- rect one. Contrary to what took pace at the morning ser- vice, the organ was not played; neither the choir nor con- gregation responded to the prayers, nor were the psalms sung or any hymns announced. But when the Vicar entered the pulpit for the purpose of preaching several per- sons rose from their seats and left the church. After waiting until the noise bad subsided, The 'Vicar, before proceeding to preach, said with some warmth of manner: I cannot any longer forbear, my friends, making a few remarks as to the present state of things. lam told all sorts of things. Some find fault with me ; some say one thing and some say another, and some say that the whole congregation is being punished because of a few. I tell you plainly that it is not my fault that any punishment has been inflicted upon the congregation in the way of depriving you of singing and playing. On three occasions I have been prepared with singing and playing, but one of the officers of the church, who is now present, said on two or three occasions that if Mr. Durman did not play the organ he would take good etre no- body else should. You have seen a specimen of it to-day. I have been at the trouble of bringing a gentleman down here for the purpose of playing the organ and leading us in our praises, which you will have heard this morning. or at least to some extent; and which has been put a storto— has been prevented—as you have seen this evening. Three other officers of the church have been planted behind the organ with the authority, as they say, and I believe it is so, of a fourth officer of the church to prevent any blowing the organ unless Mr. Durman plays the organ. Now, I dis- tinctly say that Mr. Durman shall not play the organ. I have made up my mind to it, and they may wait, and wait, and I may tell you, I can wait too. I have not acted or taken one step without the knowledge, and the consent, and , the guidance and the instruction of my bishop and his legal I adviser, although all this hasbeen set at naught, and I have been .told by cue officer of the church that bishops and par- sons can say anything—that they willAmake laws to suit themselves. All I can say to that is, other people can do so too. Here is a note I got from the bishop a short time ago:—" Dear sir,—ln all matters be- tween yourself and Mr. Corlett I advise you to be guided entirely by Mr. Glamon, whose legal opinion you can always have for nothing." That I have done. When I said the other day from this place that R was sot my fault that there was no singing I heard something like hissing— something like a contradiction of what I said. But I re- peat it, it was not my fault, nor is it my fault to-night that we have no singing. Just as I entered into the vestry to- night I received this note from Mr. Corlett :—" Dear sir,— A very strong deputation of parishioners waited upon me this afternoon, and they are determined "—But, added Mr. Matthews, it is no business of theirs, whoever they are— "that if Mr. Durman does not preside at the organ to-night no one else shall, as they consider he is our servant from vestry to vestry.—Yours respectfully, B. Corlett." Now considering these things, I ask is it fair, is it honest, is it leanly that I should be blamed for the events that have taken place? I say no, and in saying so I feel that lam only echoing the feelings of every honest heart in this place and parish generally. The rev, gentleman then announced his text as the fourth verse of the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah, and he proceeded to preach his sermon thereon. But his remarks concerning the dispute appeared to be uppermost in the thoughts and minds of the congregation, and when the close of the service was reached the choir and congregation manifested a desire to linger behind. , Those who got outside the building gathered round the doors and excitedly discussed the vicar's "speech," as it was called, until, when nearly all had left the church, a rash was made, and a large nnmber .pf persons made their way into the building to the cry of "Line up' ROvers." The vicar, his son, friends, and the new organist.walking about the chancel were loudly hissed and groaned at, while one of the vicar's sympathisers, a middle-eged man, was greeted with offensive cries, and inithe course of the commotion he was violently pushed backwards against one of the pews. On the vicar and his friends entering the vestry the large number of persons, numbering several hundreds, who had been present at the service waited around the vicarage; and when the vicar, accompanied by his friends, made their ap- pearance out of the vestry they were greeted with loud and prolonged hisses and groans.. Fortunately they had not to pass through the streets from the church to the vicar's house, but kept within the church grounds, otherwise there is reason to believe the vicar would have been as- saulted. As it was, some one shouted, " Kennel, kennel, thou grey headed old ; " others cried out " knobstick" to the new organist; while one individual, more excitable than the rest, took up a large piece of sod and threw it at the vicar. It alighted en the vicar's back, but fortunately he was uninjured. The hubbub and noise occasioned by the distuebance was heard a coneiderable distance away, and a large number of persons remained near the church. Immediately after the vicar and his friends had entered the vicarage, Mr. Darman proceeded to give a short ex- planation respecting the occurrences that had taken place. Addressing those gathered round him, Mr. Durmaa said he had had a conversatianewith the gentleman who had been requested to officiate as organist ,that day, and he happened to be a friend of his (Mr. Darman). It appeared that Mr. Darman's friend was the organist at St. Catherine's Church', ' Liverpool, at which the Rev. Gustavus Carson officiated. Mr. Caison informed him, , that he had a friend )c .11ed Matthews in gailestown, whose or- ganist Lad left, and he asked if he would oblige by going over and taking the musical part in the ser- vice. Bt he (the organist) did not know how matters Atood at St. John the Baptist's Church, Earlestown, and con- sequently replied that he would do so with pleasure. Ile, however, did so quite ignorantly, and when he found how matters stood he had asked Mr. Darman to preside at the organ, but he (Mr. Darman) would not do so. The people afterwards gradually dispersed to their homes. Since Sunday the scandalous scenes have formed the chief topic of conversation throughout the district- The enhn.ual vestry meeting is being anxiously swait!„d by the pail: ton- ers, who are desirous of expressing their opunon upoa the events of the last few months in an uarnietakeable form. The following notice referring to the vestry meeting has bean posted on the churei door :—" Notice. St. John the Baptist's Church. The parishioners are requested to take notice that a vestry meeting will be held on Monday next, the 14th of April, at seven o'clock in the evening, in the vestry of this church, for the purpose of passing the ac- counts of the churchwardens for the past year, and for the election of officers for the clining year, and for the trinsact- tog Of any other business. N. 11. &dim), B. Corlett, church- wardeas."

The Manchester Examiner and Times of Wednesday has the following comments On the subject :—" The dispute be- tween thtleVicir of St. John's, Earlestown, is proceeding fro:n had to wane, and is asmming, if indeed it has not a re irly obtained, the charact?r of a puhlic scandal. The nomilial origin or the unseemly quarrel is that the Vier yid tilt accept the services of an orgrinist who is po'pular wi ir the atteudants at the church. We say the nominal origin, V. eausa it is evident that something more than the dismis di ' of an organist is the exciting cause of the heated tealO''l which is exhibited on both sides, and what that something

we venture to think, will not be difficult to ascertain from the report we published of the Vicar's remarks at the Sunday even:ng service. Even supposing the congregation were in the first instance at fault, it would have to be said that the attitude taken up by the clergyman is little calculated to persuade them of their error, while his masterful lan- guage is only too like to have an aggravating effect upon their passions. Last Sunday he imported an organist from Liverpool, and the appearance of the stranger led to a scandalous scene, certain of the officers of the church taking forcible possessioaof the organ, and declaring that if the old organist was not allowed to play no one else should use the instrument. And not less deplorable was the defiance the Vicar delivered to the congregation from the pulpit. It was as though he said he was the dictator there, and deter- mined to have his way in spite of everybody. He would distinctly state, he said, that the old organist should not play again. He had nude up his mind to it. They could wait and wait and wait, but he could wait too.' This is not the language of a peacemaker; it is not language which becomes a clergyman. The Vicar stated that he had not acted without • the knowledge, con- sent, guidance, and instruction of the Bishop '—an asser- tion it is' difficult to credit; but since it was made it is not surprising that, according to the Vicar's statement, one officer of the church had said that 'bishops and parsons would say anything and make laws to suit tbemselyee: When the sermon began several of the congregation retired, and those who remained ended the disgraceful episode by hissing the Vicar at the close of the service. Since the Vicar has mentioned the Bishop's name, it is not too much to ask that, in the interest of decorum, not to speak of self. gion, the Bishop will administer a little more 'guidance and instruction' of a nature likely to arrest these indecent proceedings." . The Liverpool Echo says :—" Such scenes as those which happen every Sunday at St. John's Church, Eeriest-perm can serve no other purpose than that of bringing religion into disrepute, and creating are increase of malice and uncharit- ableness. The cause of the disturbance is trivial encragb-e. a mere difference of opinion between vicar and organist as to the hymns and tunes. Therefore, the organist is die- charged and a new organist appointed, who is bodily pre- vented by four sidesmen from manipulating the king of instruments. Then the codgregation who attended the service, which is minus singing and responses, hie: the clergyman whose ministrations they have attended but not , profited by. The whole affair is childish, and worse, ex- hibiting, as it does, a lack of harmony, commonsense, and Christian spirit.

div.head: MEETING OF THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: MEETING OF THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.

A monthly. meeting oittie. Newton linproveinent Com- missioners was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Mon- day afternoon. Present—Colonel McCurq uoda le, J.P. (pre- siding in the absence of Mr. Gooch, chairman), Messrs. J. E. Pardey, J. W. Emmett, T. J. Gillespie, J.P., T. Porker, James Fairclough, T. Hunt, Jamas E. Woi-sley (law clerk), and R. Brierley (surveyor). The minutes of the last meeting were read and con- firmed.

HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.—A meeting of the Highways Public Works and. Sanitary Committee WAS held on the 17th ult. ; the surveyor reported that the Rev. J. Lennon's cottages, Crew-lane, were again obstructed by the adjoining tenant, and it was ordered that the offer of the Commissioners in the minutes of the 2nd February, 1882, be again made, and if not accepted by the property owners, that the surveyor be authorized to extend the present drain, to within 100 feet of the premises, and to take such other steps to enforce compliance under section 23 of the Public Health Act, 1875. A letter, dated 11th inst., was read from the Local Government Board enquiring what steps the Com- missioners were taking to improve the sanitary condition of Wargrave. The surveyor was instructed to reply that the sewering of Wargrave would be commenced shortly, and it was ordered that the necepsary notices be given preliminary to commencing the work. Mr. Brierley submitted Mr. Bale harry's valuation of the tenants' interest in the land required for cemetery purposes, amounting to £76 2s. 8.1. Alter some discussion the same was ordered to be paid, together with Mr: Bal harry's fees £5 14s. It was ordered that the Sur- veyor do proceed to fence off the cemetery land at once, with wok posts and wire fencing. It was ordered that Mr. Glover, with the surveyor, be deputed to attend the Association of Local Boards' meeting at Liverpool, on the 19th inst. Plans for four cottages in Gas-street for Mr. J. Swann, eight houses In Wargrave New-road for the Earle,- town Industrial Co-operative Society, two houses in Sankey- street for Mr. Galligan, two houses in Sankey-street for Mr. J. Eckersley, and intended street south-east of Wargrave Bridge for R. H ,ughton, Esq , were submitted and approved. —The minutes were passed. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.—At a meeting of this cemmittee held on the 17th March, a letter dated 4th March was read from Messrs. Meadows and Son asking for a rebate from their contract prices for gas and water. It was ordered that they be informed that the committee cannot see their way to deviate from the existing contract. The Special Committee reported the necessity for additional coal storage accommodation at the gasworks, and directed Mr. Brierley to submit his plans to a future meeting of the committee. The gasworks zarbonizing account for the past month gave fuel used 315 tons 6 cwt., gas made 3,119,900 cu ,ic feet, averaging 10,022 feet per too of fuel used.—On the motion of Mr. Hunt, seconded by Mr. Gillespie, the minutes were confirmed.

SCLIOOL ATTENDANCE —At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee held on the 17th ult., the school attendancz officer read his report, and Mr. Ball having com- piled a copy of the attendance registers of the various schools in the district, it was resolved that his salary for the current year, just ending, be augmented by an addition of £lO to his present salary.—The minutes were confirmed.— Mr. Emmett said he would like to give Mr. Ball, the school attendance officer, an intimation of what he intended to speak at the next meeting. He had had a paper put into his hands showing that the average attendance at the Wes- leyan school was not quite so good as it ought to be, but was decreasing. On enquiry being made as to the cause, many reasons were assigned by the parents of the children. One cause was they had an idea that if they made eight attendances in the week that was all that was required of them. He did not know and he never understood that that was the rule, but if mothers only knew that they were expected to send their children regularly to school, and not keep them away a full day in one week, it would perhaps have some good effect. He merely mentioned the matter then so that they would have an idea he intended to speak about it at the next meeting. FINANCES.-A meeting of the Finance Committee was held on the 17th March, and accounts amounting to £1,614 2s Id were examieed and passed for payment. The accounts included one of £730 6s lid paid to the Economic Life As- su r anc e Society in connection with a loan.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Gillespie, seconded by Mr. Emmett.

THE REMOVAL or NIGIIXSOIL.—The Law Clerk submit- ted the contract of William Ellam with the Newton Com- missioners for the removal of the nightsoil, with a bond with two sureties attached. It had been duly signed, and only required the seal of the Commissioners affixing to it.— On the motion of Mr. Fairclouseh, seconded by Mr. Forster, it was resolved that the seal of the Board be affixed to the contract.—Mr. Gillespie: What is the amount we are pay- ing for the removal of the nightsoil ?—Mr. Brierley : £340. —The Chairman: It was duly brought forward before the Commissioners, and we agreed to it.—Mr. Fairclongh : How much more is it than we paid last year?—Mr. Brierley : It was £3OO last time.—Mr. Fairclough: It goes on increasing. —Mr. Brierley : Yes.—Mr. Gillespie: And I suppose New- ton goes on increasing as well. THE NEW CEMETERY.—Mr. Worsley stated that the agreement with Messrs. Lee and Houseman on behalf of the owner of the land required for the new cemetery had been duly signed, and he (Mr. Worsley) had paid over the de- posit money, and the Commissioners now had possession of the land. He had also to report that the mortgage for the cemetery was in progress with the Economic Life Assurance Company. THE RATING OF Nnwroht LAYIL—It was intimated to the Board that Mr. John Lane. who had been before the Commissioners at their last meeting with respect to his rate for the Newton landing-stage, again wished to have an. interview with the Board. The Board decided that the question could not be re-opened, but Mr. Lane was called into the room—Mr. Lane said he had come to ask them to return the money paid by him under protest. He said a policeman went to his house, marked the goods; and was going to have them removed unless the money was paid.— The Chairman said the subject had been gone into before, and it was duly recore'ed in their minutes. It was then ascertained that they had no power to return the money, and therefore they could not go into the subject afresh.— Mr. Lane : You had better go into it afresh rather than let me take it to London. I can get it at the Court of Queen's Bench.—The Chairman said he might take what action he liked, but they could not re-open the question.—Mr. Lane: Ought Ito be rated for a landing-stage when there is none. The magistrates said--Mr. Pardey : Really this is not the place to discuss the action of the magistrates. We can- not discuss the action of the magistrates here.—Mr. Lane : There is one thing. Mr. Pearson himself said---The Chairman: We cannot hear you any further.—r. Lane - Ote minute, please.—The Chairman: No, no; te: ;am me, but we really cannot go into it now. The next business, please.—Mr. Lane then retired, muttering something about having been "robbed" of his money. AUDITOR'S REPORT.—The CHAIRMAN read the following report : Newton-le.Willows, Bist March, 1884. To the Oha' rman of the Newton Improvement Commissioners —Sir —We have completed the audit of all tha books and accounts of your Board for the year ending March, 1883, and find (lit) that Mc. Brierley's books are well and correctly kept, and agree with the printed sta'ement of accounts which has been issued; (2nd) that in the books kept by Mr. Houghton we foun& several clerical errors, which 'nth, aggregate almost balance each other, with the exception of one item—an uodercharge of 100,000 feet boons of the gas accounts of the London and North- , Western Railway Company. We may, la use ver, .ention that ' taking into consideration the numerous entries Mr. Houghton ' has to make it is a matter of surprise there are not more I errors, and we would respectfully suggest that the gas anei water accounts he checked quarterly; (3rd) the books in :'Mr. Swann's charge require more care in the keeping, as we found, numerous small errors in them.—RICHARD BARTON and THOS. [ THOMPSON. Auditors, • .. . . , TiliS was the only business of Interes6, and the meeting concluded. --ref

At a late hour on Tuesday night a fire broke out on the premises of Mr. David Morton, lace and hosiery bleacher, Sneinton, Nottingham, doing damage to the amount of be- tween £12,000 and £14,000, which is covered by insurance. On Monday morning a man was found bruised and bleed- ing on his face in the yard of the Uld Swan, Liverpool. The police, on being called in, ascertained that he was dead. The occurrence is believed, to have been the result of an accidental fall. William Morewood, a person who had obtained several sums of money by falsely representing that he was heir to the Alfreton estates, Derbyshire, Was on Wednesday sen- tenced at the county sessions to nine months' imprisonment for that offence. At the annual meeting of the Manchester, Salford, and District Temperance Union, held on Monday night in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, it was reported that much good work had been done by the Union within the past year. 7,000 pledges were taken during the twelve months. RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR DUBLIN—An accident by which several persons were seriously injured occurred on the Dublin, Wicklow, and Wexford Railway on Wednesday morning, at Blacktock, a short distance from Dublin. Thirty-five persons were injured, though none seriously. Some of them were taken to the hospital, but it was not found necessary to detain any there. SUICIDE ON THE RAILWAY.—A shocking discovery was made on the Midland Railway at Brightside, near Sheffield, on Tuesday morning, when a carter, named Cottom, found the body of an old man cut completely in two on the line. The deceased, George Robinson, a labourer, it is supposed, lay down deliberately on the track of the night express, as he had previously been heard to speak about poisoning him- self. MRS. WELDON AGAIN.—In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Manisty and Mr. Justice Watkin Williams gave judgment in the application of Mrs. Weldon to have a new trial of her action against Dr. Forbes Wins- low for trespass and libel, in which she had been non-suited. Their lordships granted a new trial, and condemned Dr. Winslow's action in taking part in the proceedings for the removal of Mrs. Weldon to a lunatic asylum. SUPPOSED SUICIDE ov A Crum—While fishing in the river Aire, near Keighley, on Wednesday morning, a man found the body of a girl in the water. It was removed by by the police to Keighley Workhouse, where it was identified as that of a girl named Ada Crossley, 11 years of age, who had been missing since the 17th March. The deceased had been reprimanded by her parents for some misconduct of that day, and is supposed to have committed suicide. PERSECUTION OF Scaoraas.—At the quarterly meeting of the Manchester and District Committee of the Liberation Society, held at the offices, 4, St. James' Square, on Tues- day, Mr. Jess Boyant in the chair, it was unanimously re- solved, on the motion of the Rev. Principal A, Holliday, seconded by Mr. John Mather, "That this committee hav- ing in 47iew the fact recently stated in Parliament respecting the flogging of scholars at a National school for attendance at a Dissenting chaPel, and haying observed that this is by no means a solitary instance of petty persecution on reli- gious grounds, respectfully urges upon the Education De- partment or the Government the necessity of adopting some measures to prevent such scandalous abuse of authcrity in schools supported by grants of public money."

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 12, 1884.

"Sound the loud timbre! !" the Franchise Bill has passed the second reading, and with a majority of 130. That there would be a substantial majority nobody doubted who was not wilfully blind to the situation, but that the majority would be so large is more than the most sanguine expected. What a stag- gering blow it must be to the Toy party, who have been "fooling round" the Egyptian question in the vain hope that the Cabinet was going to pieces, and that a dissolution was imminent! It is time that they looked' facts fairly in the face and realised that the country is not to be trifled with, and that the emphatic decision of Monday night is no more than a reflex of the opinion of the nation. When Mr. Gladstone was returned to power by a triumphant majority at the last General Election, the Conservatives, as soon as they had recovered from the dire shock, comforted themselves with the assertion that "the happy family," as the Liberals were called, would lead such a cat-and-dog life that the Ministry wouldn't hold together for twelve months. But they are still alive and hearty. in the fifth year of office, with a majority on this question of questions, of, let us repeat, 130. l'his is very gratifying to one side of the House, whatever it may be to the other, and is some consolation for suf- fering from the indirect but persistent Ob- struction which has alike distinguished and discredited the conduct of the Opposition. But, perhaps, it will be said "This is shouting before one is out of the wood—there is the House of Lords." And so there is, but will they dare to throw out the Bill ? They may do it once, but they will not repeat the opera- tion, or the question will ins antly and seri- ously take hold of the public mind as •to whether they themselves should not be "thrown out." English people are long-suffering and slow to anger, but, once in arms against an abuse, they do not let the matter rest until a remedy is pro- vided. They are not good to move, how- ever, until there is a practical difficulty, and they are just now in such a frame of mind as to the Upper House that there need only to be an extra bit of stupidity to make way for a drastic reform of that "respectable," if not r6pected, old-time Temple of Obstruction. Mr. Burt, in speaking on the Franchise Bill, revealed a suggestive fact when he said, "In any meeting of working men of the north of England the mention of the Bill would be received with applause not less enthu- siastic than a reference to the necessity of reform in the House of Lords." He used in this case a two-edged sword— drawing blood from the Lords on the one hand and cutting down those of the Com- mons who have had the hardihood to say that there was no demand far the measure. The debate has been like the division—a good deal on one side. The Tories—to put it plainly—have been "cornered ;" the Bill

for adding Two Millions of electors to the present Three Millions is so grand in its sim- plicity that there has been no shirking it without showing that it was a shirk They no more like an extension of the franchise than they did twenty years ago; but, as a party, they do not now, as then, oppose it out-and-aut. There is here and there an un- sophisticated fossil like Councillor Franccrnb, of Warrington, who has ventured to speak of the measure as "a humbugging Franchise Bill which nobody wants to know anything about ;" but the older hands have acted on the cynical axiom that language was in- vented to conceal thought.' Nobody ex- pects a great speech from Sir Stafford North- cote as leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons; but even the Tories must have been disappointed with the effort he made on Monday night. He evidently felt himself in an equivocal position, and •there is therefore an air of unreality about everything he said. He approached some- thing like a point when he urged that it was not a question of trusting the people, but of trusting the Government. But why did he not go further and say whether he could trust the people in this matter—whether he was prepared, if opportunity were given him, to bring in what in his judgment was a better bill, but with the same object—that of widely extending the suffrage? It was not that such an issue was not before him—he has been repeatedly challenged in the course of the de- bate to say whether or not he is in favour of enfranchising these Two Millions of her Majesty's subjects; he is silent on the main issue, and the only inference that can reason- ably be drawn from silence under such cir- cumstances is that he dare not give an answer. It was left to a Liberal, or rather a Whig, to make the best opposition speech ; Mr. Goschen ventured to say what he thought, and what the Tories thought, but what as a party they could not bring them- selves to say. His speech may be summed up in a single phrase—distrust of the Two Millions about to be enfranchised ; and the Tories let it out that they agreed with him by cheering him at every turn. He wants to know what chance there is that the principle of the protection of minorities would be heard in a Parliament elected on the new franchise, and he corn- , plains that the Government are silent in this matter. He wants the "minority vote" ex- tending and applying to Ireland; but this is a " fad " of which sensible politicians are tired, and we must confess that No should be ashamed of the Government if, after seeking to put Ireland on the same foot- ing as England, it was proposed to stifle her. voice by applying a gag in the shape of a "minority vote.' It should always be kept in mind in considering the franchise question as it relates to Ireland that the people of the sister isle have all along had a special grievance in the matter, inasmuch as, front = a difference of qualification, the number of electors is absurdly small as compared with England. Take, for instance, the Parlia- mentary borough of Warrington ; with 3 population, roundly speaking, of 45,000, there' are some 7,000 electors on the rolls; while Cork, with a population of r 04,000, has less. than 5,000 electors And this is no outside instance; it is fairly typical of the shameful disparity as to representation which exists between the two countries--a disparity that the Liberal party have twice sought to get rid of by a spe,cial bill which has been twice rejected by the Tories in the House of Lords. Let Irish elect Ors note these things, and note, too, that the Tories cheer Mr. Goschen when he suggests the necessity of checks upon the, fair and free exprecsion of opinion in Irelana under the new Franchise Bill. Mr. Goschen asks, and he is again applauded by the Con- servatives, if they did not "sea that democ' racy at eve 7 turn was the beginning to clutch' - the arm of the Executive power ?" This sounds alarming, but what does it reallY mean? Simply that the people are taking the power in their own hands which by right belongs to them. Byron said more than a generation ago: Methinks I hear a little bird which sings— The people by-and-by will be the stronger. That "sweet by-and-by" is close at handr and, although Mr. Goschen and the Tories may dread it, the Liberal party do not hesi- tate to say they rejoice in it; it is what they are striving by the Franchise Bill to promote, for it means "government of the people, for the people, and by the people."

MILL BROW WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—In connection With this society a public meeting Was held in the school- room, on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. John Wittington. The children gave recitations in a very creditable manner, and the Sunday school brass band per- formed several selections of music. The Rev. George Hack and others delivered speeches. Mr. S. Pope presided at the harmonium. RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL SOCIETY.—The last meeting Of the present session took place on Tuesday night, when the Rev. George Hack lectured on " Scientific confir- mation of the Bible," and an interesting discussion took Place, the lecturer being opposed in his views by a young man who was a stranger to the members. Mr. James Craig presided. At the conclusion of the meeting a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Craig for his services as president during the past year. THE ACTION AGAINST WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.—It Will be seen from our report of the meeting of Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, that Mr. Jeffreys. the late contractor to the sewerage works, has commenced an action against the Local Board for damages, which amount to about £5,000. Mr. Higginsoe, the surveyor, and Mr. Copeland, the resident engineer, are also defendants to the action. Mr. C. Russell, Q.C., M.P., ha e been retained on behalf of the defendants, and the case will be heard at the next Manchester assizes. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A BOATMAN AT RUNCORN.—At the Coroner's Court, Liverpool, on Wednesday, Mr. Clarke Aspinall held an inqeiry touching the death of Thomas Burgess, aged 65, a canal boatman. On the sth ult., the deceased was proceeding with two flats frrin Runcorn to Manchester, and when near Delph Bridge, Runcorn, on the Bridgewater Canal, injured himself by getting his leg en- tangled in a rope, which suddenly snapped. It was found that his leg was broken. Subsequentey he was removed to the Royal Infirmary in Liverpool, where amputation of the limb was deemed necessary. He rallied somewhat Satisfactorily for a little time but died on Saturday last. Medical evidence was to the effect that the death of the deceased was due to exhaustion consequent on loss of blood after arriputw ion. The jury returned a verdict of " Acci- dental death." RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—At RtIllOWll County Court On Tuesday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, Joseph William Smith, surgeon, Weaverham, brought an action against John Bailey, of Aston Arms inn, Sutton Weaver, umkeeper, as administrator of Elizabeth Riley, late of VVeaverham widow, deceased. Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, Who appeared for the plaintiff, said he had to ask the court for an order that an account might be taken of the personal estate of Elizabeth Riley, and that the same might be ad- ministered under the supervision of the court. The defend- ant did not appear, and after the judge had amended the Plaint by making all creditors of Elizabeth Riley plaintiffs, and directed Mr. Fletcher to advertise this order, the order as prayed by Mr. Fletcher was granted. The other cases were not of public interest. The cause list comprised 100 original plaints and 25 judgment summonses. ADULTERATED MILK AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Sarah Norman, who keeps a farm at Penketh, was summoned on a charge of having sold adulterated milk—Mr. J. T. Allen appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Local Board ; Mr. J. O. Swift defended.—Mr. Allen said on the 16. h March Mr. Dickson, the inspector of nuisances to the Local Board, Purchased a quantity of milk from the defendant. A sample Of the milk was tested, and he (Mr. Allen) had a certificate from the analyst, who stated that upwards of 24 quarts of water had been added to every hundred parts of milk. There was, however, an informality in the summons, and it had been agreed between Mr. Swift and himself to withdraw the case on the payment of the analyst's fee of half a guinea and the costs of summons.—Mr. Swift concurred in • this course, adding that the defendant thought she had a good defence, as she had never added any water to the milk. HO'wever, there was the analyst's certificate.—The costs, amounting to 175., were paid, and the case was per- mitted to be withdrawn. WATERING WHISKEY AT RutecOnN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Martha Saunders, landlady of the Fleetwood Arms, Church-street, was summoned for selling Whiskey which was not of the substance and quality demanded.—On the 21st February P.C. Bossons purchased a pint of whiskey from the defendant, and on the 27th of thesame month Superintendent Williamson submitted a sample to Dr. J. Carter Bell, the publrc analyst. The analyst certified that the whiskey contained 29 per cent, of water, or 4 per cent, more than is allowed by Act of Parlia- Ment.—ln answer to the Bench, the defendant, who pleaded guilty, said she always purchased the spirits from the same Merchant, and then she 'let it down" according to her own judgment, and not according to any legal method.—The Rey. E. A. P. Campbell said these sort of mistakes must not be made; the public must be protected. If people Worked by rule of thumb, whether in milk or spirits, the Public would be defrauded. The penalty for this offence Was a heavy one, hut considering that the defendant was a . widow, they would reduce it to las and costs; total, £2 ld_ S.

- STONING A. CONSTABLE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police 'Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Holbrook Haskell, jour. ,(Chairman) and Mr. F. H. Gossage, Patrick Darlington, a rough looking Irishman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Snowdon. On the . Previous afternoon the prisoner was causing a great disturb- mice in Miltoe-road, near to his own house. P.C. Snowdon Went towards him with the object of remonstrating with him, when he threw several bricks at him and then ran into hie own house. After locking the door he went upstairs, and from the bedroom window threw bricks and missiles at the Officer. A crowd of about 200 persons assembled to wit- ness the affair, and P.C. Snowdon moved a short distance ray. Emboldened by this the prisoner left the house and , „.?ilowed him up the street, throwing brickbats and stones. vae of the stones struck the officer on the leg. This out- ?pens conduct had been continued for about three quarters an hour, when three other constables arrived OR the scene. surrounded the house and broke open the front door, while the prisoner was captured as he attempted to escape through the back door.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's hard labour without the option of a fine for the assault upon the c)nstable, and imposed a fine of ss. and Costs for being drunk and disorderly. HOLY WEEK AND EASTER IN THE CHURCHES—At ft ate or n Parish Church, on Maundy Thursday, there was evensong and sermon by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, MA., incum, bent of Weston Point, and Litany of the Blessed Sacrament. Good Friday: 10-30 a.m., Matins, Ante-Communion office- and sermon by the Rev. R Edwards. .3-0 p.m., Litany and sermon by. the 111 v. T. M. Armson 7-30 p.m., evening prayer and sermon by the Rev. J. Madden. At the close of the service the 51st Psalm will be sung as an act of confes- sion and penitence. Easter Eve: 8-0 a.m.-.-festal evensong and sermon by the Rev. T. M. Arrnson—hymn 122. Easter Day, April 13h, 8-0 am., first celebration or the Holy com- munion. 10-30 a.m., matins; anthem, Christ is risen (Hol- loway.) 11-30 am., second celebration (choral) of the Holy Communion and sermon. 3-0 p.m., Litany and catechising. 4-0 p.m., Churchings and baptisms. 6-30 pm, evensong and sermon. Anthem, "This is the day" (Cooke.) 8-0 p.m., third celebration of the Holy Communion.—At Widnes Parish Church there will be short services held on each even- ing during the week. Good Friday, 10-30 a.m.," Behold the man ;" 7-0 p ii, "Dead." Saturday, April 12, Easter Eve, "A new sepulchre." Easter Day, Sunday, April 13th, 7-30 a.m., Holy Communion; 10-30 a.m., service and Holy Communion, "He is risen ;" 8-30 p.m., service and Holy Communion, "Peace be unto you." Easter Monday, short Service at 9-30 a.m. Easter Tuesday, short service at 9-30 a.m. DEATH OF A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN IN AMERICA.--Tho „ death is announced of Mr. James Riley, at Waunakee, Wis- "nsio. The "Wisconsin State Journal" of March 14th has the following notice :—" Waunakee, March 12.—Mr. James Riley was prostrated early last Friday with hemorr- hage of the stomach. Medical attendance was quickly pro- cured, bait). Spite of all that could be done for him he sank rapidly, aid breathed his last on S tturday morning. Mr. Riley May properly be termed one of the old settlers of tDane County. He was born in Cheshire, England, March "tilt 1832 ; came to Wisconsin in May, 1846, settling in the town of Springfield. in this county, where he resided until the spring of 1872, when he moved into the village of Waunakee. While yet quite young he married Miss Euphemia Ford, daughter of Mr. James Ford, of Fordville, by whom he had eight children, of whom seven are living. Mr. Riley had held the various town offices of clerk, town treasurer, and justice of the peace. He was also deputy Sheriff for five years, and had ben notary public for some Years. He was a member of Harvey Lodge, No. 126, 1.0.0. F., under whose direction the burial services were conducted with appropriate ceremonies. Mr. Riley was a an of unimpeachable honesty and integrity, fearless and outspoken iu the cause of right and justice, a man of large heart and generous to a fault; he had his failings, but who amongst us has not? We will forget his faults, while we remember his virtues."

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT WIDNEB—Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Water- loo Vaults, Wellington-street, Widnes, touching the death of a child 10 weeks old, the son of Samuel Pemberton, a tinsmith, living at 20, Barnes-street. The child was found dead in bed on Sunday morning, and there were indications that it had died from convulsions.—The jury returned a verdict of Death from natural causes, probably convul- sions." RUNCORN GROCERS IN THE POLICE COURT.—h t Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Mr. Henry Reynolds, Peter Briscoe, grocer, Bridge-street, was summoned to answer a charge of carrying out bread without the proper weights and scales in order that the bread might be weighed.—The manager of the shop appeared, and said the carter had neglected to put the scales in the cart.—P.S. Lowndes proved the selling at Hallett of bread which was not weighed.—Mr. Campbell said. the Bench would look upon the offence as an oversight, and only impose a penalty of is, and costs 98 6d.--A similar penalty was inflicted upon Edward Johnson, grocer, Church. street, who has also establishments at Widnes, St. Helens, dm., whose manager, Mr. Blair pleaded guilty. It was an oversight that the scales were not put upon the cart. IfUNCORN PARISH Cnuncte—ln consequence of the death and funeral of the Duke ot Albany, signs of mourning were displayed in Runcorn Parish Church on Sunday. A deep black fringe hung from the prayer desk, each panel containing an ecclesiastical device, wrought in white on a black grout d. Above the central panel vvas a hatchment on which was incribed "Leopold Duke of Albany, 1884," sur- mounted with a ducal crown. The communion table was covered with a black cloth, on the frontal of which was the sacred monogram, boldly executed in white velvet, the north and south sides of the frontal being denoted in the absence of the orphreys by maltese crosses and feur de its in the same material. During Saturday and Sunday the bells tolled muffled peals. The pulpit was occupied on Sunday morning by the Rev. R. E twards, who preached from Ist Corinthians, xi., 23,24, and 25 verses. He alluded to the death of the Duke of Alb tny as a national leas, and said that had God granted him a longer life he would have made an undeniable mark on the more defined phrases of his country and his age. Special hymns were sung by the choir and congregation. TEMPERING JUSTICE WITH MERCY AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. E. K. Muspratt, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, Annie Whalley, landlady of the Blackburne Arms, Warrington-road, Lugsdale, Widnes, was summoned on twe informations laid by P.S.McGregor, charging her with per- mitting drunkenness on her licensed premises, and also with selling intoxicating liquor to a drunken parson.—Supririn- tendent Barker said on reading over the depositions he found that the case was not a very bad one, and he was in- formed she was a widow, and that this was the first com- plaint against the house. She unfortunately happened to go out on the day in question, and left a Man in charge of the house who had perhaps done what he ought not to have done. This was the first offence Mrs. Whalley had committed, and if she would be mere careful in future he had no objection to withdraw the informations, providing she would pay costs.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, said he appeared for the defendant. What Mr. Barker said was true. This woman had kept the house since her husband died two years ago, her husband having previously kept it for eight yehrs ; and she was struggling to keep a family of seven children. He hoped the course suggested by Mr. Barker would have his Worship's approval.—His Worship allowed the charges to be withdrawn. He hoped it would be a warning to Mrs. Whalley. RUNCORN SHOOTING CLUB —The first competition of the season for the "Challenge Cup" took place on Saturday last, on Runcorn Heath. Conditions seven rounds at 200, 500, and 600 yards, Wimbledon targets and scoring. The day was rather bad, there being a: strong wied blowing from the left and a variable light. *Appended are the scores :

P,erpoint l4 2 0 16 Private G. Littlemore Sergeant JW. Woodland PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—A meeting of this body was held on Thursday, Mr. W. A. Meadows pre- siding. The medical officer (Dr. Hall) reported that at the. present time the health of the district was most satisfac- tory. Complaint was made of nuisances arising from the want of proper drainage at'Ditton, and the member for that townsnip (Mr. Gilbodv), the surveyor (Mr. Twist) and the clerk (Mr. Hartley) were instructed to report generally on the sanitary condition of the township.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board forwarding £l7O in res- pect of a moiety of the salaries of the medical officer and the nuisance inspector. Mr. Newsome gave notice that he would move the reappointment of Dr. E. F. Hall as medical officer at a salary of £l3O a year. —Mr. Syder drew attention to the fact that a part of the township of Knowsley was obliged to get water from a ditch in consequence of a pump belonging to Lord Derby having got out of order. The surveyor was instructed to report on the subject.—The Surveyor having suggested the purchase of 100 pails for use in Whisten and Eccleston townships, where the tub and pail system is in operation, Mr. Leather- barrow strongly protested against the further continuance of the system, and as the cost of supplying the pails con- stituted a township charge, he moved that the matter be re- ferred to the township committees.--Mr. Newsome seconded the motion, and it was agreed to.—This biting the last meet- ing of the year, a vote of thanks was, on the motion of Mr. Leatherbarrow, seconded by Mr. Newsome, given to Mr. Meadows for his services as chairman during the year. Rotecome Bomar, BOARD—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Offices, on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. James Handley, J--Pe Presiding. There were present— Messrs. W. Whittaker, H. Coleburn, T. Norman, W. H. Rogerson, P. Briscoe, W. F. Salkeld (secretary).—Finance : The Chairman read the report of the Finance Committee, which stated that the fees received during March amounted to £43 18s 10d. There had been piid—Wages £lO 34 9d, sundrieS 19s, auditors' fees £2 2s, paid balance into bank £3O 14s Id. Sundry accounts amounting to £9 3s had been examined and passed for payment, and interest due to Mr. John Hazlehurst on April 11th, £23 10s, was ordered to be paid.—Annual Statement: The Secretary's report stated that the interments for the year ending March 25th were 324, corresponding period last year 370; decrease 55. The fees received during the same period amounted to £367 Oa 6d, last year £379 16s 3d; decrease £'l2 15s 9d. The total interments since the opening of the cemetery were 6,399.—8a1ance Sheet: The Chairman read the annual balance sheet, which it was decided to advertise in the local papers, on the motion of Mr. Norman. The Chairman ob- served that the total debt on the Burial Board would be paid ' off in 30 years.—Mr. Rogerson's Election: The Chairman welcomed Mr. Rogerson to the Board, and hoped he would be as useful in connection with the affairs of the Burial Board as he had been in connection with other matters con- nected with the town. (Hear, hear.) He thought it would be advisable if the Board confirmed the appointment, as there was some little doubt exprossed by Mr. Coleburn whether the meeting was held in time. Mr. Coleburn : That is set at rest now. The Chairman :If we confirm the ap- pointment it will prevent any questionieg. On the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, the appoint- ment was confirmed.—There was no further business. THE SIMON ELOPEMENT: THE PRISONER COMMITTED. —Before the Rev. E. A. P. Camping' and Mr. Henry Rey- nolds, at Runcorn Petty Seseione,'on Monday, John Lo kett, a middle aged man, was brought up on remand charged with having on the Ist April stolen boots, bed linen, child- ren's clothing, crockery, cutlery, dtc., the property of Wm. Pcvey.—The prosecutor said be lived at Sutton, near Frod- sham Bridge, and was employed an a labourer at Weston Charcoal Works. For two veers the prisoner had lodged with him. On Monday morning be went to his work at four o'clock. The house was then in its ordinary condition, but the prisoner, who was night watchman at the Charcoal Works, was not present. When he (witness) returned home at eight o'clock on Monday evening he found the house de- serted and in darkness, while the drawers had been emptied hi swif wife and of their contents, and the beds bad been stripped of their clothing.He children, was unable n to t he discoverfollowing the whereaboutsmornng,fro of information he had received, he took out a warrant for the Prisoner's apprehension. On Thursday, in company with P.C.Egerton, be went to Manchester, and f •ni saner and his wife and seven children, ow" the or three of whom were the prisoner's, living together ins house there, The articles produced were in the prisoner's possesßmn. —Wm Bennion, stationmaster at Halton, said on Monday, the 31st March, the prisoner asked him the charge for sending Manchester, and he informed him. Next morning he brought the three boxes produced to the station, and said he had disposed of the furniture. Mrs. Povey and seven children were with him, and tickets were purchased for all the nine by Mrs. Povey. They travelled by the 10-6 train.—Sarah Hardy, pastry cook, 44, Lower Bryom-street, Manchester, said on the let inst. the prisoner, Mrs. Povey, and seven children occupied three rooms at her house—two bedrooms and a sitting-room and bedroom combined. The prisoner and Mrs. Povey occupied the last-named room for two nights. The prisoner brought the boxes to the house.— P.C. Egerton deposed to apprehending the prisoner in Man- chester.—ln answer to the charge, the prisoner said : Soon after I went to reside with Mr. Povey he accused me and his wife of berng in the parlour together. That was a false ac- cusation, but in order to injure my character he went and told it all over the town that such a thing had been done. That has been the cause of us eloping together.—The pri- soner asked the Bench to deal with the case. He thought a small fine would meet the case. He did not take the goods with a felonious intent, but as he was taking the wife and seven children he thought they wouid want something. (Laughter.) He did not abduct them; they were consent- ing parties.—Mr. Campbell said the law would not permit the Bench to deal with the case, and the prisoner was com- mitted to take his trial at the next Chester Qinarter Ses- sions.—As be was being conveyed to the cells, the prisoner shouted to Mrs. Povey, who was in court, "Cheer up, Mary." (Loud laughter.)
