A NEW RATE you RIINCORN.—On the application of Mr. W. Sutton, the assistant overseers, the Runcorn magi- strates laid a pools' rate of 10d in the for the township of Runcorn. It was estitnate4 to realise £2,125. WESTON PoINT NATIONAL SeimLs.—The Committee of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Liverpool Branch) have awarded a priz3 each to Clara B. Clark and William McLean, two scholars attending the above schools, for the excellence of their essays on" Kind- ness to animals," sent in at the late competition a month ago. A WIDNES THIEF AT WARRINGTON.—At the Warring,ton Borough Police Crurt on Monday, Andrew Walsh, a disreput- able-looking man, was charged before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. John Fairclougk with stealing a coat at Widnes.—From information received, P.C. Chantler and Sergeant Bowen went in search of the prisorpr on Sunday night, and found him at a house where another man was wearing the meat in question, which was one that had been stolen from Widnes. The man who had the coat said that the prisoner had lent it to was remanded to Widnes.
ELECTION OF GUARDIANS FOR THE RUNCORN

UNION. As previously stated, the only townships in the Union where contests took place in connection with the election of Guardians for the Runcorn Union were at Runcorn and Weston. For the five vacancies at Runcorn there were 14 nominations, but these were reduced by withdrawals to eight. The candidates supported by the. " Works " party were Messrs. W. Whittaker, T. Norman, P. Speakman, W. Fisher, and S. Taylor, and on Mmday, when the voting papets were distributed, there was a strong canvas in their favour b 7 the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Mr. W. Handley fought his battle single-handed, and the same may be said of Messrs. J. Williams and S. White. There was very little electioneering literature issued. The voting papers were collected on Tuesday, and counted at Du ton Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. 'Henry Linaker, the clerk to the Board, being the returning officer. At four o'clock in the afternoon the result was declared as follows:— T. Norman W. Whittaker W. Ilandley P. Speakman 646 W. Fisher B. Tayl,r J. Williams 8 Whita 142 The first five are elected. We may point out that the number of votes for rtuncorn might be considerably in- creased. Parsons possessing property vote as owners for Commissioners and members of Parliament, but they can- not exercise the same right in parish elections unless they make a special claim. Very few owners in recent 'years claimed to vote as owners for the Guardians election, and hence many votes am lest. For the information of our readers we may state that all claims should be sent in to the Overseer before the let of February each year, giving the particulars of their ownership. The necessary forms can be obtained, we believei on application at the Overseer's office. The contest at Weston resulted in the return of the Rev. Canon Barclay with 255 votes, and Mr. E. Aaron with 163 votes. Mr. R. Clark, the defeated candidate, received 145 votes.

I of damage caused to their property by the nightsoil con- tractor and of abusive language used by him. The con- tractor denied having made use of abusive language. He was cautioned as to his future conduct. The committee recommended that a vote of thanks and an honorarium of £lO be given to Mr. Dickson for his extra services during the outbreak of smallpox ; and that votes of thanks be passed to Dr. Cooper and Dr. O'Keeffe for their services during the late late outbreak. With respect to the public Cemetery and Infectious Diseases Hospital sites letters were read from Rev. J. Wright Williams, the Rev. G. Bond, and the Rev. T. Finegan. The Market Superintendent re- ported that the receipts for the month amounted to £22 17s 9d, being an increase of £1 118 41 as comparee. with March, 1883. Eight shops were now let, and the stalls were doing better. A vote of thanks was passed to Dr. O'Keeffe kr his services as chairman during the year. —Dr. O'Keeffe moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded the confirmation 'of the minutes. Mr. Midwood said complaints of the nightsoil contractor's neg- lect cf his duties were of monthly occurrence, and he sympathised with the committee in having such a man. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Board should take some ac- tion to stop him from damaging property. He was very glad to see that the committee had recognised Mr. Dickson's services; he thought he ric'ily deserved the £lo.—ln answer to a questioe, Dr. O'Keeffe said the letters from the rev. gantleinan with reference to the cemetery, contained infor- mation as to the number of interments in the churchyards and the present accomrnod ition, but they were of a private character. He paid a high compliment to Mr. Dickson for his labours during the smallpox epidemic, and referring to the nightsoil contractor, said it was his (Dr. O'Keeffe's) dis- agreeable and painful duty to censure him month after month. If certain proof was brought before the committee they would take action, but it was a difficult matter to ob- tain proof of damage, and the committee had to centent themselves with reproving the contractor. The minutes were passed. FINANCE.—The Finance Committee had passed a vote of thanks to Mr. Handley for his servic-s as chairman during the year. Accounts amounting to £2,845 17s Id were re- commended for payment —The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Wright. THE COPYTIOLD ENFRANCHISEMENT BILL—The General Purposes Camtnittee.had received a letter from the Corpora- tion of Accrington, enclosing copy of their petition in favour of this bill, and asking for the Board's co-operation. It was recommended that the representatives of the bill be asked to support the bill,—Dr. O'Keeffe moved, and Mr. Sadler seconded, the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was carried.

ATIaIBUTE TO TEE CHAD:MAN.—At the conclusion of the business, Dr. O'Keeffe said he had great pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman of the Board for his services in the chair during the year that had just terminated ; for the courteous manner in which he had treated every member of the Board—(hear, hear)—for his great patience in attending to the public business of the ratepayers of Widnes; and for the efficient manner in which every duty devolving upon him had been carried out. He (Dr. O'Keeffe) knew that Mr. Gossage had devoted a great deal of his time, which was important, to those duties, and he was exceedingly pleased that Mr. Gossage had by the unanimous desire of the members of the Board and the outside public as well, consented to allow himself to be again nominated as a member of the Board. There was a universal expression of feeling amongst the people of the town at the result of the election and the number of votes that were given to him indicated that feeling very strongly. But independantly of that he believed, and almost every member of the Board believed, that the free manner in which discussion had been allowed, and the excellent har- mony that had prevailed amongst the members of the Board, vras chiefly owing to the way in which the chair had been filled. He had, therefore, great pleasure in pro- posing that the members accord a hearty vote of thanks to their Chairman. Mr. Wright rose with great pleasure to second the resolution. He could fully endorse everything that Dr. O'Keeffe had said. He was sure that the Chairman's patience on many occasions had been most remarkable—he had exercised a greater amount of patience than some of the members could have or would have exercised if they had had the power. It gave him (Mr. Wright) groat pleasure to have had the pri- vilege of sitting under so able a chairman. (Hear, hear.) Whether he had learned to be better or whether he fancied the chairman himself had been better, he thought Mr. Gos- sage had been a much better chairman this year than be was last, and he felt confident that he would make a better chairman next year than he had even made this year. (Hear, hear.) He did not think anything would give the members greater pleasure than to see Mr. Gossage occupying the chair of the Board next year.—Mr. Handley, in sup- porting the motion, said when Mr. Gossage took the office of chairman two years ago he followed in the footsteps of one who had been conversant with the Board's business for many years, and who was a model chairman: Mr. Gossage had a very difficult task in following a gentleman of such great business capacity and ability as chairman. In the chair they needed a gentleman who had courtesy combined with firmness and decision, and he need not say that Mr. Gossage had shown the members every courtesy, and while allowing great latitude in debate, he had known when to show firmness. In every sense, be had realised the expec- tation of every member of the Board.—Mr. Midwood said be could not allow the proposition to pass without saying one word in its support. It had been a pleasure to him to sit at the Board during the last two years, and he felt thank- ful for the courtesy he had received from Mr. Gossage.—Mr. Houghton and Mr. Sadler also supported the motion, which was then put, and carried by all the members rising to their feet, and applauding heartily.— The Chairman thanked the members for the kind way in which they had recognised his endeavours to carry out the duties devolving upon him as chairman. If at any time he had appeared harsh to any member of the Board he was sorry. He had only sat there to carry out the business in the most efficient way he knew how; to calm irritated feel- . . .

jug and to endeavour to point to a sounder judgment than might have been arrived at. He must acknowledge that he had had greater pleasure in sitting on the Board last year than he had the first year be was appointed chairman, simply because he had had some experience, and because perhaps he had commanded his temper better. He again thanked them sincerely for their kind expression of feeling towards him. (Applause.) The meeting then concluded.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday at the Board cffices, Mr. F. H. Gossage presiding. There were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst, T. Handley, D. Wright, J. Midwood, B. Duttoo, J. Houghton, J. E. John- son, S. Sadler, B. Webster, J. F. Allen (clerk), J. Carr, and Copeland (resident engineer). AN IMPENDING ACTION.—Mr. Davies (of the firm of Messrs. Do.vies, Sharp, and Kirkconnell, Warrington) at- tended at the meeting to confer wick' the Board on the action commenced by Mr. Jeffreys, the late sewerage contractor. —On the motion of Mr. WRIGHT the Board went into com- mittee to consider the subject, and it Yri9 decided that the action should be defended at the forthcoming Manchester Assizes. Messrs. Carey, Midwood, Webster, and Handley were appointed a deputation to represent the Board at the assizes. Tux ELECTION.—Dr. O'KEETFE, the returning officer, formally reported the result of the election, observing that Mr. Gossage had received the greatest number of votes (2,229) ever recorded at any election that had taken place at Widnes. (Applause.) The total number of papers de- livered was 4,188, against 3,257 last year; filled up in the presence of the returning officer 339, last year 41; total number of voting papers made out 4527, last year 3,298; papers not delivered through change of residence 1,364, last year 935; returned blank 95, last year 280; bad votes 99, last year 216; not accounte I for 136, last year 166; the good papers numbered 2,833, against 1,701 last year. The number of voting papers made out this year was greater than last year by 1.229, and the good voting papers exceeded last year by 1,132. The expenses of the election amounted to £7O 103 4d, against £59 4s, and £64 13 8,1 in 1882. This increase in expenditure was caused through the printiag hills, which were rather heavier than usual. He asked that a cheque should be signed for the amount of the costs. On the proposition of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. HOUGHTON, the desired cheque was signed. THE BYE-Laws.—The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board, dated April 4th, referring to the conference held on the 16th November last between certain officers of the Local Government Board on the subject of bye-laws which the Local Board proposed to make The letter asked if the subject had been further considered, and

if so with what result. The communication was referred to the General Purposes Committee. THE NEW BOARD.—On the motion of Dr. O'KEEFE, the first meeting of the new Board was fixed for Friday, the 18th inst., at two o'clock. TITE GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE: GRATIFYING IN- TELLIGENCE.—The minutes of the Gas and Water Com- mittee contained the following report on gas stoves, by Mr. Carr, the manager:— I beg to direct at,ention to the continned decrease in the make of gas. Tins year shows a falling off of 11 per cent, as corm ared w,th the year 1880; and with the view o, remedying this. I would recommend fr consideration the desi, ability of keeping a stock of gas cooking and heatiag stoves, and other apparatus for sale or hire. It is a system which is nwr gener- ally adopted by gasworks throughout the country, and 1 know of no piece where the system is ia vogue, that has not oem adequately remunerated by the irPreised sale of gas attending Its aoostion, bes des giving satWaction to the consumers. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 16.23. For the erection of the extra Netherly buildings the following tenders were received —5. Collins and Sons, £593 15s 7d; B. Balsham, £697 ss; T. Sadler, £565 103; and J. B. Walsh, £575 14s 9d. It was recom- mended that the tender of T. Sadler be accepted. A vote of t'sanks was passed to Mr. Panktturst for his services as chairman during the year.—ln moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. Pankhurst said: I wish, as this is the end of the financial year, to make a few remarks respecting the results of our year's working. It must, I am sure, be a source of pleasure to the members of the Board, as well as to the ratepayers at large, to know , that the waterworks this year will realise a considerable profit, and for this desirable condition we have to thank a , combination of circumstances. In the first pi ace the deter- mination of our committee to exercise the strictest economy in the management of the works, and in this matter we have been ably seconded by our officials, principally Mr. Carr and Mr. Allen, and then in the enormous saving in waste water, and finally and principally the increased use of water for manufacturing purposes. This latter item we look upon with pleasure and satisfaction, as it is positive evidence of the improved state of trade in our town. With reference to the gas works, I am pleased to be able to say that we shall realize a greater profit than we did last year, ' notwithstanding the loss sustained by the fall it the price of ammoniacal liquor consequent upon the continued de- pressed state of sulphate of ammonia ; also in the reduction of gas, gas meter rents, &c. The amount of gas tratde during the year is 69,302.000 cubic feet, being a decrease on the previous year's make of 2.2 per cent., but although there is a decrease in the quantity made we have every reason to beliete that when the accounts are made up it will be seen that we have an increased sale of gas, as compared with the previous year, and a..consequent reduction in the gas leakage. The new system of carbonizing continues to work satisfactorily, and has effected a great saving in coke and stoker's wages in the year. and has also given an in- creased quantity of gas per ton of coal carbonized. We have carbonized nearl.oo tons of coal less this year than last, but owing to the introduction of the new gas washer, which was put to work in August, last year, we have an in- creased make of the residual products—tar and ammoniacal liquor; and the cost of purification is reduced to about one- half, so that the whole cost attending the erection of the washer will be cleared before it has been at work 12 months. —Mr. Wright seconded the motion—The Chairman said he was strongly of opinion that the suggestion to offer facilities for buying gas stoves was a move in the right di- rection. The cooking at his house was done altogether by gas, and had been for the past nine years, and was a saving, while he was of opinion it would be a greater saving in a smaller house than his.

The minutes were paesed. THE LEVEL CROSSING NUISANCE.—The Highway Com- mittee had received a letter from Messrs. T. Bolton and Sons asking for permission to close West Bank-street; con- sideration was deferred.—lt was recommended that the Appleton property be offered to Leigh's trustees in payment of amount due for land for road improvements, and that the tender of Mr. D. Hirst for the lengthening of the culvert in Lugsdale New-road be accepted.—Mr. Midwood reported that many complaints had been made to him of the delay caused through shunting at Waterloo-road level crossing.— The surveyor instructed to attend and report.—The plans f three houses, Milton-road, for Mr. James Hulme • three lock-up shops, Wellington-street, for Mr. Brewis, subject to a slight alteration in the ashpit ; temperance mission rooms, Hibbert-street, for Mr. T. Reav and others, subject to the foot-wall being made 14 inches in thickness, and to have two brick pillars each, 18 inches by 41 inches, and the floor to rest on sleeper walls only, were approved. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Midwood for his services as chairman during the year.— Mr. Midwood, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said there were many complaints made with respect to Waterloo- road Crossing. The gates were often closed for periods of ten minntes, causing a great stoppage of passengers and vehicular traffic. The crossing was becoming a great nuisance. He did not think the obstruction was caused by the company, but by the man in the signal box, who was not at all careful. The other day a man had his hand crushed in the gates, and a person walking over the crossing had the gates sent against his back. Ile thought the atten- tion of the company ought to be called to the way in which their servants were treating the people at the present time at the Waterloo-road level crossing. Alluding to the work of the Highway Cemmittee during the past year, he said there had been 474 yards of flagging done.Bs yards of channel stone laid, and 657 yards of kerbs fixed. The committee bad not had the benefit of the Surveyor's assistance for five months owing to his sickness and the law suit the Board had in Lon- don, and taking this into consideration, be (Mr. Midwood) thought they had done very well. The committee had taken over 7,860 yards of land free of cost in various parts of the township, and it could be used at any time.—Mr. Handley seconded the motion, and observed that the gates at Waterloo-road Crossing were kept closed very much longer now than formerly. He hoped the Board would instruct the Clerk to write a strong repre- sentationto the Railway Company about the matter and thrt some alterations would be made.—Mr, Midwood said he forgot to state that the amount of money allowed the High- way Committee for the year was £3,500, and out of that had been expended £3,096 Os. 10d., leaving a balance of £471 19s. 2d. (Hear, hear.) He moved that Mr. Allen be instructed to write a strong letter to the London and Nertlii-Western Railway Company calling attention to the frequent stoppages at Waterloo-road crossing.—Mr. Houghton seconded. The minutes and the motion were passed. TILE HOSPITAL.—In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Hospital Committee, which contained nothing of pub- lic interest, Mr. Sadler said he had no elaberate report of the year's work to lay before the Board. He was inclined to think that the less work done in the hospital the better, bnt he might point to the fact that it had been conducted succeesf ally during the past year, and it had fulfilled all the expectations that were formed of it, while the expenses were under the estimates. THE SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.—The minutes of this Com- mittee stated that there bad been received lett-rs dated the sth and 10th March from Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., enclosing copy of statement of claim made by Mr, Jeffreys, I and stating that W. W. Copland and T. Higginson were joinecLas defendants in the action. It was recommended that Messrs R. Davies and Co. be instructed to defend Messrs. Higginson and Copland.—Mr. Midwood moved the confirmation of the minutes, and observed that the two sewerage contracts were proceeding very satisfactorily.— Mr. Dutton seconded the motion which Was carried. div.head: CHEMICAL TRADE OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE CHEMICAL TRADE OF WIDNES.

IMPORTANT ASSESSMENT DISPUTE. A dispute of unusual importance, taking the form of an appeal against an assessment, and affecting indirectly the entire chemical trade of Widnes, has been proceeding by arbitration, at the Mitre Hotel, Manchester, during the last three months. The arbitrator is Mr. Edge and the appel- lants against the decision of the Assessment Committee of the union are Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., the leading chemical manufacturers of Widnes. Their appeal was male to quarter sessions, and as questions of value and of the con- dition of trade were iavolved, the appeal was referred to Mr. Edge, who has sat on various occasions during the past few months! The works of the appellants were assessed in 1872, when the trade was said to be most prosperous, at upwards of £B,OOO. An appeal to the committee at Prescot was made against this amount in 1882, when the committee sent their valuer, Mr. Joseph Raby, to the works to revalue them. Instead of inducing their valuation, he increased it to £B,OOO, which was confirmed by the committee; hence the appeal and the protracted arbitration inquiry. Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. have been represented by Mr. Walton (instructed by Messrs. Simpson and North), and the Assessment Committee by Messrs. Leresche, Smyley, and Swift. A large number of scientific witnesses, valuers, and experts have been called on both sides in the course of the inquiry, which concluded on Tuesday with a speech by Mr. Leresche, which occupied nearly two days. Mr. Walton, in the course of his address for the appel- lants, stated that the structural valuation of the works, ac- cording to their witnesses, was £69,814, and according to the evidence for the committee it was MOO ; but he pointed oat that, in consequence of the introduction of a new system of the manufacture of soda by a patent ammonia pro- cess, which was much cheaper, the old Le Blanc process, as in operation at the Widnes works, was to a large extent su- perseded; the extent of the trade had greatly decreased, and the profits were not so large as they had formerly been. The fact that the prosperity of the chemical trade had been largely shaken must have a very considerable bearing on the question of the assessment of the works. He contended that, under all the circumstances, the valuation of the appellants laid at 3P a yard was much too high, and 24 a yard, the value deposed to by their witnesses, was ample. The , valuer (Mr. Raby) had arrived at the structural value by considering the amount of mosey invested in the premises, and he had confused that with the beneficial value, and he Ral in conflict with a number of witnesses who were, to say the least, quite as competent to express an opinion. Mr. Leresche, in concluding his vary exhauetive speech for the respondents maintained that the valuatien was a fair and reasonable one, and that the statements as to the loss of trade were all vaticinations and not realisations. If they turned out to be realised, and if Widnes became a howling desert, the rateable value of the works would, of course, be reduced, as there would be no Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. to assess. The new ammonia process that had been spoken of only affected a small portion of the trade carried on by the manufacturers at Widnes, and he anticipated that the trade would go on there as elsewhere; and he hoped the objectors to the assessments would have good reason to be satisfied, although they might not get a reduction of their rates.—The arbitrator promised to make his award at quarter sessions at an early date.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION. -This annual contest concluded on Saturday, when the votes were counted by the clerks of the Board at the offices, Alforde Chambers. The work was commenced about half- past nine under the supervision of Mr. J. T. Allen, the clerk to the Board, and considering the obsolete and cumbrous method of voting, was finished in good time. The returning officer, Dr. O'Keeffe, was assisted in his responsible duties by Mr. C. H. div.head: DARESBITRY-
div.p: DARESBITRY-

FORCIBLE LEY! or TITHES.—We are informed that another instance of the forcible levy of tithes has occurred near Daresbury. Mr. John Derbyshire of Stretton, who is a member of the Society of Friends, like so many of his co- religionists and others, has conscientiously objected to the paymeat of tithes which are levied upon him on behalf of Christ Charch College, Oxford. For the last three half- years no unusual pressure has been brought to bear upon him to secure the payment of these charges, but on Wed- nesday last, whilst Mr. Derbyshire was away from home, the authorities made a raid upon his goods and chattels, and carried off a spring cart and a calf. These were, we , understand, taken to Northwich, where they will no doubt I be held a few days, and then sold to defray the ecclesias- tical claims. The amount of tithes charged was .£4 1s sd, while Mr. Derbyshire estimates the value of the articles ap- priated at £lO la&

div.head: HIGHWAY BOARD MEETING.
div.p: HIGHWAY BOARD MEETING.

A meeting7ii—thai;loard was held in the Court-room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. There were present Messrs. T. Bennett (in the chair), C. T. Whitley, Joseph Cooper, and H. Houghton; H. E. Linacre (clerk), and John Darbyshire (surveyor). A DISPUTED POINT.—The Clerk read a report by the surveyor with respect to the condition of the road from Dutton Lodge to the Sutton Weaver about which complaints had been made to the Board by Mr. Cox, of Dutton Lodge. The whole length of the road, the report stated, was in a very good state of repair, and, with slight exceptions, where new material had been put on its surface, was in good con- I dition even for pedestrians. With regard to the portion of I Mr. Cox's letter in which be alluded to the making of the cindered footpaths, he (the surveyor) would state for the Board's information that about one-third of the length of the read from Dutton Lodge to Sutton Weaver bad already footpaths in good condition; that one-third was unsuitable owing to its narrowness for setting apart a footpath one length of which has within the last few years become so by a new fence having been planted and thereby reducing the width of the road by about seven feet less than the statute width. The other length of the road might have a footpath made on one side of it if the Board wished it.—lt was re- solved to leave the further consideration of this report over to the next meeting which will be the first meeting of the new Board.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.
It is characteristic of Parliamentary work in the present days that on the ive of the Easter recess the House meeting for a morning sitting on Tuesday should have sat far into
Wednesday morning.
Within the last few years the whole

conditions-of Parlii-mentary life have changed. It is still a green and pleasant meniory of the times when for at least a fortnight, sometimes three weeks, after the House first met it used to adjourn at about eight o'clock, never later than ten. In those days the Address was frequently hgreed . . . - .

to immediately after the speeches of the Lea'ders 'on -both sides, just as it is now in the House of Lords. To remain over dinner on the first night of the meeting of Parliament was altogether unprecedented, and a shocking thing. At the !same time, whilst the hours were short work. went
steadily forward. Bills were brought in, of course without opposition, debates on second readings were brief, and real discussion began in its proper place, in Committee. There
was no such thing as bl'ock'ing, and 'though .obstruction was
not unknown its exercise was reserved for really great fights—on the Reform Bill for example, on Church rates, " ' ' •
or—on kindred topics.

These halcyon days have fled probably never return. The change commenced with the incursion of the Irish members after the election of 1874. Supposing Parliamentary his- tory were assisted, as ether history sometimes is, by excava- tion, the New Zealander digging round Westminster and

„ coming upon the bones of Mr. Biggar would know he had reached the particular stratum from which this change dates. The House has never been the same since Mr. Biggar entered it. Not that he personally is an influential person, but the change has been contemporaneous with his appear- . . . . . . . .

ance and is in the direction of his nature. It is wit the House of Commons and the member for Cavan as the lover in " Locksley Hall "declares it is with man and wife— Thou art mated with a clown. And the grossness of his nature will have weight to drag thee
down. What is wanted now, as _would be promptly admitted any- . . . .
. . - where out of the House of Commons, is that, since the con- ditions of life in the House have altered, the conditions which control life must also be changed. Of :that there is

no present prospect. Mr. Gladstone will have no more tinkering with the Rules of Debate whilst he leads the House, and there, for the present, is an end of the matter. But Lord Hartington is very strong on the point; so is Mr. Chamberlain, so is Sir C. Dilke, and so doubtless are other members of the Cabinet. One of the first things we shall see when Mr. Gladstone seeks retirement is a thorough

reform of procedare in the House of Commons. In the meantime we must stagger and blunder along with what we have got, thanking heaven that _the Speaker is showing increasing signs of aptitude for his place. He has very wisely laid down for himself the rule to begin slowly. He is feeling his way and I think he is finding it. Certainly he came best out of the scene at midnight on Tuesday. Ac- cording to their habit the Irish members were enjoying a row on the eve of the recess. It is part of their tactics al- ways to go home to their constituents covered with the glory of having outraged order and decency in the House of Commons. Mr. O'Brien had been up, and " Wind- bag " Sexton had been pumping out vituperation by the i hour. Then Mr. Healy appeared on the scene, and it is a ' family boast that "no one can beat Tim." He had a Blue Book with him, from which he read long speeches, inter- spersing them with remarks conveying the most abominable charges against Mr. Trevelyan and Lord Spencer. Mr. Trevelyan is hard to move, but Mr. Healy's assertion that he was smiling at a description of the dying agonies of some , young patriot in Mountjoy Prison stung him to the quick. ' "That is an absolute falsehood," said Mr. Trevelyan, dis- tinctly. It was pretty to see how shocked the Irish mem- bers were at this plain language. Mr. Biggar bounded on his feet and groaned in anguish. Mr. Sexton and Mr. O'Brien were on their legs together, gesticulating. Mr. Healy was bellowing out to the Speaker, and that pink of courtesy and good breeding, Mr. Harring- ton was shouting " Shame! " The Speaker in- terposed to protest against the accumulation of violent language which Mr. Healy had indulged in. " I , thought you got up," said Mr. Healy, when the Speaker concluded his dignified rebuke, "to call the Chief Secretary for Ireland to order." Mr. Trevelyan, with the instincts of a gentleman admitted that he had been led into the use of the language

which he regretted, and here the matter seemed to close But Mr. Healy, with his cool audacious pertinacity, rose again and going back to an earlier point insisted upon hay. jug the Speaker's ruling on Mr. Trevelyan's indignant remark. But the Speaker was not to be drawn off on this false scent. He pinned Mr. Healy to a retrospect of his own conduct, and declared the point of order settled. Again Mr. Healy returned to the charge after his manner familiar in the times of Sir Henry Brand. "Well, you have settled , the point of order to your own satisfaction," he said, with I an insolence of manner intensely aggravating the speech, and having fired this shot was going on with his reading. But the Speaker would not let this pass, and peremptorily warned him of his danger. Another word and Mr. Elealy would have been suspended. But he knows bow far he may go, recognised that he had now reached the limits, and pro- ceeded with his extracts, leaving the Speaker the master of the situation. It is to be hoped that the result of this encounter will encourage Mr. Peel. Like all bullies, these outragers of order in the House of Commons are cowards, and cringe before a firm front and the certain prospect of punishment. The death of the Duke of Albany is not to be allowed to postpone by very long the marriage at Darmstadt. On Monday the Queen sets out for Germany to be present at the ceremony, which will not in any respect, other than that of the absence of the hapless young Duke, be shorn of the presence of Royal personages. The exaggerated and melodramic circumstances alleged to have occurred upon the receipt by the Queen of the news of the death of her youngest son were promptly contradicted, and uadoubtedly were the figment of the brain of a local reporter at Windsor. Nevertheless the condition of the Queen is by no means satisfactory. Before this sad blow came she did not feel herself strong enough to put in an appearance at the second drawing-room, which was held on her behalf by the Princess of Wales. For some months past Her Majesty has been subject to fits of extreme depression. For a whole day she is in most melancholy mood, and the next resumes her normal condition of health. These fits have naturally be- creased and been prolonged since the death of the Duke of Albany. The Qaeen will, of course, not join in any public festivities at Darmstadt, the wedding being made as quiet as possible. She will stay at Kranichstein, a quiet place about three miles out of Darmstadt. Here she will be visited by the Emperor and the Empress of Germany and the Empress of Austria. The Czar is expected at Darm- stadt towards the end of the month. The postponement of the Budget till after the Easter re- cess is an eve& of rare occurrence, and testifies to the dif- ficulties of conducting business in the House of Commons at the present time. It is a course which imposes much in- convenience upon business men who are left in doubt as to how the proposals may affect their affairs. Happily, or in Isome sense null ippily, the state of purturbation this year Is lens coasiderahle than usual. I mentioned some time ago the report, then current, that Mr. Childers would be able to take a penny off the income tax. Since then the anticipated surplus seems to have vanished into space, and the most hopeful expectation at the present time is that he will make both ends meet, carrying forward a small sur- plus to next year. One thing that affects current circum- stances is the ineradicable habit of the Liberal ministry to pay their way. Sir S. Northcote, had he found in his time the national finance in the present sound condition, might I have been able to remit taxation, spreading th Egyptian expedition over several yeatis,ore costs of the banding it over bodily as a legacy to his successor. The present Govern- ment have paid out of revenue !very penny incurred, and will make provision forel of debt hitherto clearing off all con- tingencies. As usual, many propositions for raising taxa- tion are submitted by amateur .i Chancellors of the Ex- chequer. One of ths most attractive s the imposition of a duty of a shilling per cent: upon speculative transactions on the Stock Exchange. It is estimated that these reach the aggregate sum of £5,0 0,000 in the year, and the proposed tax would yield a pretty revenue from the pockets of a class who can well afford to ray. The new stamps, running from a halfpenny up to five pounds, are now current, and present perhaps the ugliest and meanest agglomoration, whether of design or colour, ever submitted to a long.suffering publit. It is a remark- able thing that with boundless money at their command (which means the power of appealing to the highest art) the Post Office have within the last half century only effected a single improvement in the postage stamp, and that was rather in the direction of utility than of art. The change from the old red postage stamp with its thick, mucilage— popularly but horribly said to have as its basis old poultices brought out of the hospitals—was a decided improvement. Beyond that we have never got. The new stamps, issued fora purpose that no one can conceive, are of weak washed-

coloutours, whilst the Queen's head, crammed within an enlarged border, is inexpressibly mean-looking. It reproduces the girlish head on which the crown was placed now nearly half a century ago, an anachronism said to be due to pre- judice in high quarters against a more faithful representa- tion of the royal lineaments of to.day.
It is hard to conceive on what ground this objection is

_ . -- --- based. It in quite modern, as anyone can see, by comparing coins of the time o! the Georges, who openly grew fatter and balder and more wrinkled as the years passtd. It would seem that the coinage and the postage offer a unique and valuable portrait gallery in which might be prePerved the face of the sovereign through inicceeding epochs of years. This is recognised in the United States, where, as a special tribute, the counterfeit presentment of General Gar- field as he lived, is impressed upon the five cent stamp and handed down to all posterity. Comparing this stamp in respect of historical interest, or the French head of the Re- public on stamps and coins as a work of art, we have good cause to be ashamed of the pitiful collection of stamps now issuing from the post office as the highest outcome of its mature deliberation.

There is always a conundrum orjeu d esprit in verse go- ing the round of the Benchea of the 'louse of Commons. This week's riddle is naturally suggested by a recent trial. "Why was Annanias told to stand fort h ? " is the question. Answer: "Because the other three were Yates, Labouchere, and Bowles." This will require a little thinking - over, but it is really very good. The point will be best caught br repeating the question aloud, with emphasis en the (set word. The jest is plainly, at least as far as Mr. Yates is concerned, a subordination of the impression of fact to temptation to be smart. The feeling in the house of Com- mons as elsewhere is that Mr. Yates has been hardly dealt with, a view deepened and widened by the publication in the current issue of the World of his temperate and convincing setting forth of facts.

Ouida has reached the eminence of Mr. Ruskin, Mrs. Henry Ward Beecher, and other personages not to mend= Shakespeare. A handsome volume hai just been published containing flights of "Wisdom, Wit, and Pathos," selected from her works. Some clever people have a habit of sneer- ing at Oujda, and it must be admitted that some of her fre- quent references to classical history and personages are not so exact as they might be from one who presumably has Lempriere on her bookshelf. But Ouida can afford to smile in response as long as she commands such a vast circle of readers as she boasts. She is still at work, Messrs. Chatto II and Windus now having is the press a new novel of hers, called "Princess Napraxine." If it is only as good as " Wanda," it will coFnplete the proof that Ouida, so far from having written herself out, is improving.

THE WIREDRA.WERS' STRIKE. Sir.—Will you allow me through the medium of your valuable paper on behalf of my fellow workmen and myself to thank the public of Warrington for the valuable and generous assistance they have rendered to us during the present trying time, when through no fault of our own we have been obliged to ask for hop. The response to our appeal has, so far, exceeded our anticipations, and we sin- cerely trust it may be continued, as Mr. Henry Thornton has generously premised that if the labourers and iron- workers combined can raise £75 he will give us another £25. When I state that there are 130 labourers and 84 iron- workers-214 in all—compelled to be idle, much against their will. I feel sure that the public will appreciate this kind offer, and will help us to raise the required amount.— I am, yours truly, SAMUEL DUNSOBBIN, Secretary.

div.head: RIIRAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: THE RIIRAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Sir,—From the report in your paper it is satisfactory to notice that at last the Rural 6anitary Authority have been roused from their lethargy, and, though not in office I am evidently in power, and as long as I have the great privi- lege of living in their district they shall not aid or abet in the sacrifice of human life ignorantly. The medical officer (the man after their own heart) even supports all I have said, and at last the Chairman is beginning to learn the ele- ments of sanitary science, but a death rate of 50 per cent. in typhoid fever is not a pleasurable recollection. It seems, however, to the ex-member for Penketh that because I have ceised to be medical officer of health for the district there- fore my opinions and statements are untrustworthy. I was unmuzz!ed " long before I knew Mr. Garnett, and if he will take the trouble to read my annual reports for 1881 and 1882 and my monthly ones for 10 years past, he will find even stronger statements than those that appear in my letter to the Local Government "bard, and I hope also that they will remind him of what little assistance he was to the offi- cials of the Rural Sanitary Authority during his long term of office —I am, yours, &c, JOHN H. GORNALL. Penketh Lodge, Warrington, 11th April; 1884.

THE ST. HELENS (BOL14) MANURE WORKS. Sir,—Some person has sent me copies of The St. Helens .Exansiner newspaper of the 15th and 22nd instant, in which my attention has been directed to the prosecution and con- viction of the owners for a nuisance at the works of the above-named premises by the Corporation of St. Helens. I think it a great pity and mistake that such works as these should be allowed to become a nuisance to the public in any shape or form, and unless these works are so reconstructed as to utterly remove all ground of complaint, the owners are certain to be pounced upon with redoubled determination should an opportunity for doing so again occur. I note that evidence has been produced to show that "everything has been done to obviate a nuisance that is usually done." Moreover, the inspector under the Alkali Act says "he does not know any boiling or glue making works which were free from nuisance, but he was of opinion with regard to the defendant's works that they were as well constructed and conducted as any other works of which he had cogni- sance." That may be quite true. I know nothing of the gentleman's experience in question—but I make free to say this is net sufficient—in cases of this kind. The cause of offence ought to be entirely subdued, and no half-measures should be accepted. In matters concerning the public health and comfort, I think it right that those having experience, should give the benefit wherin they have found successful remedial measures. Having had a large experience in works of this description, is my reason for troubling you with my experi- ence and the results. In the year 1865, on my appointment to the management of one of the largest chemical manure works, etc., in the neighbourhood of Glasgow, the company had been in the court for some time for a similar nuisance to that of the Bold Manure Company—besides at the same time Messrs. Packard, of Ipswich, and J. B. ',awes, of Lon- don, were likewise in court, all for similar offences. I made it my business at once to visit both of these establishments and was shown all they had done to comb it the evil com- plained of, on the understanding that they should benefit by the result of my investigation. Both had laid out large sums of money in making experiments to overcome the escape of noxious gases from their works, but neither had conquered, though they had greatly modified the evil. Hay- ing seen where their shortcomings lay, I was thereby en- abled to form a decided opinion, and at once devised a plan which turned out a complete success. In the first place I saw that a re-construction of the works was absolutely necessary tograpple with the evil which must be dealt with, like every other sanitary measure, at the fountain head. I had, by this time, learned how fallacious it was, first, to construct water-closets to convey from our dwellings human excreta and urine, and then at great expense, independent of the nuisance, endeavour to extract the ammonia from a multitude of sewage. So with noxious gases—there must be no egress found them to get outside, and that all cause of offence be entirely sub- dued, there must be no room left for accidents or machinery out of order to perform a nuisance. To secure the end I had in view I prepared plans, which were approved, and carried out under my personal supervision. These embraced the manufacture of sulphuric acid, all kinds of manures, even guano from collections at public works, of excreta and urine, bones, green ancl dried, the slaughter of horses and Cattle, and all followings, sulphate of ammonia, 011.53 isphalte, etc. In the construction and arrangement of departments' I kept very specially is view that from no part must their escape one atom of gases or noxious vapours, each and every house being so constructed that any escape was in- stantly caught, returned to its own chamber and utilised, or conveyed by attractive power to the position assigned for gases considered unworthy of utilisation, nothing whatever being allowed to escipe outside. The late Professor Penny often complimented me upon our "Model Works," as he termed them, and never to this day have I heard of cause for complaint. It is an extraordinary fact that in the majority of cases an entire overlook of all sanitary laws has been too long the prevailing system in the erection of chemical and other works from whence noxious vapous and bad gases may be expected to generate. I speak from a long period of varied practical experience in dealing with chemical works of various descriptions, and have made upwards of 7,000 tons of sulphuric acid and used it myself in the manufacture of guanos in one season. Many of my experiments being of a revolting nature, I have satisfaction in stating these have been carried out free from nuisance, while at the the same time with much greater safety and health to the workmen employed in the manufacture. Moreover, lam thoroughly satisfied, and do hold, that no work of whatever kind—even such as you experience at St. Helens need be, nor has any right to be, a nuisance to the neighbourhood, if constructed an managed on proper scimtific principles. Independent of a greater degree of health to the workmen employed, the very utilisation of gas eecaping to the out- • side and blown with the wind, would go far to pay the cost of a reconstruction—besides giving satisfaction to all con- cerned. I mast apologise for these lengthy remarks, bat the im- portance of the subject, and the interest I have taken in sanitary matters, induced me to give my views on the sub- ject. JOHN BEGG. Manchester-road, Bolton, Lancashire, March 29th, 1884.

Form MEN KILLED AT A SHIP LAIINCII.—ShortIy after one o'clock, on Wednesday, a number of men were engaged placing launchways under a small steamer in the yard of Messrs. Allsnp and Sons, Preston, ready for launch- ing. The vessel slipped off the blocks, azhi crushed five of the men, named Lupton, Wilson, Holmes. Dickinson, and Melling. In a quarter of an hour all were got from under, Lupton being dead. Wilson, Holmes, and Dickinson were conveyed to the infirmary badly injured, and Dickenson died ti)ere. On Wednc iday night, Richard Melling, car- penter, succumbed to his injuries at the infirmary ; and on Thursday morning, at ten o'clock, Isaac Wilson, labourer, ale ) died, making four deaths. An inquest was held on Thursday on the bodies. The jury returned a verdict 91 "Accidental death."

SUPPOSED CONCEALMENT OF Etum.—On Thursday morning, at the Lymm Police Court, two young women named Mary and Sarah Forrest were charged, before Mr. Henry Stanton, with endeavouring to conceal the birth of a female child, of which one of them, Mary, had been de- livered. The body, which was much decomposed, was found in a drain on the premises where the prisoners lived. They were committed to the next Chester Assizes for trial, substantial bail being taken. LYMM Low. BOARD ELEcrrox.—The result of the elec- tion of members of this Board was made known on Saturday afternoon by Mr. H. Cameron, the returning officer, as fol- lows :—Mr. Samuel Appleton, master fustian cutter, Brook House, Statham, 542 votes; Mr. Thomas Woolley, gentle- man, Heatley, 490; Mr. James Gibbon, yeoman' Camsley, Lymm, 496; Mr. George Hall, gentleman, Oak Lea, Statham, 480; Mr. Thomas Richardson, gentleman, Statham, 286. The first three gentlemen were declared duly elected. Lout, GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY AT Lt.—On Thursday week Mr. J. F. Harrison, an inspector of the Local Government Board, held an inquiry at Lymm into an ap- plication by the Local Board to borrow the SIM of £1,650 for works of sewerage and sewage disposal. In 1882 an application was made to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £7,156 for sewerage works, bet on an in- quiry being held the amount recommended by the inspector was reduced to £6,586. The work had been proceeded with, but unforseen contingencies necessitated a number of extra charges' which amounted to £1,193 143 lid. The new loan weuld make an addition to the rates of fid in the pound, and it was remarked that a rate of 2s in the pound would cover the Board's expenses. FREEMASONS AND TFIE LATE DUKE OF ALBINV.—At a recent regular meeting of the Earl of Chester Ledge of Freemasons, held in the Masonic Hall, Lyme, immediately after The opening of the lodge, the Secretary, Bro. J. H. Evans, P.M., proposed "That the brethren of the Earl of Chester Lodge, now assembled, desire to express their heart- felt sorrow at the painfully sudden death of Prince Leopold, George Duncan Albert, Duke of Albany, and beg most re- spectfully to convey to her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen, his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Duchess of Albany, and the rest of the Royal family their sincere sympathy in their very painful bereavement, and to assure them that the brethren of the Earl of Chester Lodge (unswerving in their devotion) are at all times keenly alive to whatever affects their intereks, and sincerely de- sire their happiness." The resolution being very feelingly seconded by the J.P.M. Bro. Sudlow. and supported in ap- propriate terms by the W.M. Bro. Kenworthy, was unani- mously carried.
