div.p: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETING AT LATCHFORD.

The annual meeting of the Conservatives of the Latchford Ward was held in St. James's Schoolroom, Latchford, on Tuesday evening, when there was a moderate attendance. Captain S. Reynolds, J.P., occupied the chair, and amongst those also present were Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Harrison), Messrs. John White, Henry Greenall, John Lee, R. Kern, George Woods, T. Barber, T. Ashcroft, W. J. Burgess, J. V. Taylor, R. Isher- wood, Joseph Grine, T. Sutton, W. Dickens, W. S. Abra- hams, W. Wallace, R. Pierpoint, George Cropper, John Hartley, John Roberts, J. B. Buckton, W. Bennett, John Hartley (hon. sec.), and John Hampson (Coneervative agent). The Cuatiarate, in opening the meeting, said that on the occasion of every ward meeting they had held they had oc- cupied a schoolroom for the purposes of the meeting. He thought a schoolroom was a vary good place, inasmuch as in that room were taught a good many Young people to fear God and honour the Queen. (Hear, hear.) He hoped and believed and trusted that no young children who were brought there would be brought up with those ideas which were held by Mr. Bradlaugh, who believed in no future state. With regard to that meeting, it was more for organisa- tion than for speaking. They knew there had been a bill lately posed called the Corrupt Practices Bill, and that bill would not permit them, as had been done before, to pay people to help them at times of an election. Therefore they who had the cause of Conservatism at heart must give them good voluntary aid. ,In Sir Gilbert Greenall they had a man from whom they might expect many acts in Parliament. If Sir Gilbert had not been heard in Parliament, as the other party were always very fond of saying, he could only ask what their present member had done to be heard within the walls of Parliament He made it no complaint that the present member had not spoken because he thought if there were less said and more done they should then get many acts that wanted passing in Parliament. He (the chairman) saw there were some remarks made in a newspaper in the town which he did not think worth their while to take much notice of for when people could not make Use of argument they usually used abuse. So in the present case. He thought it was for them to so they did not believe in protection; they did not believe in putting any taxes upon any of the necessaries of life, but it was a question for them whether a commission of inquiry into the causes of the pre- sent bad trade was necessary or not. He believed it was, and he believed a lot of working men in this town and other industrial towns would think the Same. If there was nothing wrong, if there was no cause for change they had done no harm, but a search- ing inquiry would lay bare many Oings which at that moment they were possibly not aware of. The trade of the country was one of the greatest things they had to live by, particularly in towns, and, therefore, it must be one of the things that they must look after. At the time when the elections Came he had no doubt that the Govern- ment which would give up their time to searching and in- ' vestigating these things would be worth more than a Govern- ment which would not listen to them. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. WILLIAM DICKENS moved "That the undermentioned constitute the officers of the Ward Committee, delegates to the council of the Conservativ. Association, and Executive Committee of the ward—viz., Captain S. Reynolds, J.P. (chairman), Messrs. John White, J.P., James Moore, W. Tinsley, J. Woolfall, and J. Jones (vice-chairman) ; John Hartley (hon. secretary), and Messrs. William Wallace, T. Ashcroft, William Tinsley, William Whaley, William Dickens, and Thomas Wright (delegates)." The resolution also appointed a representative committee. As, Mr. Dickens continued, the chairman had told them they were now under the Corrupt Practices Act, but if they were under it, their Radical friends were equally *tmder it. He believed it wonld tell against them (the Radicals) much more than against the Conservative party. Take Warrington, for in- stance at the last election. They all knew how money was distributed—he was going to say in bushels, but it was given in handfuls to various people to distribute amongst the voters. They knew perfectly well what took place in Latchford ward. Mr. Dickens then referred to the Ship- ping Bill, with which, he said, Mr. Chamberlain wanted to ruin entirely a very great industry in this country. The Government, he added, had brought in the Franchise Bill to cover a multitnde of sins—to cover themselves with a cloak of iniquity. Mr. JNo. HARTLEY seconded the above proposal, and

Mr. JNO. LEE supported it. He said they (the Conser- vatives) had the advantage of having a very good candi- date. Then they had another great assistance—that was bad trade. (A laugh.) Bad trade they knew played a very important part in the last election. He had no doubt from his own observation that it perhaps did more than anything else towards turning the late Government out of power. If it was a good argument then it certainly ought to be a better argument now. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GEORGE WOODS moved the following resolution "That this meeting pledges itself to do its utmost to return Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, to Parliament as member for this borough at the next election." Referring to a letter written by Mr. F. Flood, Mr. Woods said that Mr. Flood was a most estimable man. He was a pattern working man, a man who in his spare moments was ever trying to do good, but he was a Radical, and, like everybody else when they got talking about subjects they didn't understand, they were sure to put their foot in it. The object of his letter was to damage Sir Gilbert Geenall in the minds of the working men of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He said "without being considered impertinent he should like to 'know what Sir Gilbert contributed to the welfare of the town of Warrington and the country." He (Mr. Woods) was astonished at Mr. Flood, who was a man of intelligence ; he was astonished that the proposition he put forward in the form of a question should contain such am amount of ignorance. He might ask in the sense that Mr. Flood put the question, "what did the present member contribute to the welfare of Warrington ?" He was not going to say one word to the detriment of their present member. He con- tributed to the welfare of another place, and therefore con- tributed to the welfare of the country, that was to say to the national wealth. But no man in his senses would have asked the question relat;ve to Sir Gilbert Greenall. Sir Gilbert was an employer of labour in the firm with which be was associated. The wages paid by the firm were spent amongst the shopkeepers of the town. Again, Sir Gilbert was a shareholder in Parr's Banking Company, and banks were very necessary now-a-days to enable manufacturers to extend their works and pay the wages of their workpeople. Every shareholder in a bank contributed his proportion to the wealth and the welfare of the town. Sir Gilbert Greenall was a shareholder and director of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. which gave, it may be,employment to thousands of men. They also knew that Sir Gilbert was a large landowner. He (Mr. Woods) did not know how many farms he had, but be had no doubt that if all the families of the farmers and the workmen employed upon the farms were in that room they would be a very gopdly com- pany. (Laughter.) When they came to consider that every article for the sustenance of life—whether it was for comestibles or whether it was for the rent— hey must go to the nearest town to provide it. There was no subj• rt about which more nonsense was talked than the land question. It would be a bad thing for England when the land fell into the possession of paor landowners. It was necessary that the land should be kept in the highest state of cultivation, and it was net possible to do that unless the owner had large capital. The result was when such was not the case that there were a certain number of people in the country and they required a certain quantity of food, and if the land -was not made to produce as much as it was possible the I deficiency of produce was to be supplied from elsewhere, and the buyer had to pay the cost of the carriage from the place from where it was exported. If there was more in the country tbay. perha ,s might be absolutely required there I was a fall of prices, and they got their living the cheaper in consequence. In conclusion Mr. Woods said that another claim Sir Gilbert had upon the constituency was the fact 1. that he was a large shareholder in the London and North- Western Railway. Mr. JouN ROBERTS, in seconding the resolution, drew at- , tention to a letter that appeared in our last issue signed A North-East Ward Elector," which he proceeded to , criticise at length. This " North-East Ward Elector," he said asked his Liberal freinds to be up and doing and not to forget the laurels that they won in 188(1. This elector said that if they were up and doing and did not forget those laurels they would get their c indidate in -by double the majority that thcy had b fora. He (Mr. Roberts) was never aware until now that they bad any laurels, and if any were gained by them they were not gained honestly, which he was prepared to prove. lie could only say that laurels
THE EXA.WINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 12, 1884.

gained in such a way as those were most disgraceful, and they as Conservatives would have been sorry to have sent Sir Gilbert Greenell to Parliament with any such disgrace- ful laurels. He maintained that the laurels of the Liberals were not gained honestly, and said that I e was prepared at• any moment to prove his assertion. This writer referred in another part of his letter to a gentleman who had mili- tary honours, and he thought they would all guess who was referred to. It was a gentleman against whose name there was not one in the tewn of Warrington would put a black mark. When they had such a gentleman to lead them, he thought it was quite enough to give them encouragement to follow his eximple, and he was thoroughly satisfied that he was a gentleman who would never deceive them and who was a credit to the town of Warrington. The writer in this letter referred to a cer- tain tannery with which this gentleman with military honour. was connected, and went so far as to say that it would ba as well if that gentleman with military honours would not talk so much about wiredrawers' wages, but would look after the labourers in some of the tanneries. He (the speaker) was prepared to prove to them that the writer had got hold of the wrong end of the stick, and that before he made such assertions again he should well consider what he put into the newspapers. He could prove that these la- bourer, as they were termed, in some of the tanneries at Warrington got wages second to none in any of the other firms of any description. Sir GILBERT GREENALL, speaking to the resolution, said that this was not the first occasion on which he had been present in that room, and he had always found, as he per- ceived was the case now, that he was associating with true and faithful friends. (Applause.) The inhabitants of Latchford especially—when he said especially, he did not mean to say in a greater degree than he had received kind- ness from other friends—but the kindnees, the consideration, and the feeling towards himself had never been greater or more thankfully received by himself than the reception he had always had given to him when be had been there. (Applause.) With regarl to The Examiner, he said he had never known anything of the paper, and he never would know anything of it. He thought that it had been, as he said it would be, a most miserable production from the hour of its creation to the present moment, and he thought unless it greatly improved it would expire—it would expire, a lean, wretched, and attenuated object. So much for The Examiner! He was speaking of days before the flood. (Laughter.) He did touch, he did read, the first production of The Examiner. He said to himself—and be had kept his word—that he would never either finger, touch, or read another production in that paper. He felt that he had then a good reason, and he had never regretted the decision that he had come to. Proceeding, Sir Gilbert said that no man in the neighbourhood of Warrington had expended so mach upon, the labour of Warrington as Gilbert Greenall. He had been, and he was now,most loyal to the working men of Warrington—(applause)--and not one jch had he taken from Warrington when he was not compelled by arrangements or circumstances which ex- cluded the Warrington man, to do so. He had never taken any advantage whatever, his inclination was always given towards Warrington men and there had not been a single instance where, if he could give a job to a Warrington man, that he had not done so. He said, and asked any person to disprove it, that no man spent as much money in Warrington as did Gilbert Greenall. (Ap- plause.) Well, when a flood raged, it was a most splendid thing, but there was no fuel in the flood's kettle. When the flood raged and the stream ran violently —in the case to which one of the speaker's had alluded as in all other cases—it was an irregular, agitated flood, pro- ducing nothing but a heap of rubbish. (Applause.) He was thankful to be able to say that what he had expended and what he did expend, as far as he could give a fair pre- ference to Warrington it was invariably given. As to the wretched allusion to the church at Walton made by Mr. Flood, he pitied the misery of the man who could introduce such a subject into such a letter. That was his answer to the turbid, muddy authors of this flood. (Laughter.) And now, did they intend to ivork if he intended to stick by them. No distance, no separation, a perfect combination, a perfect union, a respect and affection for each other, a con- fidence in the political creed that they held, and their cry was "no surrender." (Applause.) Their cry was charity to others, firmness amongst themselves, and the fixed, un- wavering resolution to win when they fought. (Applause.) The resoluion was then put to the meeting, and carried. Mr. Jouer WHITE proposed the third resolution, which was as follows :—" That this meeting is of opinion that the recent horrible slaughter in the Soudan, the critical position of Khartoum, the state of anarchy existing in Zululand, 'and the unsettled state of Ireland have been entirely caused by the weak and vacillating policy of the present Govern- ment." He said that there could be no darker page of his- tory written than that giving an acconnt of England's actions in Egypt and Ireland during the reign of the pre- sent Government. Her Majesty's Government had not, 80 far, condescended to reply to the many questions that had been asked as to what was their intention with respect to Egypt in the future, and what was the meaning of all the blood that had been spilled. They did not know what good was to come of the bloodshed in Egypt, but they did know that the Government was discredited throughout the country, and that it was being deserted by its own sup- porters. The Government had played their last card in General Gordon, and they had left him te his fate. If any- thing happened to Gordon it would be the last stroke of policy that the government would carry out, for, he was sate, an indignant nation would deprive them of their power. Mr. TAYLOR seconded the resolution, which was carried. Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT proposed the fourth resolution. It was "That this meeting expresses the fullest confidence in the leaders of Her Majesty's Opposition, in the noises of Parliament,and trusts that they will receive the cor- dial support of every Conservative member, in their efforts to preserve the constitution, and main- tain the true interests of this country." Although some thought, he said, that Sir Stafloid Northcote and Lord Salisbury might exercise a little more fire and go, still they had had great difficulties to contend with, and had led the party well through them. Speaking of the franchise, he claimed that the Home Rule party. had greatly swelled the majority, and voted in favour of the Reform Bill. That party seldom did anything ;or nothing, and they would find when the time came for a redistribution of seats that there had been a little Kilmainham transaction, and that the Horne Rule party had not supported the bill for nothing. Mr. W. J. BURGESS seconded, and Alderman KEAN sup- ported, the resolution, which was carried. A vote of thanks accorded to the chairman, on the motion of Captain LITTON, concluded the meeting..

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

MAY DAY—The committee of the May-day festival met on Monday last, and arranged for another day of enjoyment for this town and district. LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—The election of the members for this Board has been narrowed down to a contest in the Vale Royal Ward only. The two candidates before the public were Messrs. Garfitt (retiring member) and Mr. E. Pickstock (candidate). The papers were collected on Mon- day, and on Tuesday examined, when it was ascertained that Mr. George Garfitt stood at the head of the poll by 90. THE RIFLE CORPS.—The first of a series of competition trials as to which of this company shall represent this sec- tion of the battalion at its prin shooting and for the other county prizes took place at the range on Saturday. The firing was at 200, 500, and 600 yards. The wind was not favourable for good shots, but out of seven rounds those above 60 were as follows :—Private Reith 70, Col.-Sergeant Phillips 65, Private Bratherton 64, Private Jones, 61, Sergt. Hulse 61.

Trin LIBERAL CLUB.—There was a first-class lecture de- livered in the Winsford Town Hall on Thursday, under the suspices of the above club, by Mr. Thackney, of the National Liberal Federation. Mr. Joseph Slater was pre- sident, and was supported by Messrs. Cooke, Tolfree, Picker- ing, and the lecturer. There was an excellent attendance of the leading Liberals of the town and neighbourhood, whose hearty appreciation of the subject, "Gladstone as a model Statesman," was often shown as one good point after another was displayed. Evidently the lecturer was quite at home in his subject. The chairman, before and after the lecture, spoke warmly on the subject. Votes to lecturer and chairman were pas•ed. During the evening Mr. Hongh sang a political song, and was accompanied by Miss Lydia Atherton, who also played a solo before the lecture and dur- ing the collection in an unusual style for one so young. Mr. Cohen, from Manchester, also sang a song. OVER SCHOOL BOARD.—Meetings have been held of this Board both ordinary and extraordinary. At the first the attendance officer's report was received, showing that 1,558 Scholars are in attendance in the public elementary schools independently of those attending the private schools, which would probably raise it to about 1,700. The matters on the agenda raper were gone through, such as school clean- ing, examination, audit, petition against the sale of in- toxicating liquors en th 3 Sunday, which the Board refused to sign as not a part of the educational duties they hada to perform; the appoiotment of new treasurer (Mr. Grant) in 'place of Mr. Ellison, late of Parr's Bane ;land buying from Mr. Finney, which the extraordinary meeting of this week confirmed, subject to the auditor's surcharge. This was an extension of land to be purchased from Mr. Finney to make a separate entrance for the boys; but most important to levy a precept of £3OO, not quite 3d in the £. PRESENTATION TO MR. JOHN ASPEY.-011 Saturday, an interesting event took place in the United Free Methodist Sehoolroorn, High-street. It was a presentation to Mr. John Aspey, who has been foreman 21 years for Mr. Evans, whose slit works are at Winsford. The illuminated address setting forth his long and faithful services, together with his and his wife's portraits and a packet of cartes de visite, formed a. very handsome mark of the estimation in which Mr. Aspey was held by his fellow workmen. After hymn land prayer by Mr. T. H. Massey, Mr. John Smith took the , chair, and spoke warmly of the kind manner in'which Mr. Aspey had exercised his rule during the 30 years they had been in connection.—Mr. T. Hulse also spoke feelingly of •long and faithful service, aril praised the late foreman as a master, friend, and brother.—They then made the presenta- tion.-2 Mr. Aspey suitably responded, saying he had tried to do his duty both to the workmen and his masters. He had a good lot of workmen under him or he could not have got on as well as he had done. He should still feel an interest in them, and of en go dawn to see them.—The other fore- men, Mr. Tkomason, Mr. Heath, Mr. Hough, and Mr. Ben- nett had a few kindly words to say. Between the speeches the choir gave a few well-sung pieces, which enlivened the evening, Miss Buckley, the organist, presiding at the har- monium.
General Sir Gerald Graham will visit England in a few days on leave.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

Local. BOARD ELECTION.—Gre.tt interest has been mani- fested in the election of four members to serve on this Board, the vacancies being caused by Messrs. C. Spencely and T. S. Preston retiring in order this tear, and Messrs. J. Wycherley and J. Mawdslcy resigning their seats. Nine persoms were nominated for the four vac metes, and all went to the poll. The voting papers were delivered on Widnes- day, the 2ad of April, and collected again on Monday last, and the task of counting up the votes was begun on Tues- day morning, at ten o'clock, at the Board offices, under the superintendence of the returning officer, Mr. H. Fogg, as- sisted by Mr. H. Cross (clerk to the Board), Mr. H. Makin (assistant overseer for Prescot), and Mr. J: G. Dunn (as- sistant overseer for Eccleston). After a careful count and scrutiny of the papers, the number of votes obtained by each was declared at 5-30 p.m. aa follows :—Mr. T. Beesley, 117; Mr. J. Berry, 320 ; Mr. T. Dennett, 159 ; Mr. J. T. Hall, 368 ; Mr. T. P. Hewitt, 414; Mr. T. S. Preston, 321; Mr. T. Prescot, 144; Mr. C. Spencoly, 427; and Mr. J. Sagger- son, 189. Messrs. C. Spencely, T. P. Hewitt, J. T. Hall, and T. S. Preston have been declared duly elected by the Re- turning Officer. WORKING MEN'S SOCIETY.—The sixteehth and last popular entertainment of the season, under the auspices of this society, was given on Thursday evening week, by the Star Minstrels, in the Town Hall. The first part of the programme, which consisted of a variety of songs and choruses, was opened by the overture to the " Caliph of Bagdad," and, after an ooening chorus by the minstrels, the ballad "Chiming bells of long ago" was given by Mr. J. H. Wilson. Mr. D. Wallace next sang "PH meet her when the sun goes down ;" and Mr. J. Johnsen's rendering of the ballad " When you and I were young, Maggie," well merited the applause which was given him. The humorous song "Oh ! dem golden slippers," by Mr. W. Lorenzo, and the ballad "Wait till the clouds roll by, Jennie," by Mr. T. Nightingale, were much appreciated by the audience. After the song "The old wooden rocker.', by Mr. H. Bowen, Mr. Bryant gave the humorous song "I'll throw myself away," which was loudly applauded. During the short interval between the songs of this part of the programme, the audience were amused by the answers and sayings of Messrs. Lorenzo and Bryant, Mr. J. Johnson acting as interlocutor. The second part was opened by the quartette "Come, brothers, tune the lay," and was followed by a Darkies' ghost seance, in which Mr. Bryant played a prominent part; as be also did in the Grand Review of the Guards, under the command of Capt. Swords. A humorous lecture and discourse on "Temper- ance," which amused everyone, was given by Professor Marengo; and the evening's entertainment was brought to a close by a Negro instrumental prize contest, conducted by Prof. Johns, which created roars of laughter. The atten- dance' was rather smaller than usual, but the entertainment throughout was a decided success.

GOVERNMENT REPORT ON THE WORKHOUSE. The guardians of the Prescot Union have had under their consideration for some time the question of enlarging the workhouse buildings at Whiston, and, as the result of a representation to the Local Government Board, Dr. Monett, one of their inspectors, and Mr. P. G. Smith, architect to the Central Beard, were sent down to make an inspection, and at the fortnightly meeting of the guardians on Thursday week the report of those gentlemen was submitted. The premises, they state, comprise altogether about eleven acres of land, excellently situated on an open country rather more than a mile from the town of Prescot. The workhouse buildings comprise the original main building— cruciform in shape—with the old infirmary be- hind it. After dealing with recent arrangements for the accommodation of paupers, rendered neces- sary by the increased population, as shown by the fact that the population of the union in 1871 was 92,551, and in 1881 was 117,939. and that the children were being accommo- dated in Kirkdale Schools, the report c mcludes ;—*. Look- ing, therefore, at the question as a whole, we come to the conclusion that, as there appears to be no immediate chance of the Liverpool Poor-law authorities desiring to have Pres- cot children removed froln Kirkdale, they had better be al- lowed to remain there for the,present, and the Prescot guar- dians be recommended to increase the accommodation for adults at the workhouse. We cinnot advise that additions should be made to the main building. The old infirmary, being a corridor building, is not worth extending; and the more modern infirmary, being upwards of 300 feet long and three storeys in height, cannot properly be enlarged. We accordingly think that a new infirmary should be erected on the high ground to the east of the present work- house. The present infirmary would then become available for the infirm and old of each sex, the imbeciles would re- main where they are in the old infirmary, and the able- bodied and the younger inmates would remain in the main building. The present Infectious Hospital should be given up to some other purposes, such as accommodation for the so-called " fluctuating" children, perhaps, and a small iso- lation hospital erected for the separation of the few cases of infection that might occur in, the workhouse, or be acciden- tally brought there, for whom probably eight beds would be ample. The guardians should at the same time be advised to consider the best way of providing proper vagrant wards and improved receiving wards, new laundry offices, proper workshops, &a., audit will likewise be necessary to consider the question of improving the kitchen and scullery accom- modation, and the dining-hall, with the view of rendering them adeauate to the altered conditions of the workhause.

Mr. Meadows said it was very evident they would shortly have to move in the matter, and he saggested that the report be referred to a building committee. The Chairman (Mr. Tyrer) said the governors had placed themselves in the hands of an architect (Mr. Sumner). and he thought it might be desirable for him to meet Mr. smith and go into the matter. Mr. Hall moved that the report be referred to a building committee, to be appointed along with other committees next Board day. The Rev. T. Chambers seconded the motion.

The Rev. T. Finegan said he had heard it mentioned on many sides that there might boa movement for a division of the union in the direction of St. Helens and Widnes, and he thought if anything was going to be done in that direc- tion now was the time. It might save having to enlarge the workhouse at all.

The Ghairman said they could not take those things into consideration then. Mr. Fidler : The wise men of Widnes will look what Bosthport has done—applied and got refused. The motion that the matter stand adjourned until next Board day, and that the clerk request the Local Gov ern- ment Board to allow their architect to consult with the architect to the Guardians at the Workhouse was carried.
THE FRANCHISE BILL: LIBERAL MEETING
AT PRESCOT.

' A public meeting in support of the extension of the county franchise to all householders, was held in the Town Hall, Prescot, on Wednesday evening, under the auspices of the . Prescot Liberal Club. There was a large attendance, and 1 the chair was occupied by W. W. Pilkington, Esq.' J.P., ; who was supported by the following gentletmen :—Messrs. , Alexander Eccles (Rainhill), Alfred Crilly (Liverpool), Alan . Jones (Rainhill), W. C. Rawlins (Rainhill), G. W. Rawlins 1 (Rainhill), W. Tyrer (Prescet), W. McKenzie (Prescot), and I J. Lawrenson (secretary of the Liberal Club). The CHAIRMAN, who was warmly received, said they might think it strange that they should hold a Liberal meet- log in Prescot at the present time, seeing that , they had a very strong Liberal Government in . power, backed up by the large majority of 130. , (Hear, hear.) Yet stranger still was the fact that I thoagh they had a Liberal Government in power, I little or nothing was being done as far as actual government I of the cauntry was concerned. That was not simply strange, I but it wet a serious thing„ and it was a disgrace to the country. (Hear, hear.) The Conservative party, of all parties, ought to be that which did its best to uphold the institutions of the country for the Tory party were the most inclined to talk about the "grand old institutions." Bat Lord Salisbury, as the leader of the Conservative party in the 1 House of Lords, was the man of all others in that chamber I who had , dragged the chamber into the dirt. I Coining to the House of Commons • they would ' find that the Opposition of the irrepressible members of • the Tory party was doing all the mischief, but that mischief , was connived at by those who ought to know better—by the ;leaders of the Opposition. Conservatives talked about the I prestige of England and proudly said that the system of government in this country was better than the American, German, or French system, and yet they were doing their best to destroy that system bring it into disgrace, and make it utterly useless as a power' for the government of this great empire. (Ap- plause.) The object of it was as mean as , the means were illegitimate. It was to fritter away the last remaining years of one of the ablest men that ever ruled over England. (Loud applause.) England had determined by a large majority that Mr. Gladstone should rule over the country, and the Opposition were doing all they could in the way of obstruction to prevent it. They were simply doing it in order that they might be at last sent back to office ; but was it likely that while Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote were unable to govern their own party the coun- try would trust them with the government of the nation ? He believed not, and thought they had better put their own house in order first. (Applause.) Mr. A. ECCLEs (Rainhill) moved: "That this meeting heartily concurs with the provisions of the bill introduced by the Government into the House of Commons for the ex- tension of the county franchise to all householders." He remarked that after the overwhelming majority in the House of Commons there was very little doubt that the bill would ultimately become law. Pe did not know what would take place in the House of Lords, but he thought the members would scarcely dare to resist the wishes of the people of the country, which had been expressed so strongly by their representatives. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Gladstone had been sent to Parliament to bring about a better state of things in relation to home and foreign matters, and that he had suc- cessfully accomplished. (Applause.) Among the many questions which had been raised none was mare impor- tent than that of Reform, and the residents of the counties were quite ' justified in asking that they should be recognised as being as good as those who resided in boroughs. He held that the interests of working men in the good government et the country were quite :In great as those of men of properity, and they wanted the people, and not interests to be properly represented. (Applause.) He proceeded to ctit:cia,; at some length re- cent remarks of Sir Richard Assbeton Cross, and concluded by pointing out that when the Franchise Bill became law the new electors would have to carefully and wisely fulfil the trust confided to them. (Applause.) Mr. CRILLY (Liverpool), in seconding the resolution, ex-

plained the grounds on which the Franchise Bill could be commended to the country. The resolution was then carried with aczlim :Con. Mr. W. C. RAWLINS (Rainhill) prooosel ti next re- solution, as follows :—"That this meeting deeply deplores the organised obstruction which is being calried out by the opposition for the purpose of impeding the Progress of the County Franchise Bill through Parliament, and hopes the Government will persevere with the Bill in spite uk all op- position." He contended that the Egyptian question was I but an excuse for the Tory party to attempt to obstruct legislation in the House of Commons, for the Tories knew well enough-that when the Franchise Bill became law their chance of regaining office would be very small indeed. Mr. A. JONES (Rainhill) seconded the motion in a lengthy address, in which he pointed out that the Goverumeut were determined to persevere in the course they had laid out for themselves. Never had there been a time when the party whi,ph insolently regarded itself at the Constitutional party had been so utterly regardless of Coustitutional forms it had during the last few years. He next alluded to the benefits which would follow the passing of the Franchise Bill, and said they could look forward to its being carried to a successful issue now that they had got so far. (Ap- plause ) .

The resolution was unanimously passed. On the motion of Mr. TYNER, seconded by Mr. G. W. RAWLINS, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the speakers; and after a similar compliment had been paid to the Chairman, the meeting concluded.

HIGHWAY BOARD MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Prescot Highway Board was held at the offices of Mr. Cross, on Tuesday forenoon, when there were present—Messrs. W. L. Evans (in the chair), J. Newton, jun., Captain Willis, IL Cross (clerk), and W. Goldsworth (surveyor). THE AUDIT OF THE BOARD'S ACCOUNT. After the minutes of the last meeting had b3eo read and confirmed, ' Mr. Cross reported that the Government auditor had held his audit. There had been some correspondence with re- ference to the holding of the audit at PrescJt and not at the Workhouse. The Local Government Board thought it desirable that it should be held at the Workhouse, but he (Mr. Cross) wrote in reply that that Board thought it more convenient to hold it in Prescot in conscqn3r.ca of Living all the evidence ready that might be required at the audit, instead of having to run backwards and forwards from Pres- cot to the Workhouse. He had since received a letter stat- ing that future audits of the Highway Board's accounts would be held at Prescot as requested.—The Chairman: As a matter of fact he held it here yesterday 7—Mr. Cross: He did, and he certified that the accounts were correct. THE SUGGESTED TELEPHONE TO WHISTON.—With re- ference to the suggested telephone between Prescot and VVhiston, mentioned at the last meeting.—The Surveyor re- ported that he had communicated with and had had one or two meetings with the person who had to arrange the lines, but he held out little hope of being able to do any good, but he would submit the matter to his superiors. He (Mr. Gohisworth) had since received a letter stating that they wou'd be happy to give a quotation for a line to Whiston post office if he could obtain permission from the postal authorities.—The Chairman asked what the telephone had to do with the postal authorities.—Mr. Goldsworth : I don't think it has anything to do with them. —Captain Willis thought the manager of the Telephone Company had misunderstood the matter.—The Chairman : It really means that if you arrange with the company they will put down a telephone.—Mr. Goldsworth : Yes.—Cap- tain Willis observed that it was not to obtain facilities to his house alone, but to give facilities to the district generally—to the collieries and so on.—The Clerk pointed out that before the telephone could be placed along the highway the consent of that Beard would have to he obtained.—Captain Willis said that in the Roby district they compelled the telegraph people to put their wires under ground. They would not allow them to go through Rqby along the highway, because, as he supposed, they were a nuisance and an eye-sore to the neighbourhood.— After some further conversation it was decided to leave the matter in Mr. Goldsworth's hands, and that the consent of the Board be granted, subject to the poles being placed in positions satisfactory to the surveyor, and to their removal in ten days' notice.

THE E'STIMATES : THE STEAM-ROLLER QUESTION. —Mr. GOLDSWORTH said that he supposed it was the wish of the Board at the last meeting that a Copy of his estimate then submitted should be forwarded to the waywardens with a view of giving them an Opportunity of considering the estimates. In the estimate for the whole district he put in a sum of £135 towards the cost of a steam breaking machine.—Mr. Newton: Have we much money in hand? —The Chairman : We are owing the bank £232 now. It might be perhaps as well if we waited a little while longer until—(Mr. Newton: We are in a better position)—wo are in a bad position.—Mr. Goldsworth said he and the chairman bad had a conversation about the matter, and they had thought it might be well to leave the purchasing of the steam roller and stone-breaking machine for a year or two so that they could in the meantime get a little money in hand. By postponing it they would have some funds in hand, and they would certainly be in a better position.— Mr. Newton: We ought to have something to begin with if we are going to have a steam roller.—The Chairman : There will be plenty of time to consider the matter during the next twelve months.—Tho discussion of the estimates then dropped. This was the only business of interest.
THE LATE DUKE OF ALBANY. _ . THE FUNERAL.

In accordance with the ceremonial which had bean pro- scribed, the funeral of the late Duke of Albany took place on Saturday at the St. George's Chapel, Windsor, and was at- tended by the Queen and all the members of the Royal Family at present in England, besides many Ministers of State and representatives of foreign monarchs. The scene I was an imposing one, and the day, though occasionally showery, was, en the whole, sufficiently fine not to mar the outdoor procession and the military display. A specid train with mourners from London arrived about 11 o'clock, and shortly after that hour her Majesty, accompanied by the I Princess of Wales, Princess Christian, Princess Beatrice, I the Grand Duchess of Mecklenburg-Strelita, and Princess ' Frederica of Hanover, left the Castle for St. George's Chapel. The Prince of Wales, the Crown Prince of Ger- many, the Grand Duke of Hesse, and other Royal person• ages soon afterwards drove up to the Memorial Chapel. Minute guns announced the approach of he body, which was borne from the Memorial Church by a party of the Seaforth Highlanders, while the Guards' band began the solemn strains of Chopin's " Funeral March." The procession was led by servants of the late Duke. On the coffin rested a number of beautiful wreaths, and behind the coffin came the Prince of Wales, anpported by the Crown Prince of Prussia and the Grand Duke of Hesse. On reach- ing the west door of the Chapel the procession was met by the Dean of Windsor, who read the opening sentences of the burial service as the coffin entered. The Queen occupied a seat on the north side of the "sacrarium." The Archbishop of Canterbury, Lord Granville, Lord Hattington, Sir Wm. Harcourt, Lord Oalisbury, and Sir Stafford Northeote occu- pieti the knights' stalls on the north and south sides. When the Prince of Wales had reached his place the Highlanders I laid the eolith, on wich were the Union Jack and the late Duk 's coronet, upon the bier. The Dean read the first part of the burial service, and after Spohr's anthem "Blest are the departed," the coffin was partially lowered into the vault. The Queen remained until the close of the service, retiring from the chapel after the hymn "Lead kindly light.' The body was afterwards fully lowered into the vault and the impressive ceremonial concluded, and the procession filed elowly out of the chapel by the south door. The Queen and the Princesses drove to the private apart- ments, but the Prince of Wales, the Crown Prince of Ger- many, and the Grand Duke of Huse went on foot. In the metropolis and throughout the provinces special marks of respect to the Royal family, and sympathy with their great sorrow were evident. At the afternoon service at Westminster Abbey the Dead March in " Saul " was played, and Canon Rowsell delivered an appropriate discourse. At the York Minster a special service was held in the morning, and was attended by the Lord Mayor and Corporation. Similar observances took place at Saliabury and Canterbury Cathedrals. Most of the London theatres were closed in the evening, and the Stock Exchange and many public and private establishments were closed during the day, and bells tolled from church towers. The Queen attended Divine service in the Private Chapel at Windsor, on Sunday morning, with the other rnembeas of the Royal Family staying at the Castle. The Dean of Windsor officiated and preached a sermon, after which Her Majesty went for a drive, accompanied by Princees Beatrice. Her Majesty continues in good health. DEPARTURE OF VISITORS. The Crown Prince of Germany left Windsor Castle on Saturday evening for Berlin. The Prince of Wales, Prince Albert Victor, Prince Christian, and the Marquis of Lorne accompanied him to the Great Western Railway Station' where they bade him an affectionate farewell. On Satur- day evening the Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont, father of the Duchess of Albany, and his son, drove from Windsor Castle to the South-western Railway Station and left by special train for Claremont. Mr. 'Collins, Master of the Household, accompanied them to the station, and on the platform the Prince of Waldeck shook hands with him re- peatedly, and thanking him for having faithfully executed the wishes of the late duke. Later in the evening the Duchess of Albany left the Castle and drove to Claremont, accompanied by her mother, the Queen of the Netherlands. The Duchess, notwithstanding her delicate condition and grief she has suffered, bears up remarkably well, and is in the enjoyment of comparatively good health. Before leav- ing the Castle her Majesty took an affectionate farewell of the Prince and Princess of Wales, and the Marquis and Marchioness of Lorne, who remain at the Castle.

div.head: SERVICE AT ST. GEORGE'S CHAPEL.
div.p: SERVICE AT ST. GEORGE'S CHAPEL.

_ A. large congregation assembled on Sunday. morning at St. George's Chapel. Most of those present were attired in mourning, and this, combined with the sombre appearance of the chapel, had a most iMpresslve effect. Toe sermon was preached by, the Hon. and Rev. Canon Courtensy, from the words, "Jesus wept." He referred to the grief and sor- row in mothers and Q'qers, and more especially to the grief of a widowed wife at the death of a prince whose loss was regretted by all for the noble qualities he possessed. Near the altar of St. George's Chapel was displayed an itnmens numbet of handsome wreaths which had been sent to deco- rate Prince Leopold's coffin. Only the wreaths that had been contributed by members of the Royal Family an.l other Royal personages had been placed in the vaults. Many of those placed near the altar were objects of admira-

lion, among them b-ing several from distinguished Frenck personages, and from the French Government. There wall likewise a magnificent wreath from the Mayor and Cor- poration of Windsor, and another from the Corporation of London. The Mayor and Corporation of Windsor attended divine service on Sunday morning at the parish church, but without their robes of office, being attired in mourning, and the Corporation mace wee draped in black. The Dead March in "Saul " was played at the conclusion of the service. At Holy Trinity Church, Wind. For, the congregation included the regiment of the Royal Horse Guards. At the commencement of the service the organist played the hymn, "Blessed are the departed," and all other hymns were of an anpropri are character. The ser- mons were preached by the Roy. Arthur Robins, chaplain le the househotd Croon', and hon. chaplain Co the Queen, and , ee referred to the late Duke as an admirable Prince in the opinion of his contemporaries as well as of society. At the close.of the service Beethoven's " March Funelre " was Per- formed at all the places of worship in Windsor. Most of those present wore mourning. On Sunday afternoon the Marchioness of Lorne visited the Memorial Chapel, and at five o'clock the Prince and Piincess of Wales, PrinCese Beatrice, the Marchioness of Lorne, the Grand Duke of Hesse, and Prince Albert Victor attended service at St. George's Chapel. The Royal party, who entered the edifice through the Deanery, occupied seats in the stalls of the Knights of the Garter. The chapel was crowded, and the service was very imposing. SPECIAL SERMON AT WARRINGTON. On Sunday evening the Rev. John Yonge preached a sermon, suggested by the death of the Duke of Albany, itt the Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington. His teat was Psalm ciii., 15 c, 16 v., "As for man his days are ati grass ;as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth. For the wind passeth over it and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more." These words, he said, conveyed a lesson which God by His recent providence was seeking tO enforce with new power upon the attention of this nation. The lesson was one with which all should be abundantly familiar, for it eras brought into prominence repeatedly and variously. It was taught with every invasion of the fatally circle by death; by every funeral which passed along the street; by every black-edged letter that came to hand; the graveyard in every-town and hamlet; by the mourning' clad persons who mingled with the crowd. It cold not be without value that this familiar but shunned lesson should sometimes be set for men with peculiar emphasis and CO mand. It was set in such fashion now before the nation b/ means of this sudden and unlooked for death in the fatnili of the Queen. Death seemed now to challenge the attelr tion of the nation to the fact that he claimed all " sorta and conditions" ae his own without exception or favouritism; and God, whose messenger death ever was, appealed forcible, to the people td' consider the brevity, uncertainty, and frailty of this mortal life. He thought that as a congrege• lion they should be greatly out of harmony wi`h the wide' spread national sentiment if they did not suffer that mourn- ful event to make its direct appeal to them. WhateVer theories they might affect respecting monarchs and WWI and courts be believed that they were all alike moved w real and de ilt' deep sympathy for the Queen, again sudden]," called to mourn the loss of one of the dearest of her believed ones, and by no means less for the youthful Duchess 50 early and unexpectedly thrown, in what was to her a foreign land, into the deep and bitter solitude of widowhoOde The distress that filled the Royal household had metered in measure into the homes of all classes in the land. The national heart had thrilled with the Royal grief. The life of the nation had been hushed into sympathetic quietness ea loving hands had laid the mortal remains in the tomb. In these days of clashing parties and divided classes it was re- assuring to discover that still one touch of sorrow rendered all akin. Even in,that respect the event, so lamentable ill itself, was not without significance and value. But their attention must be held that night by the larger and deeper significance of that Providential event. He called it a "Providential " event, for such it was. It was certainll not an accident, however much whet men called "accident' might have apparently brought it to pass. They did nOt believe in human lives and destinies being the sport Of chance. The Greatest Teacher the world had ever kneel% declared that not a sparrow falls to the ground " withont the knowledge of the Infinite Father. They were sure, therefore, that a man who was "of more value than mini sparrows" never died without similar divine knowledge and thought and care. They might not b 3 able Is see how that truth workel out in every case or in any; but still upal Christ's authority they accepted and rested in it. And in this case for the nation at large they thought there wile some lesson of serious searching, saving wisdom. Men were set in high places not only for themselves. Rank and royalty were always far I ess huno unable than they were respon- Bible ; less for personal aggrandisement than for large and in- fluential service. Both in their lives and in their death the great ones of the earth were meant to be teachers of their race. He repeated then that God was giving new force to familiar truth by means of this melancholy event. As the ycung prince—se exalted in position, so worthy in life, 80 surrounded with advantage and opportunity for widest ser- vice--was laid in his early grave God's voice seemed tO sound forth to the nation in the very language of the teat. At the best human life hung upon a thread which at any moment, and by any trifle, Might snap asunder ! How trivial an accident might crush out a life. A slip of the foot might do it or might cause it. It might be that, all unconsciously., they had all of them stood or even stumbled many a time upon the brink of death, lied not a Hand Unseen upheld them, theY should hake fallen to rise no more. It was surely a cause of much satisfaction, in viewing the early death of Prinee Leopold, that there was so much in his his that bore the closest scrutiny, and so little, if anything at all, that needed to be veiled in silence. Never had any whisper of evil tarnished his fair fame. There was no page in his his- tory that would ever occasion remorse to his friends or to his country. After the manner of his great and noble father he had shown how it was possible for a prince to live an irreproachable and unblemished life, and to devote himself quietly and unostentatiously to the service and benefit Of his fellow men. Evidently Prince Leopold hid cherished it as hi a ambition to walk worthily in the footsteps of bie father. He had shorter opportunity of knowing his father than had either of his bothers, but it might at any rate be said that he had at least caught more of his father's spirit than had they. At one time, it was said, that he aspired tie become a clergyman, and why he did not realise his wish had never been explained. Had he done so he would at any rate have been a thoughtful and earnest teacher. fla.f that he became without being a clergyman. During Ille short public life he made several speeches, from which it was manifest that he was a man of deep and earnest con; victim, and of considerable independence and freedom thought'. In conclusion, Mr. Yonge said the influence of a pure life was of unspeakable value anywhere, and not lead in the inidet of rank and wealth. It was to be hoped that the prince's influence would not depert with his life. UI left a lesson for his peers; and he trusted they might wile tingly learn and follow it out. He advised young men'33 devote to highest purpose their early powers and endea- vours, and then they would best La fit either far long and useful life on earth, or for early death and greater and grander service in the perfect world.

A REDUCED ACCOUNT.—The Surveyor said that in pnr' smarms of the instructions of the committee he had taken steps to get the account of Mr. Moore, solicitor, for Pro' ceedings in connection with water rates, Ste , reduced. MT' Moore had now reduced it from £ll 13s 4d to the motion of Mr. Feints it was agreed that the reduced te. count should be paid. SEWERAGE WORKS, &c.—The Surveyor asked that n cheque should be signed for £lO to meet current expeneen in connection with lighting, water, and sewerage. He had a cutting to make in Barn-lane to drain Mr. Entwhistle'll and Mr. Mitchell's property.—The cheque was signed. THE HEATH-STREET ENCROACHMENT.—The Chairman asked what had been done in regard to this affair.—The Surveyor said he had called upon Mn Wakefield and Mr. Parr, and they stated they could do nothing in the matter, but they should see Mr. Unsworth. Since then he (the Surveyor) had heard nothing at all.—The Chairman : Unsworth has not seen you about it.—The Surveyor : rie has uot.—The Chairman suggested that the matter be left over for the new committee to deal with—Tots suggeB- - was agreed to. NIGHT-8 or, REMOVAL.—The Surveyor, in accordance with instructions reported as to the best system of night' eoil removal. He was of opinion that the ashpit System waft very bad indeed, the removal being totally in the hands Of the farmers, who removed the night-soil at any time of dal. He had come to the conclusion that the work would be done most efficiently by purchasing a cart and horse and con. I stantly engaging three men. Unfortunately the cost wenid I be more, but more could be realised by the sale of the night.. soil. He estimated the cost of maintaining the horse aria three men at £lB9, the sale of manure at £l2O, thus leaving a deficiency of .£69. Under present circumstances he thought the simplest way would be to enter into a contract witb some person to remove the night-soil at so couch per an• num.—lt was agreed that a meeting of the committee should be held next Thursday to take this nsatter into considefa. tion. THE EMISSION OF SMOKE.—Soine conversttion took place with regard to the emission of smoke frost the factOri chimneys, but the Chairman stated that was a subject which they had no power to deal with, and the sobjec dropped. APPLICATION FOR WATER, &C.—The Surveyor said Mr• Gritnke had barn at his office and wanted a supply of at to the colliery offices. Their mains. the Surveyor added, did not go in that direction. Mr. Griznke aloe wished t, have a closet on the pail system built in connection with lit offices, and wanted to know if the commictee had any o,h; potion to it. The committee would have to remove tn. a contents of the closet —lt was agreed to refer these pplt.•

cations to the Sewerage Committe'e. NEW COTTAGES—Mr. Mitchell submitted plans of Vivi° e,ttages which he propond erecting in Leh-street, whie' r.-nild be in every ropec similar to the cottages ahead,' eiected theie.—The plans having been 37,proved, the meet- log ended.

ITALTON.—These clubs 'sleet on Saturday at Rattan, when, as on the previous occasion, the Runcorn players,cems off victorious: Each tram worked very hard to win, and whoa at half-time. the Ha,ltoulans bad seared a try and seven minors ,to three touchdowns. the Chance of the Wanderers seemed rather small. Soon after the ball was re-started, the home trans was gradually forced back, and for some time is territory was beseiged during which e,try Was obtained f r the visitors, the kick at goal failing. As this equalized mattes. the cont st became still nine lively, and both sides played up t • their be.,t form, Halton eventually adding anotter try, which was not Improved upon. The Wan- derers now began to force the ball back into the htinne quarter. Where for a while they held it, shortly bet re time was relied they got their second try, W. Riley converting it iuto a goal. After this a few minor points were scored, but nothing of Importance took place, and the score at the dose stood— Wanderers, 1 goal, 1 try, 6 minor points; Halton, 2 tries, 12 minors FOOTBALL: EARLESTOWN JUNIOR offILLENGS 'CUP: BAHLESTOWN (2ND TNA.M)•V. T/re Earlestown Lid team journeyed to St. Helens on Satur- day afternoon to meet the St. Thomas's Ist team In the second round of the competition to the Eariestown and District ,! Junior Challenge Cup. As this was one of the most impor ant ties in the compe ition, there was a large attendance of spec- tators. The vintors won the toss, and shortly alter three o'clock 18 attbews locked off for St Helens. Tue home team Possesred an advantage for the first few minutes, and the Ilarlestown go.' was seriousty endangered. Green defended well, however and the game afterwards asmmed a pretty even Character. The two goalke,pers were in turn called upon to M 5 their hands in order to save their charge, but about ten Minutes before half-time Perter scored for St. ffe ens. On the game being resumed, the Earlestonlans ran the bail into their %Moments quarters, and quickly tecured two corner kicks. Holoroft nicely placed the ball in front on both occasions, and James succeeded in equalising the score by a good shot. On the change of ends both elevens worked hard to secure a lead- ing point, and the play became very exciting. The score re-. Maimed unaltered up t ) within ten minutes from the call of time, when after is ,crimmage in front of the Farlestown goal, Porter again mired for St.. Helens sued considerable cheers. But no sorter bad the leather been again started for Eariestewn than the latter agile tan to the front, and Ogees, by a long low shot, stored a second goal for tile vleiters—a rather lucky point, as one of the backs and a goal keeper al- lowed the ball to roll by them. As neither team were able to 1 scere again the game resulted in a draw of two goals each. They wit again meet at Earle town to-day (Saturday) to de- cide the tie. Teams :—Earlestown J. Gray, goal; J. Green and W. Thompson. backs; T. Fairclough and C. Birkhead, half-backs; li. [(aura and J. Appeeton right wing; J James and W. Cameron, renter; T. Oldham and J. Ogden,•.eft wing; Tualifire, G. 0 Roberts. St. Helens: J. Tyrer, goal; 11. Tickle and J. T. Mills backs; R. Ellison, H. Roberta, and W. Wright, half-backs; W. Porter and C. Cousins, right wing; P. Matthews, centre; J. Williams ant G. Evans, left wing; um- pire, H. Miller; referee, J Whalley, Earlestown. "DEFEATED, BUT NOT DESGRAOED." [BY "LEATHER HUNTER."] The progress of the Eariestowe lade has been especially • marked in connection wirh the Challenge Cup competition. This was their first season'e entry in the contest, anti a more spirited and brilliant bid for the trophy was never made. The success which attended their efforts throughout the various stages of the contest is fresh in people's recollection. and suf- fice it to say that in the first round they easily, dispesed of ' Buiscaugh by four gnats to one; in the second round they eaeltaleashed Liverpool Anfield by five goats to none; in the third —Maid they met Bantle (last year's winnees), and after a bril- liant performance they defeated them by four teals to none, While in the fourt round (the semi-fins' tie) they were drawn against Liverpool Stanley, a club whiter boasted ate an un- beaten certMotere dueng the season. The match was played on the Bootle cricket field. After one of the most stubbornly-ought games ever played in Liverpool, Earlestown amid a scene of excitement again came out with flying colours, Stanley (although they scored the first goal) being beaten by two goals to One. Now cause the real tug of war I Earlestown were left to fight in the final tie with their old opponents—the Everton ""atn. From various cause a most bitter feeling of rivalry and animosity had sprung up between the two clubs, and their m in the final tie evoked an interest which spread itself °I, rough rut South-West Lancashire. The Liverpool players Journeyed to Blackpool, so it is said, to undergo a week's special training preparatory to the conflict, while the Eta lee- town lads had thee days of it in their own immediate.district The well known rivalry between the teams drew together at Bootle a large concourse of spectators—he largest by far ever seen at an Association match in the district. About 809 were s‘aPPorters of the Earlestown team, and as the latter tripped lightly over tee boundary they were eagerly scanned by the thousands who had gathered from Liverpooland surrounding towns The Eariest :Mans cettatnly seemed in rare trim, but In size and s'ature were a marked contrast to the Evertonians, r; big, burly set of men, weile the former vemed a body of (gist lads. Evidoetly one team bad weight and build' on its Side, but the other was possessed of nimbleness, activity and (swam ance. As the game progressed the extitement among the rival supporters of the two teams thereased, and shouts of eneouragement we e heard over all parts of. the field. The Play continued very fast up to half-tinse.-when ends were ,changed, and no score made. Up to that time weight and build nad had the best of the play, but when put to a test of real 4._trength and enduranc, the stamina of the Earlestown lads began to show itself. When the game had been resumed the latter rushed forward with great beJ Ili may and Mel opponents were forced to act on the defen- Zve. for ten mieutes Everton (ought desperately .e.erl to save their goal, but evidences that they were nearly ragged out" were visible to nearly all the spectators. MR. BRIGHT ON AMERICA, PEACE,

The New York Tribune publishes the followibg letter recently received by Augustin Jones, of the Friend? Boarding School, Providence, in reply to this announc- ing that a marble bust of Mr. Bright was • to be erected there:—

"London, March W. "Dear Friend,—l regret that I have so long delayed an answer to yonr most kind letter, which reached me some weeks ago. It informed me of the singular and great com- pliment you were about to pay me by placing a marble bust of me in the lecture hall of your noble school. I was surprised to hear of the project; but I cannot but' be much gratified at-the friendly feeling manifeated to me by your- self and the authorities •connected with .your institution. You say that FeVssa friend to yout country in the day of need. I did what I could to prevent discord tetween the two English nations, and to teach our people the nature of the great issue which depended on the conflict in which 20 years ago your people were engaged. I lamented the' conflict; but I wished that England should offer her sympathy on the side of freedom to the slave, and in favour of the perpetual union of your great Republic. I look back on the *part I took with unalloyed satisfaction, and Would withdraw no word I uttered in connection with a contest on which England and the civilised world looked with a profound interest. "The question of peace, to which you refer, claims the sympathy of all Christian nations. On your Continent we may hope your growing millitins may henceforth know no- thing of war. Nona can assail you; and you are anxious to obstain from mingling in the quarrels of other nations. Europe, unhappily, is a great camp. All its nations are armed as if each expected an invasion from its neighbour, unconscious, apparently, that great armies tempt to war the moment any cause of dispute arises. The potentates and , Governments of Europe, I doubt not, dread war. They seek to guard themselves against it by arrangementge "We. in England, are not free from blame; but with us the love of peace is increasing, and no Government can en- gage in war without risking, and even losing, the support of our people. We are so involved with territory and popula- tions over half the globe that difficulties are almost con- stantly arising, and our elanger of war is greater than that of any other nations. I am however, confident that our feel- ing against war is sensibly increasing, and I trust and be- lieve the moral sense of our people will more and more con- demn it. "I have read with much interest the report of your great school which you sent' me. I hope your efforts in behalf of a sound, liberal education may prosper, and that your students as they enter and pass through, the world may strengthen the moral sentiment which pervades so large a portion of your population. I can only wish you success in your great work, and thank you and all connected with your institution for the kindness .you have shown me. . "England and your United States are two nations, but I always like to regard them as one people. On them the growth of all that -is good in the world greatly depends. Believe me your sincere and grateful friend. "JOHN BRIGHT."

THE UNIVERSaI BOAT RACE- Considerable enthusiasm was required to infuse the aver- ag- sightseer to honour the Thames river banks on 'Monday morning, as rain fell pretty persistently. and the aspect of the weather wee very threatening. Asythe hour fixed for the start of the University Boat Race (half past eleven) drew near, there was every indication of a wet day, while the wind, blowing fitfully from a damp quarter, W.N.W., had evidently a marked effect upon the attendance, the towpath and other coigns of vantage being rather less densely packed than on many occasions, though the change of Nours from nine to eleven, owing to the funeral of the Duke of Albany, n 6 doubt afforded many visitors from a distance an oppor- tunity of reaching the scene of action comfortably. Cam- bridge took the Middlesex station: . Four steamers accom- panied the race, besides the launch Lorna Hoene, which has been nied by the Cambridge coach during the training, and carried the umpire, Mr. Lewis Lloyd. The first sign of movement on the part of the competitors was made at 11-25, when the Can- tabs launched their boat from East's yard, and were loudly cheered while paddling down to their station. Oxford did not show until their opponents were fairly afloat, when they put out from the London Club quarters, and were also in turn greeted with loud applause, which their neat style in pad- dling certainly merited. The start was effected at seven minutes to twelve, and Cambridge was soon a trifle ahead, having caught the water first. At Craven Steps Cambridge led by nearly half a length, both crews rowing 39. At the Grass Wharf Cambridge were nearly clear, both crews in the centre of the river, and catching the full force of the wind, 'which blew strongly, although the water was not much roughened. Cambridge were very badly steered near- ing Hammersmith Bridge, brit led by 4sec.---time, Cam- bridge 7min. 29sec., Oxford 7min. 33sec.---utnd opposite the Doves quite held their advantage. Off the Oil Works Oxford flattered their supporters by drawing up a trifle, and, aided by • Cambridge's' atrocious steer- ing, looked for a moment like going by. The Cantabs, however, got away again, and along Horse Reach kept well ahead, the Oxford stroke-oar doing very little work. Both were badly interfered with by the swell from a tug-boat below Barnes Bridge, where the steering, especially of Oxford, was very faulty, and the Light Blues led by a length and a ball clear through the bridge—time 16-roln. 50sec., lisec. to the good. The race was now practically over, Oxford, pulling a game stern wager, being defeated by two clear lengths. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A MOTHER.—EarIy OD Tues- day morning a shocking attempt by a son to murder his mother was made at &nth Shields. John Sutherland, glass-cutter, his mother, and brother were drinking on Mon- day, when a quarrel took place, and Mrs. Sutherland struck the accused on the head with a glass. lie said he would do for her before the night was over, and after she WAS asleep he cut her throat with a razor, causing a dangerous wound. The prisoner was brought before the magistrates on Tuesday, and remanded. PROFESSOR MAX MULLER AND THE ILBERT BILL.—The following letter from Professor Max Muller, addressed to Mr. Chesson, was read at the Indian meeting which was held in the Kensington Town flail on Friday evening :—" 25, Pembroke Gardens, Kensington, W., April 4, 1884.—Dear Sir,—l have just received the Royal command, which was sent first to Oxford, to attend the funeral of the Duke of Albany at Windsor to-morrow morning. This, I regret, makes it impossible for rue to at tend your meeting. I was particularly anxious to be present to congratulate you and all true friends of India, to whatever party they may belong, on the great triumph which you have obtained. Every great triumph is mixed up with some small disappointments, but these can be corrected by and by. The essential point is that the fundamental principle on which the Proclama- tion of the Empress of India rests has been maintained against all quibbling!, that the honour of England is saved land the Imperial word be been kept sacred. Do not trust 11 to party, but trust to the great heart of England, or if that I sounds too poetical, trust to the good sense of the English people.—Yours faithfully (Signed) F. MAX MULLER.' div.head: FARLESTOWN.
div.p: FARLESTOWN.
LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

A public lecture on " En-gia-n-d and Egypt, or four years of Liberal foreign policy, and what It has led t 0,,, was given in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, by Mr. Frank John Leslie, solicitor, Liverpool, on Monday evening, under the auspices of the Conservative Club. There was a large and enthusiastic audience. Mr. M. B. Westhead (president of the club) occupied the chair, and he was supported by Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, IP.. B. B. Glover, Thomas Stone, J. E. Pardey, Barron, G. Clarke, and other gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN said be was sorry to announce that their late respected president, Mr Pearson, was unable to attend. He had written to say that it would have given him great pleasure to have been present and listen to the lecture. Be had also expressed to him verbally that it was no false ex- cuse, as he had so many engagements in relation to the railway undertaking that he was utterly precluded from be- ing present. Letters had also been received from Mr. John Brewis (chairman of the Golborne Conservative Associa- tion), the Rev. Canon Whitley, the Bev. Ho Monks, and a telegram from Mr. Robert Stone. Proceeding to introduce the lecturer, the chairman said he hoped that at the termi- nation of the lecture they would be able to say that he had successfully waded through ,what he would call such a quagmire of mud and slush. It streck him (the chairman) that if he did successfully accomplish the task of travers- ing over such a slough of despond without having good goloshes and gaiters almost up to his hips— (laughter)—he would be deserving of their thanks. The chairman at a recent Liberal meeting in that neighbourhood had referred to him (Mr. Westhead), and said that he was very much surprised that a neighbour of his, who was once a Liberal, should now assert himself to be a staunch Comprvative, and that the reasons why he did so were never given. He thought nearly all present would know that the change of politics with him (Mr. Westhead) was certainly attributable to that which he con- sidered a very dangerous precedent, and that was the Dis- establishment of the Irish Church. (Applause.) It was certainly not merely a matter of so much money to Ireland, but it was a stepping stone to the solicitation of the dis- establishment of everythinT, which had hitherto proved and was satisfying to our forefathers. (Applause.) When he looked and considered what had taken place since that time he thought he had not formed a very erroneolac opinion. (Hear, hear.) The subject of the lecture was of importance to them, for he could hardly conceive any community of Englishmen, whether they were bigoted Radicals or bigoted Tories, but what they must feel their country's interests were deeply endangered by the policy and conduit of the present Government. (Applause,) The gentleman now at the head of Her Majesty's Government, with that wonderful talent which he possessed, was trying to keep the miAC.s of the people from Egypt to the rural Franchise Bill. But the subject before them was one with which their lecturer Was well acquainted, and he would therefore call upon him to deliver his address. (Applause.) Mr. F. J. LESLIE said the story of tbc present Government was one which could not be told too often. it, however, did not run consecutively and in order, for the fact was that the Government policy had, Leen a policy of fits and starts, never ending, and never', ,knowing wkat was going to happen, or what they were go- log to do next. The Liberal Government and the Liberal', patty were trying to prevent in every possible way a dis- .ol:melon of the Egyptian question. Why did they shrink ' from every discussion which bad been raised upon Egyptian mentos, and why did they always raise the parrot cry of 4' Obsteuction," which really meant nothing at all ? It was simply the red barring thrown across the path to prevent their Conservative friends from raising the Egyptian ques- Con. They were aimply ashamed of the whole business, and they.wanted to wipe out the recollection of it from the minds of the people by centring their attention upon the all-absorbing question of the franchise. (Applause.) They did everything they possibly could to wipe out the recol- lection of what had happened in Egypt • and abroad during the latt fottr years, but it was for the people to say if their scheme had been successful, after going owl: again the blun- ders, mistake, acid disasters which characterised the period the Littoral party had been in power. The lecturer proceeded to allude to the various phases which the Egyptian crestion had assumed, since it came prominently before the public, strongly con- demning the action of the Government in connection there- with, and stating that they had made confusion worse con- founded. The events leading up to and includiag the Sou- dan rebellion were touched upon, and he concluded by asking what possible reason they could give for such a series of inconsistent actions on the part crf the Liberal Government. One reason was that the Cabinet was so constituted that what one member proposed and thought ought to be done another member opposed and thought ought not to be done. They wanted by some means to wipe out of the recollection of the English Den.ile the humiliations which had crowded upon them in the Last four years, and it was for evezy constituency in the United Kingdom to follow the example set them at Brighton, and to say to tilt. Liberal Government " We have seen your policy, we have marked the disisters which have crowded upon us, and we say we have had enough of it, and we will have no more." (Applause.) On the motion of fir. T. J. GuramPtx, J.P., seconded by Councillor Surrote (Warrington), a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Lecturer; and a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman en the motion of Mr, Bonaore, peconded by Mr. THOS. STONE. The meeting tiaen concluded,
