WIDNES. WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. - MEETING. The annual meeting of the member' of Widnes Liberal Association was held on Wednesday evening, in Lacey- street schoolroom. The audience, Which displayed much enthusiasm, was presided over by Mr. E K. Muspratt, and 1 there occupied seats on the platform Messrs. R. (taken, I astir., If. Grastcell, janr., Captain Brunner, E. Carey. J. Mor- rison, W. B. Bowing and C. H. Bosomwortla (of Liverpool). and If. B. Shores (secretary). Mr. SwouEs read the following letter, which he had re- ceived from Mr. Thomas Snaps :—" A previous engagement prevents my attendance at the meeting to-night. It is to be hoped that Witilleal Lib3rals will speak out in no uncer- tain tones upon the necessity of passing the Franchise Bill, and the urgency of dealing with the obstructive tactics of those who are endeavouring to discredit Parliament by wasting its time by thus making legislation impossible.' Mr. James S. Muspratt wrote—" I much regret I shall be unable to be at your meeting to-night. I hope that a strong expression of opinion will be sent to our members against the evident policy of obstruction which the Tory party are raaking use of to damage the Government. The report of the committee was taken as read. It con- .. . -

- tained the font:min; extracts : '• In June, your Becret4r7 attended a conference of Liberal i agents, vrhils met at Manchester to consider the clauses of the Corrupt Practices Bi•l, the various alterations and addi- tions there suggested were reported to the Attsrney General (who bad charge of the inmate), and many of them were em- bodied in the int. °lithe 17th and 18th October. a conference of delegates ap- pointed by the various Mei al Atia3ClatiOrl3 throughout the lillgdOM was C nvened in the A.!bert Hall. Leeds, to ascertain and formulate the opinione of the Liberal party on the Fran- chise (Zonetion ; the decietery atteaded on your bah di and votet in favour of asking priority on the Government pro- gramme for a measure extending the suffrage in the counties. On isa 2l h November, a conference of delegates was con- vane 1 tire National LP2eral Federation in the Colston Hall, Brist o pass resolutions de-sling wide extension of the Fran- chise assl redist-ibutim of seats,eat which your Secretary at- tended -vs 1 to,ils part in the procee tings- Coder rise instruinime of the °dicers. the Secretary attended the re lent York elect,on for the pop ,se 01 watching the work- ing of the Corrupt Practices Act, in operation for the first time at Ms election. The Secretary WAS also present at the L.adrn c -inference of Liberal lie glstration Agents, which was convened for the pur- pose of discussing methods of working under the Corrupt Frac- tices Act, 1883. During the year a number of pamphlets bearingupon various subjects of Interest to the party, have been distributed by the Association. Your Committee desire to call ymr attention to impending legislation for the extension of ti`le Franchise in the counties. They are of opinion that every e it should be made to de- velop Liberal principles &mom:At the future electorate, and with this object they are arranging a series of lectures to which they invite your attandance and for which they ask your

support. In conelusion, your Committee have to place before you the following detailed report of the late revision, 'hewing a nett gain of 30 votes to the Liberal Party in the Widnes Polling District, a total which again corn ,ares favourably with other out die Wets of the county ; but. whilst offering you their cm- gratulations, they must stronAly urge upon any who may still be claimants the necessity of their personal attendance at the next Revision Court, as it will doubtless be the last opportunity they will have of registering before a General Election." The details of the revision have previously appeared in the Examiner. The CIiaIRMAN moved the adoption of the report. They would find on referring to the report that dering the past year the association had not been idle. They had consider- ably increased the subscription list, and were thus provided with the sinews of war should a contest occur in that divi- sion, while they would see that all the Liberals of the district who had the present right to the franchise should be pot on the register. They had daring the past year succeeded in the registration courts to a considerable extent, and in view of the extension of the franchise the committee had thought it desirable to educate the people of the district in Liberal principles. For that purpose they had had one or two lec- tures. These lecturers lead been very well received, and he hoped the association would continue that good work; and he thought the commit-ea, the vice-president, Mr. Carey— (applause )—and the eectetary, Mr. Sher es—(appl ause ) —de- served the thanks of that meeting. At the last annual meet- ing they, in common with other Liberals, deprecated the system of obstruction which had evidently been adopted by the Tories as a policy, and asked the Government, by amend- ing the rules of the House of Commons, to secure an oppor- tunity for the business of the country being properly con- ducted. They were aware that an autumn session was held for the purpose of amending the rules, and those rules were amended, and partly owing to this add to the expression of opinion in the country, the Government were able to carry out during the last session of Parliament the bills which they had introduced. He referred more especially to the Bankruptcy Act, the Patents Act, and the Corrupt Practices Act. These measures were useful measures, but they were only measures which the Government desired to bring forward before they undertook the great question which they promised to take at the general election of 1880, namely, the exte union of the franchise to the counties. (Applaese.) The system of obstruction had in the present Parliament reached a point wh ch it had never reached before. That obstruction was carried on by two parties, one being the party led by Mr. Parnell. He must say they bad at any rate some excuse for the obstruction they had practiced. lie could to a certain extent sympathise with them when they directly , obstructed a bill of which they disapproved like the Coercion Act. But-they carried ob- struction further. They did not only obstruct measures inimical as they think to Ireland, but they used obstruction tactics to put a stop to the business of England. He thought that if they c ontirmed in that -course they would really defeat their own object. Another made of obstruc- tion was that of asking questions. Undoubtedly some of the queseions were pertinent and necessary as Ireland was to acme extent governed despotically by England. When he came to the Conservative party he found that they exactly resorted to the tactics of the'lrish party without any excuse whatever. What kind of questions did they ask? He could quite understand Lord Randolph Churchill's ignorance of the geography and politics of the Soudan—(applause)but he did not think the House of ,Commons was exactly the place where he should learn his lessons. After alluding to the form of obstruction by moving the adjournment of the dehate and to the extent it had been carried in debating the Egyptian question, he went on to speak of the Fran- chise Bill. The Tories would extend the fran- chise to the people provided that they would vote Tory ; but the Liberals would extend the franchiee to the people because they thought it wrong that a person living on one side of the street should not have a privilege which a person of the same rank of life, in the same interest in good government, possessed. (Applaatee.) The Liberals supported the extension of the franchise because they thought it was just, whilst the Tories opposed that extension of the ,franchise becanse they were afraid that the people would not vote in favour of Tory rue muzes. (Applause.) The Government had brought in a bill which was admitted by impartial per sons to be on the whole a most Conservative measure, but it was opposed by the Tories indirectly, although they had not the honesty to say so, aalike Mr. Goschen. Hewes glad to see that the Government, notwithstanding the cbstruction which they bad met, had, by their persistence and patience been suc- cessful in -dein' out the Tories, and had at length brought the extensionmf the Franchise Bill tee a vote, and it had been carried byu the glorious majority a 130. (Applause.) He had great pleaeure in moving the adoption of the report, and he thought everyone would be satisfied that the Asso- ciation was doing a good work, and that the report would meet with the approval of the members. (Applause.) Mr. E. CSILET Seconded the motion. The work which that report represeeted had been almost entirely performed by Mr. Shores, and he thought great credit was due to him for the way in which be had carried it out. He (Mr. Carey) had been connected with the Association far many years, and he was pretty well acquainted with the date of their register; and he conk: say, without hesitation, that they were better prepared at the present moment fee an election, should such an event take place this year—which he did not think would,ef coutsa—than they had ever been in the history of the Aesociatien. (Applause.) There wee no place in the country inure Leyal to Liberal princteles than :Widnes, and he belieeed that the capable citizens GC Widnes who had a vote now, and those 3,400 who would have the wote by and bye, would prove_leyal supporters of the Liberal Jeans°. (Applause.) The motion was carried. blf. J. Monsoon moved : ".Tat this meeting desiees to express its thorough approval of the bill of Her Majecty's Government for the more complete representation of the people, its gratification that the ;abject of the franchise has been separated from that of .redietribution of seats, Lie hearty satisfaction that Ireland is included in the provisions of ambition terms of equality with the rest of the United Kingdom, and sincerely congratulates the Government on the large majority they have obtained efor the second read- ing." It was the feeling ef all true Liberals, he obeerved, that oar Irish fellow subjects should ,enjoy the same rights and privileges that we enjoyed, audit would be most deplore able to deny Ireland any participation in this measure of reform, rbecause there were indications at tee present time tbatt eland .was settling down to ap era, which he thought they ell hoped might be eme of prosperity and progress. (Hear, hear, and app la ) There was a fear expmssed in one or two of the most important organs of political opinion in Ireland that the °House of Lords will not reject the Franchise ;Eel, but that the iieliminate was from it that part which referred to Ireland.wi r he further fear that the Hones of. Commons at the end of he session might be ladled to accept the Bill in its trnutilated form. He thoright these fears were groundless' and from the feeling remeree which Mr. Gladstone made on Monday night it was evident he had determined to cart, the Bill in its entirety. (Applupse.) It the House of Lode determined to frustrate his intention, supported as he was by a large majority of the representatives of the people, and the matter was referred to the conctry, the people of Widnes at any rate would know bow, and be prepared, to respond to such as appeal. (Applause.) Mr. H. GSSICELL, Jun., who was cordially greeted, said, in second ieg the resolution, that be did not think the House of Lords in the face of the lags majority by which the second reading pealed would be so inalne as to reject the Franchise Bill. ft was probable now that the Tories would endeavour to postpone the operation of the bill, and he saw that Mr. Albert Hay had proposed thd the bill should net come in force until the beginning of the year 1887. (Laughter') If the bill was a good thing they ought to have it at once —(hear, hear,)—and ha thought that the liberals through- out the country would be determined to have it at once. Mr. Gladstone had asked them to render him assistance by agitating for the bill, and they in Widnes were that night ping their beat to de Do? awl he hoped that go bibaral

associations throughout the country would agitate for the immediate operation of the bill. (Applause ) - Mr. W. B. BOWRING, of Liverpool, supported the resolu- tion, and in doing so he remarked that at the last census there were 36 millions of persons in the country, and of this vast number, every one of them more or less interested in the well being and prosperity of the country, there were only three millions who had a direct interest in the govern- ment of the country. ("Shame.") Ile did not, therefore, think it was too much to ask that that number should be largely increased, for there was a system of education in the country which was undsubtelly having its effect. Alluding to the redistribution of seats, he said they must agree that Mr. Gladstone was right ia not tacking it to the Franchise Bill, as in that case the Tories would have undoubtedly wrecked both schemes. But the present distribution of seats in the House of Commons was a ridiculous absurdity --(hear, bear,)—aud after the passing of the Franchise Bill would no doubt be attended to. In conclusion the speaker expressed his gratification that Ireland was t 3 be put on an equality witda England as regarded the franchise. (Ap- plause.) The resolution was passed with acclamation. • Mr. HaLBROOIE GASEELL, s na who was received with loud applause, moved" Fast in the opinion of this meeting the policy of obstruction whether open or veiled, by which the Tory party in the -House of Commons is seeking to impsde the action of Parliament, to divert public atten- tion from domestic legislation, and to prevent the passing of measures of reform, is deserving of the strongest con- demnation of all who value representative goverument." II He said he could net imagine any feeling but that of great I indignation seta iting any meeting of Liberal leaders and Liberal politicians when they considered the grievous and discreditable obstruction with which the present Govern- ment had been met in the Houses of Parliament. (Ap- plause.) lie thought he might go a step further and said that every faithful friend of l!arliamentary Go- vernment must view with great misgivings the attitude of the two Houses of Parliament towards popular legislation and towards the people of the country. (Applause.) They all knew the difficulty of carrying any Liberal measure through the House of Lords. Many of them could remember—he could remember well—the state of excite- ment into which this country was thrown some fifty years ago at the passing of the first Reform Bill, when the people were in a condition bordering upon civil war before the House of Lords would consent to grant such a modicum of representation as was included in that Bill. The seine sort of opposition to popular measures and to Liberal Parlia- ments had actuated tke Houses of Parliament from that day to the present, and there could be no doubt that the time was rapidly approaching when the country would feel called upon to reconsider its Parliamentary institutions with a view to bringing both Houses of Parliament into harmony with the sentiments of the people at large. (Loud applause.) The speaker pointed out that the members of Parliament who obstructed public business were not the re- promentatives of the great centres of intelligence and in- dustry such as London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Man- chester, and Liverpool, but the representatives of the pocket boroughs in the south. He felt perfectly sure that whatever might be a man's politics, if he were returned for a great constituency he dare not trifle with the time and patience of the country. (Applause.) He trusted the time would arrive before the present Parlia- ment catne to an end when the small pocket boroughs such as Eye, Bridport, Hertford and Woodstock would be swept away. (Applause.) He trusted more to the effect of the re-distribution of seats for putting an end to this lamentable state of things, and he hoped that the worn out and decayed placm in the t•outh of England would be merged from their individual existence as boroughs into the county con- stituencies around them and that great centres of industry and intelligence in the north, in the midlands, and in Scot- land would be enfranchised. (Hear, hear.) If his antici- pations should be wrong, and the House of Commons failed 'to recover its freedom of action then a most grave contin- gency would have arrived. Parliamentary government would be on its trial • the people of Great Britain and Ireland would be the tribunal to try them and he had no doubt that if the people were roused to take this question and faced the problem as to how the business of the nation was to be carried on, there would be such a united cry from the nation at large as would put an end to the present wretched system. (Hear, hear.) They would have the vox poincli which was the vox Dei—the voice of the people speaking in a just cause like this would be like the voice of God, and would not be denied. (Applause.) Mr. C. H. BOSOMWORTH seconded the proposition. He thought that the House of Lords would be sufficiently wise not to obstruct the measure which was now before the country. (Applause.) If the House of Lords had not learned in the past the wisdom et sub,nitting in respectful silence to the voices of the people the time was not far dis- tant when the people of England would beein to ioquire "I it necessary to have a House of Lords at all." (Applause.) The resolution was carried with loud applause. On the motion of Captaia BRUNNER, seconded by Mr. S. OWENS, a vote of thanks was passed to the visitors, and Mr. BUMMING, and Mr. BOSOMWORTII, in replying, moved and seconded a vote of thanks to the Chairman.—The motion was heartily carried, and the Chairman having replied, the meeting separated.

BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHFORD.—The annual tea meeting in connection with the above was held last evening and proved a thorough success, the schoolroom being filled with members of the congregation and their friends. Subse- quently, a meetfng was held in the chapel, which was crowded, and songs, anthems, and choruses were given by members of the choir. The Rev. W. Pilling, addressing the meeting, said that, surrounded as it was by so many privileges and opportunities for doing good, the Christian church at the present day was not occupying the position that it should. The great question for them all was how to remedy that, individually and as a whole to try and bring about a batter state of affairs. There was now a great lack of naturalness in religion, and there was not that reality in the lives of many Christians to create that impression upon the world that it was intended that the Gospel &mule:. If they could convince the world of the purity of their motives he believed that they would be far more successful than they were. In these 'lays there was a tendency to associate with people abut whom they should be very careful, and it seemed to him that many people were trying to solve the guestion how they could have the world and the Gospel together.—The Rev. E. Moore also gave an address, speaking principally upon the divine command to spread the Gospel. Christanity, he remarked, was uot in its infancy now, and there was no need of the convincing power of miracles. They had the ex- ample of eighteen centuries of Christian tectimony of the truth and power of the Gavel, but the need of that Gospel to men was just the same as ever. Some people said that the organisation of Goepel work, on such an extensive scale, did not produce very great results, and unfortunately the visible results of their labour were not such as they thought that they had a right to expect. The fact of the celebration they were then holding ought to stimulate them ~to unite more firmly together to secure the success of the ..cause.—The addresses were listened to with great at- tention, and the musical selections were heartily applauded.

A. RUNAWAY HUSBAND: THE MAHRIED WOMEN'S PRO. TEETY ACT.-At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Mcaday morning, Mr. Cook (of the firm of Messrs. Barrow and Cool.;) applied for a protection order on behalf of Alice Gar- nett, wife of Richard Garnett, who had deserted her.—Mrs. Garnett was then sworn, and stated that she was married to her husband on the 9th January, 1878, at the pariah church of Orms;:irk. She lived with him for five years, but on the 23rd November last he deserted her, and she had not seen him since. He kissed the children, and said "Good bye, perhaps lahall never see you again." She had received the letter produced from him, and she had reason to suppose that he had.deserted her.—Mr. Cooks: I shall nut in the letter. Is it in his own handwriting? —Mrs. Garnett : It is. —Mr. Cooke: Amongst other things in this long letter he say., "I do not set sail until 2nd January, 1884, when I sail for Brisbane, South Australia. No one knows where I am, not even my solicitor." The letter was dated 26,11 November, Liverpool, without any other address. Mr. Cooke added that Mrs. Garnett had six children to maintain cut of her own earnings, and some little property which was left her by her father. It would be a serious thing for her under the circumstance.; considering that her elder children were not on very good terms with him, if, when she made herself once more comfortable he returned, and seized what she had got. She was a widow when married to him in 1878 and was in a fair position, but he had disposed of a considerable portion of her property and also what she bad , since come iptc possession of under her father's will.—The Chairman: You have no idea where he is now I—Mrs. Gar- nett : No.—The Chairman: Has his solicitor been com- municated with about these proceediega?—Mr. Ceoke replied that he could not very well say who was Ms solicitor.— The Chairman thought some difficulty might arise with the creditors as to the wife's property.--,Mrs. G-arnett was thereupon re-sworn, and she deposed that the furniture now in her dwelling-house was a portion of that left her by her late husband. A BOY DROWNED.—A sad occurrence took place at War- rington on Wednesday, when a boy namen Benjamin Cox, 11 years of age, the son of Joseph Cox, fergeman, 15, Pitt- street, was drowned in the canal near Bewsey Locks. The deceased, it appears, was playing with a stick at the edge of the water, when be fell in. Henry Hamper, a boy of eleven, was in company with the deceased at the time and tried to get him out, but failed. He then called out to EOM water- men who were on the opposite side of the canal, but the bridge was turned at the time, and 20 minutes elapsed before the deceased was got out of the water. He was then quite dead, and the body was taken to his home to await an in- quest. IIIARRELSOME WOMEN. THE Muscat Socurry.—lt is satisfactory to learn that the difficulty which has for some time threatened the severance of Dr. lilies' long connection with the Musical Society has at last been removed, The question of changing the nii,ht of rehearsal so as to meet the exigencies of Dr. Hiles' numerous other professional engagements has been put to the test of an individual expression of opinion by each member of the society, the result being, we understand, that except in a few instances the proposed alterations will cause no serious inconvenience. The decision of the society thus to modify its arrangements so as to secure the con- tinuance of Dr. lilies' services will, we feel sure, be a source of satisfaction, a feeling, too, which will ba shared in a great measure by the outside public. SUDDEN DEATH ON • WARRINGTON MAN AT ST. HELENS. —Thomas Norman, a labourer in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and residing at 121, Mersey-street, Warrington, died very suddenly at St. Helens on Thursday morning. It appears that he left Warrington early that morning, and a man named Roberts, another labourer, accompanied him from Earlestown. .They went to work near the bridge over the canal in Raven-street, and as the deceased was stopped working while a boat passed the bridge he suddenly fell to the ground. On his fellow- workers reaching him it was found that the poor fellow had instantaneously expired. Dr. Skipton (assistant to Dr. Gaskell), soon afterwards attended, but his services were too late to save the man's life. It instated that the deceased had suffered from heart disease for some time, and that is sup- posed to have been the cause of death. WORKMEN'S CLI7B ENTERTAINMENT.—The Faraworth Amateur Negro Troupe gave an entertarnment in the Work- men's Club, Warrington, on Monday evening, to a good audience. The Rev. R. Pilcher presided, alad said that he thought that every movement like the one in which he was then taking part, should have their most earnest support and co-operation. He was satisfied that one great lack of modern society was not that there was too much amusement in this world, but that there was too little, and especially so with the working classes. THE WIRE TRADE.—The Ironmonger says :—The strike now existing in Dm wire trade at Warrington is in many respects a lamentable occurrence. It is—as are all strikes— a libel on modern progress, besides involving a most regret- table waste of time and money. The men, we are afraid, are blind to what is going en around them, and appear to I entertain the opinion that, whatever successes may attend foreign competition with Warrington, they and litheir wages should go on exactly in the same manner as when England enjoyed a virtual monopoly of the wire trade. Either they do not believe that the German manufacturers are obtaining the bulk of the business in certain kinds of wire, or, if they credit the statements to that effect, they blindly insist upon having the whole loaf or no bread at all. The manufac- turers, being better informed, and having practical experience of the realities of Continental competi- tion, have arrived at the conclusion that the rate of wages must be reduced, but, they are of opinion that the actual earnings of the men may still remain at a respectable level provided the new arrangements be accepted. At Birmingham, Halifax, and Manchester, we are told by Mr. Claude J. Morris, the wiredrawers have agreed to the reduction, and for three weeks past have earned frem 303. to 603, per week, with an average of 403. to 453. for a week's work under ordinary conditions. This being so, the stub- born refusal of the Warrington men appears inexplicable, not to say suicidal The employers point out that they are compelled to make the reduction, which they regard as being the only means of preserving the wire trade in this country. They show that we are making less wire than formerly, whilst other countries have been making more and securing later proportions of the export trade. These are facts well within the knowledge of all who are acquainted with recent business developments. Neither the employers nor the men can withstand the course of events ;:but if the masters believe that they may retain or regain their trade by a moderate readjustment of wages like the present, it is the duty of the men to accept the inevitable,and to do their best under the circumstances. Self-interest, if no other motive, should lead them to this conclusion, which we hope to hear they have arrived at without further delay. MR. THOMAS MOULDING, FORMERLY OF WARRINGTON. —We have no doubt there will be a considerable number of our elderly—and a still larger number of our middle-aged— subscribers who will remember with strong feelings of per- • sonal regard Mr. T. Moulding, overlooker of the factory of the late Messrs. J. and R. Allen when it was burned down, and who soon after, early. in 1851, with his wife and family, • went to Illinois, United States of America. We copy the ; following account of tke celebration of the 59th anniversary • of their wedding-day at their home in Blackberry (Ill.) • from the Elgiri (I 11. Courier, believing it will be read with L interest by all who remember the sterling worth of the aged , .couple, borne witness to when they left England by the presentation of a watch with a suitable inscription, pur- chased by a subscription which included a large number of the leading men in Warrington, of all classes, parties, and I :creeds :—"A Notable Event.—Mr, and Mrs. Thomas , Moulding, early settlers of Campton, were married March , 16, E. 325, and therefore had been married 59 years last • Sunday. In commemoration of thatday, the worthy couple , were agreeably surprised by having a whole houseful of , their, children meeting with them to celebrate the day. They have had a large family of 15 children, anl 47 grand children. Seven children, 34 grandchildren, and one great grand child are still living. In their life, and that of their children, they have proved that we can live without intoxi- cating drink, as neither of them have tasted of it for 52 years. Neither have they used tobacco in any form. Their eldest son, new in his 59th year, does not know the taste of intoxicating drinks. He is one of the largest brick manu- facturers in Chicago, and is widely known throughout the United States as an active temperance worker. Thomas Moulding, jun and wife, and William R. and wife, of Chicago; Dr. F. C and wife, of Watertown (Wis.); Chas. and wife, of Campton ; John and son, of Milwaukee (Wis.); Mr. and Mrs. J. E. White, F. J. Bennett, and H. Bennett, of Blackberry, and 14 grand children were pre- sent, and had an exceedingly pleasant visit with ' the old folks at home.' A beautiful sofa and painting were presented to the aged couple by their chii'dren, while with thanks the father and mother united in a Prayer that all might be spared to meet one year hence, n'ben time shall have marked their 60th anniversary. For three score years, with lack of one, We've:trode the way together, And hand in hand, as man and wife, We've battled through turmoil and strife In storm and sunny weather. We've seen the friendirof earlier years Go down the Murky river; The ones we loved in youthful time, And those who met us in our prime. Have passed away for ever. We've seen our children leave our door, Their faces turning eon-ward; We've prayed Oh, Father, keep from ha,m, The heart that with our own throbe warm, Whose weary feet press onward.' And now, good wife, our harvest filled, We're waiting but the Gleaner ; At His commanel we',e gathered in, And cleansed pure from every sin, We'll sing with our Redeemer." 1

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.

Mr. John Bright my now be considered to have corn- pletely recovered from his recent illness, and no further medical reports will be issued. The right hon. gentleman will probably leave London to-day for the seaside. DEATH OF MR. CHARLES READE.—Mr. Charles Reads, the novelist, died at his residence, at Shepherd's Bush, at half-past one yesterday afternoon. He was unconscious to the last, and passed away without a struggle. THE HEALTH OF THE PREMIER.—Mr. Gladstone, who continues to improve, attended divine service at Christ Church, Epsom Common, yesterday. He will remain at the Durdans longer than was originally arranged, and will probably not leave until the middle of next week at tLe earliest.

THE WAR BETWEEN CHILI AND PERU : BRITISH CLAIM, —List night's Gazette publishes tha text of the convention signed at the beginning of last year for the settlement by means of the United International Commission of the claims of British subjects arising out of the acts and opera- tions of Chilian forces during the war with Peru and Bolivia. The Foreign Office notify that particulars of claims must be sent to Mr. James Drummond Hay, British Consul at Valptraiso, and that further notice will be given lof the date of the first meeting of the Commission.
THE ARREST OF AN ALLEGED MURDER CONSPIRATOR.

The man Fitzgerald, the Fenian, arrested on Thursday in London, arrived in Dublin yesterday morning in the custody of Inspector Littlechild, of Scotland Yard. Fitz- gerald is not charged with treason-felony, but with con- spiracy to murder certain landlords and Government officials at Tubbercurry, County Sligo, and at Cork. He is a commercial traveller and is said to have been an asso- ciate of P. J. Sheridan who fled to America some time ago, and against whom true bills were returned by the Dublin Grand Jury in connection with the Phenix Park murders. Fitzgerald has been handed over to the Royal Irish Con- stabulary and will be conveyed to Tubbercurry. THE RKCENT DEFEAT OF OSMAN DIGNA. The Gazette of last night publishes Commander Rolfe' despatch describing the part taken by the Naval Brigade in the battle of Tainasi. Commander Rolfe commends the se vices rendered by Lieutenant Graham, his second in command, by Rev. C. J. Todd, who acted as chaplain, and by Dr. Gunlette. He also specially recommends for some mark of approval the conduct of Midshipmen Edward Bis- coe and Edward Hewett, of the Euryalus, who, in a critical moment, when three lieutenants had been killed, took com- mand of the sub-division and acted with great coolness and gallantry. Admiral Hewett, in endorsing these recommen- dations, strongly recommends Coriamander Rolfe, and also mentions Captain Baldwin, of the Marines, as having done good service as adjutant of the Marine Battalion.
DOUBLE COLLISION IN THE MERSEY.-EXCITING
SCENE.

An almost marvellous rescue was effected on Thursday night in the Mersey. About 11 o'clock at night an unknown steamer, supposed to be Spanish, was proceeding up the river on a strong flood tide, when it came into collision with the Wallasey Ferry steamer Water Lily, lying at anchor off Egremont, the result being that the moorings of the Che- shire vessel were burst and other damage done. The un- known craft afterwards ran into the Belfast steamer Electric, outward-bound with 200 passengers and the usual crew. A scene of great confusien ensued on board the Irish vessel.

The captain, officers, and crew behaved splendidly, and so did the majority of the passengers, even though the peril seemed greater that it really was. The cries of those on board the Electric aroused the atten- tion of the crew of the Water Lily, who hastened to their rescue, even though their own vessel was disabled. They were, however, helped and superseded in their work by the steamtug Rock Right, which stayed by the Electric until she was safely beached between Egremont and Seacombe. There were, unhappily, many strong men of the class of roughs who ruthlessly pushed the women and children aside in order that they might save themselves. Although the damage to the vessels was comparatively small,.and although there was no loss of life; many of the passengers for Belfast lost their trunks, bags, and boxes with their contents The passengers were all brought safely to the Prince's Landing.stage shortly after midnight.

div.head: THEFT OF LEATHER.
div.p: THEFT OF LEATHER.

On Thursday, at the Warrington Police Court, before Captain Litton (in the chair), and Alderman 'Webster, Martin Macnsahon, assistant storekeeper, was charged with stealing, on the sth of February and at various other times within the last six months, from the stores at Dallam Forge, 301bs. of leather, valued at 35e, the property of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles.—P.C. Taylor (39), said that at about eleven o'clock on Monday morning last he received infor- mation that the prisoner had been suspected of having leather in his possession, and witness, in consequence, went to his house in company with Inspector Bpinks. They searched the house, and upstairs, underneath the stairs, and in a drawer, they found the whole of the leather produced. Witness then went to Dallam Forge and apprehended the prisoner, and asked him to account for the leather that had been found at his house. Prisoner replied "Jim Royston gave me a couple of pieces to tap my shoes with." Witness asked him to account for the remainder of the leather, and he replied "The other I took from the stores." He also said that a man at the stores gave him a couple of old barrels, and he put the leather at the bottom ef them and spovered it over with chintz. That was the way in which he got the leather from the stores. Witness found fifteen packages of leather, weighing 301b5., and valued at 355, at the prisoner's house. Prisoner had been employed at the forge for 16 or 17 years.—Mr. Moore, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the prisoner, and in defence, said that the case was one of a very painful nature. The prisoner was nearly 50 years of age, and .up to the present time he had borne an irreproachable character. He had been an industrfous man, and during the 16 years that he had been employed at the forge he had given satisfaction, and had always been con- sidered trustworthy. He admitted having committed the theft, and the only question now was as to the punishment to be inflicted upon him. The magistrates had the power to inflict a fine instead of sending the prisoner to prison, and he thought that the case was one in which they would be amply justified in exercising that power.—The Chairman said that the Bench were of opinion that the case was too serious to be met with a fine, and that only punishment would prevent such offences being repeated. The prisoner would be sentenced to two months' hard labour.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday after- noon at the offices in Sankey-street, ander the presidency of Mr. R. Houghton, the other members present being Messrs. Hartley (vice-chairman), James Fairclongli, Edward Marsh, James Turner, Woolfe, George Lawton, William Royston, James Houghton, John Grounds, H. B. White (clerk), Longland (assistant clerk), and Thompson • (nresor).

. LinaPOOL-RoaD, SaIfICEY.—A. letter was read from Mr. John Hatton, Sankey Lodge, stating that he had sustained considerable damage by cattle trespassing on his land from the want of a proper fence. Cattle being driven along the road ceuld walk into the field, and there were so many drivers that something must b 3 done to prevent further darn- age.—The Surveyor said that originally the brook under- mined the road, and to prevent the road from slipping away, and save the expense of putting up a new wall, pipes were laid in the brook, which was filled bip with earth.—The Clerk observed that there was no liability on the part of the Board to put up a fence.—The Surveyor: The brook be- longed to Mr. Hatton, but we took possession of it after the pipes were put in —The Clerk said that did not throw the liability on the Board of putting up a fence.—The Snr- vevor. suggested an improvement to cost about £8 which would widen the road at that point by three or four feet, and be was directed to report further on the matter at the peat meeting._

THE Silt; CAwAL—The Clerk said the promoters of the Ship Canal Bill had agreed to give the clause asked for at the last meeting. THE FINANCES. The Clerk read a statement of the receipts and expenditure for the past year. It slated that the number of highway parishes was 14, the rateable value, £112,843; inalp roads, 13 miles 6 furlongs; district roads, 101 miles 2 fullongs, The receipts, which consisted of con- tributions from parishes, from county authority, grant in respect of main roads, compensation for damage caused by excessive traffic and other receipts, amounted to £5,350 is 7d. The expenditure had been £5,017 5s 61 The follow- ing are the balances which stand to the credit of the several townships :—Bartonwood, £65 5s 10d; Cuerdlev, £4l 14s 10d; Culcheth, £lO6 Is 3d; Great Sankey, £27 9s 5d ; Houghton, Middleton, and Arbury, £26 19s 3d; Kenyon, £64 is 6cl; Lowton, £63 us 5l; Poulton with Fearnhead, £33 3s 6d ; Rixton with Glazebrook, £l3l 12s Pd; South- worth with Croft, £76 19s 7d; Winwick, £lO5 55 lid; Weston with Martinscroft, £5l us 7d; Warrington (extra municipal), £7 38 4d; total, £BOl Os 2d. THH OYERSEEIIS AND RATE COLLECTION.—Mr. Hartley said it had been stated at the Board of Guardians that the overseers might not collect the highway rates unless speci- ally paid for it. They had always collected them in his time, but the question had nor been raised before.—The Clerk: They are bound to collect it, and the remuneration must be considered as part of the overseers' salary.—The Chairman said that in former times the parties who col- lected the rates looked after the roads. That had been abandoned, and the new regulations of the Poor Law had come into force. The surveyor now did not collect the rates, which were collected along with the poor rates.—A Mem- ber: And the overseers have had their salaries raised ac- cordingly. NOTICE or MOTION.—Mr. Royston gave notice that at the next meeting he should move that the Clerk be instructed te apply to the magistrates for licences to the waywardeas to cart and supply materials for the Surveyor. VOTES or Twaxxs.—On the motion ot Mr. Royston, seconded by Mr. Woolf, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman; and a similar compliment was paid to the Vice-chairman, on the motion of Mr. Houghton.
